Iran will prevail over economic terrorism, Khatibzadeh says
TEHRAN — Iran will overcome 'economic terrorism' through national resilience and coordinated government action, Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh said, accusing Western countries of pursuing a failed strategy of pressure and sanctions against the Islamic Republic.
Khatibzadeh, who heads the Foreign Ministry’s Center for Political and International Studies, made the remarks to reporters on the sidelines of a ceremony marking the International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism.
He said Iran is engaged in a “historic, national, patriotic, revolutionary and Islamic struggle,” adding that victory would ultimately belong to those who demonstrate perseverance.
“Iranian governments and the entire system have a duty to safeguard national interests and security,” Khatibzadeh said, stressing that President Masoud Pezeshkian’s administration would mobilize all available capacities, in cooperation with the heads of the three branches of government, to neutralize the effects of sanctions.
He was referring to the continuation of the United States’ maximum-pressure policy and economic sanctions against Iran, which Tehran has long described as a form of economic warfare.
Khatibzadeh said the latest pressure campaign was rooted in the failure of Iran’s adversaries during an earlier stage of the conflict. He accused Western governments of repeatedly attempting to weaken Iran by exerting economic pressure and promoting 'flawed narratives' in international media.
“They explicitly say they impose sanctions to make the Iranian people desperate and exhaust their resilience,” he said.
Khatibzadeh also argued that the current pressure campaign was not fundamentally different from policies pursued by previous U.S. administrations. Referring to former President Barack Obama’s sanctions policy, he said earlier attempts to bring Iran to its knees through so-called 'crippling sanctions' had failed. He predicted that those pursuing similar policies today would eventually 'be consigned to the dustbin of history.'
He further described Iran’s adversaries as a “terror front,” accusing them of employing different forms of 'terrorism against the country.'
The official cited the Shajareh Tayyebeh school massacre in Minab as one manifestation of terrorism and said Iran was now also confronting what he called economic terrorism, whose victims, he argued, were ordinary Iranians.
Khatibzadeh said the Foreign Ministry regarded documenting and pursuing such cases as part of its institutional responsibility. “We cannot and must not overlook the blood of each and every child of this nation,” he said.
According to Khatibzadeh, hundreds of international documents concerning 'new acts of terrorism' have been prepared by the Foreign Ministry over the past year and several months and submitted to international organizations.
He also accused the United States, Israel and some of their allies of seeking to prevent such cases from reaching international bodies. 'Tehran would continue efforts to pursue accountability through diplomatic channels,' added the diplomat.
'Terrorism has no good or bad side,' Khatibzadeh said, arguing that international relations should not be governed by 'the logic of force.'
He pledged that Iran’s diplomatic apparatus would continue pursuing those responsible for 'acts of terrorism and would not allow alleged perpetrators to remain without accountability.'
Khatibzadeh’s remarks came as Tehran continues to frame economic sanctions and maximum-pressure policies as part of a broader confrontation with Iran, while emphasizing domestic resilience, coordination among state institutions and diplomatic efforts to challenge the measures internationally.
Despite the pressure, he said, Iran had prevailed in previous confrontations and would do so again.
“If Western countries follow the same wrong path a thousand times, they will fail again,” Khatibzadeh said.

HONOLULU (AP) — Tropical Storm Moke advanced toward Hawaii on Saturday, likely bringing more heavy rainfall and strong gusts to the Big Island, where residents are still dealing with the aftermath of heavy flooding and damaging winds from Hurricane Lala.
A roadway is washed out by mud on Monday, Aug. 17, 2026, in Naalehu, Hawaii, following heavy rains from Hurricane Lala. (Aina Akamu via AP)
Moke, which formed Friday in the Pacific Ocean, was located about 425 miles (680 kilometers) southeast of Hilo and moving west-northwest at 12 mph (19 kph). Maximum sustained winds were around 50 mph (85 kph), the National Hurricane Center said.
As with Hurricane Lala, the Big Island was expected to bear the brunt of Moke’s rain and heavy winds as it passes south of a direct hit late Saturday into early Sunday.
Moke was then forecast to continue its westward path near the islands through early Tuesday, said Casey Oswant, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Honolulu.
“There will still be impacts, especially to the windward and southeast sides of the Big Island, but it will probably be a little bit more limited than what we saw with Lala,” Oswant said.
Lala downed trees, swept buildings off their foundations, damaged roads and bridges and left roads covered in mud and rocks. Two storm-related deaths were reported.
Ka’u Auto Repair Shop is seen surrounded by a field of debris after Hurricane Lala in Naalehu, Hawaii, Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via AP)
Weekend rainfall predictions for the southeast and windward sides of the Big Island were 5 to 10 inches (13 to 25 centimeters), with as much as 15 inches (38 centimeters) in isolated areas, Oswant said. Across the rest of the island chain, 1 to 2 inches (2 to 5 centimeters) of rain was expected, though parts of east Maui could see up to 4 inches (10 centimeters).
There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but people were urged to closely monitor the storm’s progress. The rainfall has the potential to cause dangerous rip currents, life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep areas and places where the ground remains saturated, the center said.

The northeast coast of the Big Island saw the heaviest total rainfall from Lala, at 43.54 inches (1.1 meters), according to the weather service. More than 8,000 customers on the Big Island remained without power, according to poweroutage.us.

A teenager wades through a pool of water in a washed-out section of a damaged road in Mountain View, Hawaii, Sunday, Aug. 16, 2026, after a severe weather system went through the area. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via AP)
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green and other state officials held a news conference ahead of Moke, urging people to prepare by restocking food, medicine and other essentials.
“There’s definitely tension in the air” at the thought of more rain in communities that floodwaters turned into rivers, said Tiffany Edwards Hunt, a teacher living in Keaau, on the east side of the Big Island.

Canada to retaliate for US tariffs, worsening ties after talks fail
- Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs on US imports starting Sept 8 to match President Trump's new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods.
- The tariffs affect multiple sectors, threatening jobs and businesses, with Canada planning support measures for impacted industries.
- Negotiations failed due to last-minute US demands seen as unfair, and no new talks are currently planned between the two countries.
AI generated
OTTAWA - Canada will impose tariffs on some US goods in retaliation for 50 per cent levies ordered by President Donald Trump on Canadian products, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Aug 22, after trade talks collapsed between the two neighbours.
The “dollar for dollar” tariffs on imports of US steel, electronics and other products, to take effect on Sept 8, mark a further worsening of relations between the longtime allies and major trading partners.
The two countries failed to reach a trade deal late on Aug 21, with each side blaming the other for derailing three days of intensive negotiations.
The breakdown complicates the future of a US-Mexico-Canada free trade pact.
Trump’s new tariffs hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, and cover some US$20 billion (S$25 billion) of Canadian exports to the US.
These duties do not exempt Canadian products under the USMCA, which has shielded most Canadian exports to the US in the last 18 months.
“Canada will match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses,” Carney said at a news conference.
“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said when asked a question about whether Canada was engaged in a trade war.
Carney is one of the few global leaders to retaliate against US tariffs and has pledged to forge new trade and military alliances, despite Canada’s dependence on the United States for nearly 70 per cent of its exports.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called the breakdown “a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States,” saying no new talks were planned with Canada.
“We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation,” Greer told Fox News. “They’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.”
The White House, the US commerce secretary’s office and the US trade representative’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comments.
Canada will impose tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, along with some products the US previously targeted in Canada, Carney said from Ottawa’s Parliament building.
The government will release details on its response in the coming days, he said.
“We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked,” Carney said.
Trump had expressed hope that a deal with Canada could happen on Aug 21.
But Carney said the US administration’s last-minute demands halted progress.
“In recent days, the US proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits to Canada, calling into question the reliability of any deal,” he said, adding these demands included curtailing Canada’s ability to forge new trade deals.
Larger vehicles, other sticking points
Carney said Canada would announce support measures next week for industries that are hit by the new US duties, adding these measures could last years.
The new US tariffs cover around 5 per cent of Canada’s exports to the US.
They could expose some vulnerable industries such as softwood lumber and wine to severe damage and lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.
“We will be mobilising our network of businesses in all regions and all sectors to brace for impact and make the best of a bad situation,” said Candace Laing, chief executive officer of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most vocal opponents of US tariffs, supported Carney’s decision to retaliate.
“I’m glad he didn’t sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector, and manufacturing sector,” Ford told reporters on Aug 22.
One of the main sticking points was the treatment of larger vehicles.
Three sources said Canada wanted favourable tariff terms proposed for light-duty vehicles to extend to medium- and heavy-duty trucks, something the US resisted.
Carney said the US position would have excluded Canadian-made models, including Ford’s F-350, F-450 and F-550 trucks and General Motors’ Silverado, making Canadian production less competitive.
There were also US proposals that affected Canadian culture, language and sovereignty, Carney said, without elaborating.
Carney was elected in 2025 on a promise to be a tough negotiator with Trump, and remains broadly popular.
Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to the US.
“Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses,” Pierre Poilievre, the leader of the official opposition Conservative Party, said in a statement. REUTERS

Qatar approves Iranian expert team’s access to captured pilots, Iran says
TEHRAN — Qatar has agreed to allow an Iranian expert team to meet with Iranian pilots being held in the Arab country, a military official said, as Tehran continues efforts to determine their condition and secure their return.
Brigadier General Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Missing in Action Search Committee of Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff, said on Saturday that his efforts concerning Iranian prisoners in Qatar and Kuwait were continuing.
He called on the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to send an air ambulance to Qatar as soon as possible to repatriate the captured pilots, whom he said were seriously wounded and ill.
The general welcomed the Qatari government’s decision to receive the Iranian expert team and called for the necessary cooperation to be provided.
He also expressed concern about the conditions in which the prisoners were being held, saying that “the place where the prisoners are being kept on water is not suitable.” He urged the Qatari government to transfer them to land and to a well-equipped hospital as soon as possible to protect their health.
Regarding other Iranian prisoners in Kuwait, Baqerzadeh referred to the Kuwaiti government’s initial agreement to allow the Iranian ambassador to meet with the prisoners held there, saying, “This action has created a glimmer of hope for the swift release of these dear compatriots.”
He called on Kuwait to respect the rights of the four Iranian prisoners in accordance with the four Geneva Conventions and to facilitate initial contact between them and their families.
The Iranian military commander also urged the ICRC to facilitate video calls between the Iranian prisoners and their families, pointing to an initiative through which the organization has for years arranged video communications between prisoners at Guantanamo and their relatives to reassure their families.
Baqerzadeh said the ICRC was therefore expected to take similar action for the Iranian prisoners while urgently pursuing their release. He called on the ICRC office serving Arab countries in the region to take the lead in this effort and undertake the necessary measures.
Iran recently made public, for the first time, its assessment that three pilots who went missing after a March 2 operation against the US-operated Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar were captured alive by Qatari forces.
Brigadier General Baqerzadeh raised the issue in a letter to ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric Egger on August 15, expressing grave concern over their fate and urging the organization to investigate their condition and facilitate their release.
According to Baqerzadeh, two Iranian Air Force Su-24s carried out the mission but were hit by enemy air defenses while returning, forcing their crews to eject. One of the four pilots, Brigadier General Majid Kazemi, was killed, with DNA testing later confirming his death, and his remains were returned to Iran. Baqerzadeh identified the three other pilots as Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian and Omran Behraveshian, saying they had been captured alive by Qatari forces.
The Iranian military official said Tehran had been unable, despite diplomatic follow-ups, to meet or interview the three pilots or establish contact between them and their families. He cited provisions of the Third Geneva Convention concerning prisoners of war and called on the ICRC to urgently establish contact with the pilots, report on their health and help secure their “swift release.”
The disclosure followed months of uncertainty over the pilots’ whereabouts. Iranian officials have repeatedly urged Qatar to clarify their status and act in accordance with international humanitarian law, while Qatari authorities have said they had no information about the missing airmen.
The March 2 operation came amid Iran’s broader military response to US and Israeli attacks that began on February 28.

26/11 case: Mumbai Police seek Interpol route to try Pakistani terrorist Hafiz Saeed, 5 others

Edited by: Rajeev Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 22, 2026, 22:35 IST
Comments

Text Size
Small

Large
Among the six includes Lashkar-e-Taiba founders Hafiz Saeed.
NEW DELHI: The Mumbai Police have asked the Union home ministry to use Interpol to serve court proclamation orders on six Pakistani nationals wanted in connection with the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks.The move is part of the process to bring the six accused to trial in absentia, meaning they could be tried by an Indian court even if they remain outside the country and cannot be arrested.The six include Lashkar-e-Taiba founders Hafiz Saeed and Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, along with Sajid Mir, Abu Alqama, Asim alias Abu Qahafa and Major Abdur Rehman Pasha.
Special public prosecutor Ujjwal Nikam told the special court hearing terror cases that the Mumbai Police had submitted an interim report on Friday regarding the proclamation orders issued against the accused in July."We have written to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) for taking necessary steps in serving the proclamation order, through Interpol, against the accused residing in Pakistan," Nikam told the special court hearing terror cases.The home ministry has acknowledged the request and is examining the next steps."On August 3, the MHA had acknowledged our request, and sought time for filing a status of the same," he said.
What trial in absentia means
The proceedings are based on Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. The provision allows a court to conduct a full criminal trial in the absence of an accused who has been declared a proclaimed offender, has deliberately remained away to avoid facing trial and is unlikely to be arrested in the immediate future.The court dealing with the 26/11 case issued proclamation orders in July against the six accused, all of whom are Pakistani nationals and remain absconding.The orders are an important step towards potentially beginning their trials without their physical presence in India.
Evidence links accused to 26/11
The alleged involvement of the six men in the Mumbai attacks has been referred to by Ajmal Kasab, the only attacker captured alive during the assault, as well as David Headley, who later became an approver in the case.
The 26/11 attacks began in Mumbai in November 2008 when 10 Pakistani terrorists launched a coordinated assault on several locations across the city.The attacks lasted for more than 60 hours and targeted iconic and strategically important places in Mumbai. A total of 166 people were killed, including six US nationals.Kasab was convicted of murder and waging war against India. He was sentenced to death and hanged at Yerwada Central Jail in Pune on November 21, 2012.The latest move by the Mumbai Police seeks to advance the legal proceedings against the six accused who have remained beyond the reach of Indian investigators since the attacks.

NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Saturday conducted searches at 10 locations across Srinagar, Kupwara, Anantnag, Pulwama and Budgam in J&K to unearth a cross-border conspiracy involving Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba handlers and a network of local over ground workers (OGWs) allegedly providing logistical and other forms of support to terrorists infiltrated from Pakistan.The relevant case was registered after a motorcycle-borne Kashmiri, Mohammad Naqeeb Bhat, was stopped at a naka in Zakoora, Srinagar, for checking on March 31, and one grenade and 15 rounds of ammunition were recovered from his possession. During the investigation, Pakistani terrorists allegedly connected with the conspiracy were arrested and the identities and alleged roles of members of the local support network, ascertained.
Saturday’s searches across multiple locations were aimed at securing further documentary, digital and material evidence relating to the conspiracy and at ascertaining the roles of persons allegedly associated with the local support network.According to the NIA, the probe so far points to linkages between Pak-based handlers and local OGWs who were allegedly used for communication, logistical arrangements, movement and concealment of terrorists, provision of shelter, reconnaissance and other forms of facilitation.
The investigation is also examining the financial trail, communication channels, movement of the accused, and the source of arms and explosives, with a view to establishing the complete network and the extent of its activities.The searches conducted today form part of the continuing investigation into the larger conspiracy and the alleged facilitation mechanism supporting cross-border terrorism. Further evidence relevant to the investigation has been secured and is being examined and corroborated with other material collected in the case.
NIA on Saturday said it shall continue to identify all persons involved in the conspiracy and ascertain their respective roles. Further legal action, including arrests or recoveries, may follow, subject to the outcome of the investigation.

US push to unify opposing Libya sides faces transparency calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:58:00 UTC
01:58:00 KST

Breadcrumb
US push to unify opposing Libya sides faces calls for transparency
Washington has stepped up engagement with Libya’s western-based government as well as the rival eastern forces led by Khalifa Haftar, seeking an arrangement that would bring together rival executives, military structures and economic institutions after years of political paralysis.
But the reported deal has drawn concern over its lack of transparency and over the prospect of Saddam Haftar, the son of the eastern commander and a powerful military figure in his own right, taking the country’s top post.
In a new briefing published this week, the International Crisis Group said the US initiative could help consolidate Libya’s fractured institutions but warned that its political component risked provoking destabilising opposition if it was not opened to wider domestic participation.
Claudia Gazzini, the Crisis Group’s senior Libya analyst and author of the report, told The New Arab that Washington should make the terms of any deal available for public scrutiny.
"We consider that a good effort, but what we’re saying is that the US needs to see this through," she said. "So, ensure that the terms of that deal are disclosed, for public scrutiny."
She said particular clarification was needed over provisions relating to the development budget, which remain unclear.
Gazzini added that public scrutiny of a proposed "Unified Agreement" could also help address corruption and illicit financial flows.
"Allow for scrutiny of the so-called Unified Agreement because on the basis of that we can also determine how and whether to stop all the other parallel flows of illicit financing," she said.
The US has publicly pointed to progress in its Libya engagement. At the UN Security Council this week, Washington said rival military leaders had agreed to establish a joint operations centre in Sirte, an air-training centre in Misrata and an integrated command structure.
US senior adviser Massad Boulos has also welcomed a UN-brokered agreement reached in Tunis on electoral legislation and the High National Elections Commission, while backing efforts to form a unified executive.
Yet the precise terms of the broader political arrangement have not been made public. Reporting around the initiative has suggested it could retain Abdulhamid Dbeibah as prime minister while handing Saddam Haftar the leadership of the Presidential Council, an arrangement intended to reflect the balance of power between Libya’s west and east.
Gazzini said the idea behind the proposal was a "realistic approach" in which the principal actors from both sides of the country hold positions of authority. But she warned that the prospective role of Saddam Haftar was causing concern and alarm.
"The risk is that, given the track record of Saddam Haftar – who is at the head of military grouping, who has been accused in the past of silencing opposition and possibly, also, involvement in the disappearance of activists – they fear that Saddam Haftar, if he were to be given the country’s top position, he could soon after sideline the Prime Minister," she said.
"The legal framework would allow for the President to call, for example, a state of emergency and rule with an iron fist."
The other immediate danger, she said, is that negotiations are being carried out by a narrow circle, without the political and local actors needed to make an eventual agreement stick.
"This process is happening behind closed doors and only involves those few affiliates to Dbeibeh on one side and Haftar on the other, and has not involved any institutions, any municipalities or civil society organisations," Gazzini said.
"When I say that there needs to be domestic buy-in, it means to ensure that also influential political groups or individuals with ties to powerful militias are also signing off on this deal because otherwise the risk is that they can mobilise and not accept this new set up."
Uptick in attacks deepen fears of wider instability
That risk is playing out against a worsening security backdrop.
In recent days, unclaimed drone attacks have hit fuel storage, refinery and electricity infrastructure in Zawiya, a strategic western city whose refinery and associated fuel networks are contested by rival armed groups. The attacks damaged a substation and contributed to major power cuts across western Libya, while no group has claimed responsibility.
On Saturday, Khalifa Haftar’s General Command said its forces had clashed with armed groups near the al-Sarah military base in Libya’s far south-east, claiming arrests and the seizure of armed vehicles.
The Southern Liberation Operations Room, which is opposed to Haftar, denied the account, calling it unfounded and saying its forces remained deployed in their positions.
Gazzini said influential groups in western Libya had signalled that they would not accept the proposed arrangement, raising the possibility of armed resistance in Tripoli and other key western cities.
"Influential personalities in western Libya who oppose the deal have only stated that significant groups in the west will not accept the deal and will mobilise," she said. "The risk is of mobilisation, of some armed groups in Tripoli, possibly from Misrata and maybe Zawiya."
"Of course, there is the possibility that the Haftar side can by that time buy loyalty," Gazzini added. "But it’s very much fluid and in the making."

Early Motown songwriter Janie Bradford Hobbs dies in Los Angeles after illness at age 87
Early Motown songwriter Janie Bradford Hobbs, who helped pen hits including “Money (That’s What I Want)” and “Too Busy Thinking About My Baby,” has died following an extended illness at a Los Angeles hospital, her family said Saturday. She was 87.
Bradford Hobbs was born in Charleston, Missouri, and later moved to Detroit.
She was introduced in the late 1950s to Motown founder Berry Gordy by neighbor and singer Jackie Wilson. She joined Motown as a receptionist in 1958 and like many of the company’s employees took part in the creative process that helped make Motown a music industry powerhouse.
She and Gordy co-wrote “Money (That’s What I Want).” The song was recorded in 1959 by Barrett Strong and became an early hit. It was covered by The Beatles and also became one of that group’s hits.
“Too Busy Thinking About My Baby” first was recorded by The Temptations and later became a hit for Marvin Gaye. Bradford Hobbs also wrote songs for Stevie Wonder, The Supremes, Martha & The Vandellas and others.
“Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown, and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family,” Gordy said in a statement.
“Janie was one of a special group I have always thought of as the original Motown family — the unsung heroes who believed in the dream before anyone knew what Motown would become,” Gordy continued. “She was one of the people who helped make Motown what it became.”
Bradford Hobbs later became head of Writer Relations for Jobete, Motown’s publishing company. After leaving Motown, she founded the annual Heroes and Legends Awards. The event spanned about 30 years, honoring music icons and awarding scholarships, according to her family.
She is survived by her husband, Wardean Hobbs; daughter, Nicole Hobbs; son, Lance Finney; and two grandsons. Funeral services have not been completed.

Trump’s trade war with Canada: A timeline of how we got here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:53:02 UTC
01:53:02 KST

Trump’s trade war with Canada: A timeline of how we got here
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump’s barrage of tariffs has quickly strained the United States’ longstanding relationship with Canada over the last year.
Since taking office in January, Trump has threatened Canada’s economy and sovereignty with steep import taxes on its goods. He’s even claimed that America’s neighbor to the north could be “the 51st state.” That rhetoric — paired with volleys of on-again, off-again new tariffs — has outraged Canadians and created wider uncertainty for businesses and consumers across both countries.
Canada has responded with retaliatory trade measures. And just this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney outlined plans to double its non-U.S. exports in the next decade. Trump also promised to end “all trade negotiations” with Canada over a television ad from the Ontario government opposing his levies — although the province has since said it will pause that campaign.
Here’s a timeline of how we got here.
January
On his first day in office, Trump says he expects to put 25% tariffs on imports from Canada starting on Feb. 1.
February
Trump signs an executive order to impose 25% tariffs on imports from Canada starting Feb. 4 — invoking this power by declaring a national emergency, ostensibly over undocumented immigration and drug trafficking.
Then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau promises to respond by matching 25% tariffs on up to $155 billion in U.S. imports. But days later, Trump agrees to a 30-day pause, cooling tensions at least temporarily.
March
Trump’s 25% tariffs on imports from Canada go into effect on March 4, though he limits the levy on Canadian energy to 10%. In response, Trudeau announces counter tariffs on more than $100 billion of American goods over the course of 21 days.
But Trump soon grants a one-month exemption on these tariffs for U.S. automakers — and later postpones his 25% tariffs on goods that comply with the US-Mexico Canada Agreement, a trade pact from his first term. The action thaws relations with Canada somewhat, which suspends a second wave of its retaliatory tariffs, although uncertainty remains.
Worldwide, Trump’s new steel and aluminum tariffs — which now tax imports of both metals at 25% — still go into effect March 12. Canada then imposes more retaliatory tariffs worth $29.8 billion Canadian dollars ($20.7 billion) on U.S. imports, beginning March 13.
April
Trump announces his long-promised “reciprocal” tariffs on nearly all of America’s trading partners April 2, but doesn’t unveil additional levies on Canada.
The White House says USMCA-compliant imports can continue to enter the U.S. duty-free — and once Trump’s demands on immigration and drug trafficking are satisfied, the tariff on the rest of their imports may drop from 25% to 12%.
Still, as part of further levies impacting trading partners worldwide, Trump’s sweeping 25% tariffs on auto imports begin April 3, starting with taxes on fully-imported cars. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matches the 25% levies with a tariff on non-USMCA compliant vehicles imported from the U.S. starting April 9.
Trump later signs an executive order to relax some of his auto tariffs, but relief is limited.
May
On May 28, the U.S. Court of International Trade blocks Trump from imposing the bulk of his most sweeping tariffs — ruling that the president overstepped his authority when he invoked an emergency powers law to slap import taxes on almost every country in the world, including levies imposed on Canada. But just a day later, a federal appeals court temporarily halts the order.
June
Worldwide, Trump’s new 50% tariffs of nearly all foreign steel and aluminum take effect June 4. Carney later threatens to impose new tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum starting in July, pending progress of trade talks. The Canadian Prime Minister says that Trump’s trade war is running the risk of a global recession.
Trump says he’s suspended trade talks with Canada over its plans to continue with a tax on technology firms. But days later, Carney says Canada will rescind implementing that tax, called the Digital Serves Tax, and says that talks will resume.
July
Trump sends a letter to Canada warning that the U.S. will heighten its tariffs against the country to 35% starting Aug. 1, up from 25% imposed in March — although some goods are currently protected under the USCMA pact. At the time, Carney maintains that Canada will continue to work towards a deal by the new deadline.
August
Trump’s heightened 35% tariff rate on a range of Canadian goods take effect on Aug. 1. Globally, the U.S.'s new 50% levy on imported copper also kicks in.
Later in the month, Carney says that Canada will drop many of its retaliatory tariffs to match U.S. exemptions for goods covered under the USMCA pact. Critics decry the move as capitulation to Trump, but the prime minister maintains Canada is in a good position and that such exemptions would jump-start further trade talks.
Low-value imports coming into the U.S. lose their duty-free status with the end of the “de minimis” rule on Aug. 29. The withdrawal applies to all countries, including Canada.
Meanwhile, a federal appeals court rules that Trump illegally used emergency powers to impose sweeping tariffs worldwide — but leaves the import taxes in place for now. The Trump administration later appeals to the Supreme Court.
October
For trading partners worldwide, Trump’s new tariffs on kitchen cabinets, bathroom vanities and upholstered wooden furniture go into effect on Oct. 14, starting with a 25% levy on many of these imports — ahead of steeper rates scheduled for Jan. 1.
On Oct. 22, Carney outlines plans for Canada to double its non-U.S. exports in the next decade. He points to Trump’s tariffs — noting that affected jobs across Canada are “under threat” and that the new levies are causing a chill in investment.
A day later, Trump says he’s ending “all trade negotiations” with Canada — in an abrupt move over a television ad opposing U.S. tariffs, which Trump claims misstated the facts and was aimed at influencing court decisions. The ad was paid for by the Ontario provincial government, not the Canadian federal government. Ontario Premier Doug Ford later says he’s pulling the TV ad so trade talks may resume.

Iraqi speaker confronts Iran's Ghalibaf over militia support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:48:34 UTC
01:48:34 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraqi speaker confronts Iran's Ghalibaf over support for armed factions
Iraq's parliament speaker reportedly confronted his Iranian counterpart this week over Tehran's support for armed factions, asking whether Iran would accept Baghdad establishing and funding militias on Iranian soil.
Haibat al-Halbousi posed the question to Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf during talks in Baghdad, according to Alhurra, citing people who attended the meeting.
Ghalibaf reportedly replied that Iran would "certainly not" accept such a situation and said Tehran supported the decisions of the Iraqi state.
"Then you must stop anything that appears to support what runs contrary to the direction of the Iraqi state," Halbousi responded, according to the report.
The exchange came amid attempts by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's government to bring the weapons of powerful Iran-aligned militias under state control.
People present at the meeting told Alhurra that Halbousi pressed Ghalibaf to support Baghdad's efforts to establish a state monopoly over weapons and urged Tehran not to encourage factions resisting disarmament.
The confrontation is particularly significant because Ghalibaf reportedly used the same visit to push an alternative proposal allowing armed factions to retain effective access to their weapons.
Three sources told Alhurra that Ghalibaf proposed either allowing the factions to keep their arsenals or depositing them with the Popular Mobilisation Forces rather than handing them directly to the Iraqi government.
A member of the ruling Coordination Framework coalition of pro-Iran parties said Ghalibaf supported the principle that weapons should ultimately be restricted to the state, but argued that this should happen "not now".
Under the proposal, the weapons would remain available in the event of an "emergency", according to the source.
The Popular Mobilisation Forces are formally part of Iraq's state security structure but include several powerful factions closely aligned with Iran.
Ghalibaf reportedly argued that Iraq lacks sufficient air defences to prevent US and Israeli aircraft using its airspace, including for operations against Iran, and linked this vulnerability to the need for the factions to retain their weapons.
His intervention followed a visit to Baghdad earlier this month by Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Quds Force.
According to separate Alhurra reporting, Qaani urged Iraqi factions not to surrender their weapons and sought to convince Baghdad not to weaken the groups.
The dispute comes as the Iraqi government appears to be softening its previous deadline for disarmament.
Government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said on Friday that 30 September was the date set for the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq and "not the final deadline for factions to surrender their weapons".
That contrasts with the government's position in June, when Aboudi said armed groups had been informed that 30 September marked "the end of this issue" and warned that weapons outside the state framework after that date would face legal action.
The State Administration Coalition, which includes Iraq's main Shia, Sunni and Kurdish political forces, had also described 30 September as the deadline for factions to surrender their weapons.
Kataib Hezbollah, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada and Harakat al-Nujaba continue to reject calls to relinquish their weapons, while Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Imam Ali have announced steps towards bringing their weapons under state control.
There is no evidence that Ghalibaf's intervention directly caused Baghdad's subsequent shift in language over the deadline.
However, the reported exchanges highlight disagreement between Iraqi authorities and Tehran over how far Baghdad should go in dismantling the autonomous military power of Iran-aligned factions.
The Halbousi-Ghalibaf meeting was also reportedly strained by disagreements over Iran's restrictions on Iraqi oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz and what Halbousi described as interference by Iran's ambassador in Iraqi corruption cases.
The official Iraqi statement following the meeting made no reference to the dispute over armed factions.

Erdogan, Netanyahu trade jabs after Turkey seeks arrest warrant for Israel PM

South Korea sending first container ship through Arctic route
The PanStar Acro, bound for Europe via the Arctic, is testing whether a route opened by melting sea ice can be commercially viable.
A South Korean container ship is sailing to Europe via the Arctic, in the nation’s first commercial voyage on the route to test its viability as the war in the Middle East rattles global shipping.
The PanStar Acro set sail from Busan New Port on Saturday. “We would like to inform you that the vessel for the Arctic route trial voyage departed” at 9:30pm (12:30 GMT), Seoul’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said in a statement to the AFP news agency.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4South Korea footballers urge safety after extreme heat statistics
- list 2 of 4Putin warns of tit-for-tat seizures of European vessels
- list 3 of 4Activists’ bid to sue Russia over climate change gets off to shaky start
- list 4 of 4Can China’s new Arctic sea route to Europe replace Middle East chokepoints?
The PanStar Acro will sail north, the Reuters news agency reported, hugging eastern Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, then cross the Bering Sea, and take the Northern Sea Route, stopping in Felixstowe in the UK, Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and Poland’s Gdansk before returning.
The 2,758 TEU (twenty-foot equivalent unit) container ship operated by South Korea’s PanStar has secured 837 TEU of cargo, including car parts, chemical products and about 100 empty containers on the government-backed voyage.
The journey is expected to take 40 to 45 days, according to the Oceans Ministry.
President Lee Jae Myung has made Arctic shipping a priority for South Korea, with the hope of turning the southeastern port of Busan into a global maritime hub and position the Arctic as a regular trade route by 2030.
But this new route has been criticised for several different reasons. Environmental groups have warned the route could accelerate polar ice melt, meaning the increase in shipping could worsen global warming.
The project also risks increasing friction with Western allies hoping to keep Russia isolated in its war with Ukraine. Seoul has consulted with Moscow about the journey, Reuters reported, including whether the ship needed help to tackle any problems, such as getting stuck in ice.
Last year, 103 transits through the route were made by 88 vessels, up from 97 in 2024 and 43 in 2022, chiefly from nations such as Russia and China, according to Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics.
But with the Iran war affecting global shipping, governments and shipping firms are scrambling to seek different routes, with the Arctic route increasingly viewed as a viable alternative due to technological advances and environmental degradation.
South Korea’s Vice Oceans Minister Nam Jae-hon said the Arctic route was “bound to become an alternative” to Middle Eastern shipping lanes.
The usual maritime route between Asia and Europe runs through the Suez Canal, but travelling through the Arctic can cut the journey by approximately 7,000 kilometres (4,300 miles) and about 10 days, according to the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.
However, major carriers including CMA CGM, MSC and Hapag-Lloyd have pledged to avoid Arctic shipping routes due to pressure from environmental groups. The Arctic sea route is believed to be accessible only during the time of year when the ice is melted enough to allow transits without icebreakers.
“The Northern Sea Route has become increasingly viable as the Arctic warms about four times faster than the global average, leading to a sharp decline in sea ice,” South Korean environmental group Paran Ocean Citizen Science Center said in a statement last year. “But making the route commercially viable would require further warming, putting the policy at odds with efforts to combat climate change.”

The Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) on Friday night said that it received an apology from Etihad Airways, after a Taiwanese passenger complained that an inflight announcement on a flight to Taipei referred to Taiwan as “Taiwan, China,” prompting the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to request an apology and correction.
A Taiwanese passenger last week posted on social media their experience of taking an Etihad Airways flight from Abu Dhabi to Taipei earlier this month.
They said that upon arrival at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, the inflight announcement said “Welcome to Taiwan” in English, but “Welcome to Taiwan, China,” in Chinese, and also warned that bringing meat products from abroad could result in a penalty from the “Chinese government.”
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
The passenger said that they immediately asked a flight attendant whether referring to Taiwan as “Taiwan, China” reflects the airline’s policy. The cabin manager said that the announcement was read from a script and that the passengers could raise the issue with the company.
In response to the post, the ministry on Friday issued a statement strongly protesting against the Etihad Airways’ inflight announcement in Chinese calling it unacceptable.
“The Republic of China, Taiwan, is an independent sovereign nation, and is not subordinate to the People’s Republic of China, which is an objective fact and the internationally recognized ‘status quo,’” the ministry said.
“Any improper practice that belittles Taiwan’s sovereignty will absolutely not be accepted by the Taiwanese government and the people of Taiwan,” it said.
The ministry said that it has asked its representative office in Dubai to coordinate with the CAA to lodge a complaint with Etihad Airways’ headquarters and the UAE’s representative in Taiwan, requesting that the airline make an apology and correct the announcement script.
The ministry said it will continue to follow the situation and defend national dignity and sovereignty.
The CAA on Friday said that it received a letter from Etihad Airways’ headquarters in which it apologized for causing a negative perception of the airline through the announcement.
It also said it will continue to improve content oversight and staff training to ensure that its services meet passenger expectations.
The letter said the company has already reviewed and corrected the terms used in its inflight announcement, and that it would also revise any phrasing that might be confusing or inconsistent with local usage, the CAA said.

Trump tariffs hit as Canada tries to curb US reliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:58 UTC
01:45:58 KST

US President Donald Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on certain Canadian goods, which took effect yesterday, delivered another blow to bilateral trade, renewing focus on Ottawa’s efforts to reduce dependence on its southern neighbor.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s strategy involves a search for new markets, a focus on domestic trade and the launch of major projects.
The two economies are heavily inter-connected, with about 70 percent of all Canadian exports heading to the US.
Photo: Reuters
Previous Trump levies on autos, steel, aluminum and lumber have hit Canada hard, forcing job losses and stunting growth.
Canada has even entered a technical recession this year after two consecutive quarters of economic contraction.
The latest tariffs came into force after days of negotiations failed to produce an agreement.
They impact about US$20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the US, targeting products ranging from hockey sticks to cement.
Carney said Canada would match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”
The exports affected by the US tariffs include products that were previously protected under the North American trade pact, the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).
At first glance, “that’s frightening,” Laval University international economic law professor Richard Ouellet said.
“Until now, the USMCA acted as kind of a shield. The Americans are opening a breach,” he said.
Trump declined to renew the USMCA on July 1, making it subject to annual reviews.
While Trump ditching USMCA exemptions could forecast more extreme measures to come, Canada’s largest bank, RBC, predicted that the first package of 50 percent tariffs would not “significantly change broader Canadian growth.”
“That’s because the new tariffs, while significant, will still impact a small segment of total trade,” RBC said, adding that about 80 percent of Canadian goods would still enter the US tariff-free.
Since taking office in March last year, Carney has focused on diversifying economic partnerships to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US market.
“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said in a statement following the breakdown of negotiations with Washington. “We will not allow any nation to determine our future.”
Carney has headed to China, India and Saudi Arabia, and made several stops in Europe seeking deals to expand Ottawa’s economic relationships overseas.
In January, he signed a preliminary agreement with China, providing for the import of electric vehicles to Canada.
Relations with Europe have also been bolstered. Canada last month selected the German firm TKMS to build its new fleet of submarines.
Canada’s central bank last month said the economy was “showing signs of improving,” adding that some businesses were adjusting to US protectionism, including by finding new customers abroad.
A report from the Canadian minister of international trade said that last year, the value of exports to non-US markets jumped by 11 percent, hitting 33 percent at one point — the highest level in more than four decades.

Kaohsiung family falls ill from eating wild mushrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

The Kaohsiung Department of Health yesterday urged people not to eat wild mushrooms, as it reported that a family had sought hospital treatment after reportedly eating unidentified mushrooms picked in a grassland.
High temperatures and rainfall in the south made it easier for poisonous mushrooms to grow in grasslands, the department said.
A hospital on Friday reported that a family of three had sought emergency treatment for symptoms including vomiting, diarrhea and headaches after reportedly eating wild white mushrooms.
Photo courtesy of a member of the public
The family on Thursday evening cooked unidentified mushrooms that a friend had picked in a grassland and given to them. Later that night, they began experiencing symptoms of food poisoning and sought treatment. One family member was hospitalized due to severe symptoms, the department said.
The department said some poisonous mushrooms look similar to edible mushrooms, making it difficult for members of the public to identify them safely based only on appearance, color or comparisons with online images.
The “green-spored parasol” is commonly found in Taiwan and is one of the poisonous mushrooms frequently eaten by mistake, it said, adding that it is medium to large in size and often found in open outdoor spaces at low elevations and on Taiwan’s plains.
Its gills are initially white, turning greenish-yellow or grayish-green as it matures, and it can easily be confused with edible species such as the parasol mushroom (Macrolepiota procera) or the termite mushroom (Termitomyces eurrhizus), it added.
Accidental ingestion can cause intense gastrointestinal distress within one to three hours, with common symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloody stool and dehydration, the department said.
The severity of symptoms can vary depending on a person’s condition and the amount consumed, but anyone who accidentally ingests a wild mushroom or feels unwell after eating one should seek medical attention as soon as possible, it said.
People should remember never to pick, cook or eat unknown wild mushrooms to prevent food poisoning, it added.
Separately, the Penghu County Health Bureau last month urged the public to avoid picking or eating wild plants and mushrooms or giving or receiving them as gifts, and to be mindful of the sources of food ingredients and their storage conditions.
It also promoted its “five do’s and two don’ts” principle for preventing food poisoning: people should wash their hands before handling food, choose fresh food ingredients, keep raw and cooked food separate, cook food thoroughly, store food in appropriate temperatures, and should not drink unpurified mountain spring water or pick and eat wild plants and animals.

As Europe rearms, Italy’s  space sector faces a scale test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:56 UTC
01:45:56 KST

Italy’s fragmented space industry is facing growing pressure to consolidate as defense and government customers increasingly favor larger suppliers capable of handling complex programs.
The shift reflects a broader push across Europe to build strategic autonomy in defense and critical technologies, as governments respond to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, tensions with China and uncertainty over future US security commitments.
For Italy, whose space sector is known for niche engineering expertise, but remains dominated by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the challenge is whether firms can build the scale and financial strength needed to compete for large contracts without losing their flexibility.
Photo: Bloomberg
Limited access to capital remains a major obstacle, industry executives say.
“In Italy, we used to say: ‘Small is beautiful,’ but that’s not true,” said Alessandro Franzoni, CEO of optical instrumentation specialist Officina Stellare.
Leonardo, Italy’s largest aerospace and defense company, said new projects require integrated technological capabilities, industrial reliability and the capacity to manage growing complexity.
“When selecting and developing its supply chain, the group favors suppliers capable of offering solid expertise, production capacity, resilience and operational continuity,” a spokesperson said.
Satellite navigation and cybersecurity specialist Qascom said customers now expect suppliers to provide products, hardware and industrial capabilities, not just engineering know-how.
“You need to grow, because remaining small doesn’t work,” cofounder and CEO Alessandro Pozzobon said.
The pressure has intensified as Europe’s space sector becomes more closely tied to defense and security priorities.
Europe’s defense build-up and growing demand for dual-use technologies, which can serve civilian and military purposes, have increased the importance of resilient industrial capacity.
The rise of Elon Musk’s SpaceX has also highlighted the advantages of scale, vertical integration and access to capital enjoyed by larger industry players.
“I see a trend towards aggregation, driven by the market,” said Giuseppe Acierno, president of the DTA aerospace hub in Apulia, southern Italy. “It is a trend that should be supported.”
Renato Panesi, chief commercial officer at Italian space logistics company D-Orbit, said Europe remains disadvantaged by fragmented programs and weaker access to private funding than the US.
Yet consolidation brings risks. Qascom said much of Italy’s fragmentation reflects deep technological specialization, with smaller firms occupying globally competitive niches in navigation, cybersecurity and advanced communications.
The challenge is finding ways to build scale without sacrificing innovation, executives said.
Building larger companies would require funding.
Last month, Intesa Sanpaolo, the European Investment Bank and the European Space Agency (ESA) launched a program expected to provide up to 300 million euros (US$350.3 million) in financing for aerospace SMEs.
“For too many of our space SMEs, the barrier to growth is not technology, but access to capital,” ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said.
The Italian Interministerial Committee for Space and Aerospace Research Policies estimated the country’s aerospace sector would receive 7.8 billion euros in investment and program funding by 2028, including 3.5 billion euros linked to Italy’s contribution to ESA programs.
For some companies, acquisitions have become the quickest route to achieving the scale customers demand.
Officina Stellare merged with Global Aerospace Technologies Group in June, creating an aerospace and defense platform with a pro-forma order backlog of 192 million euros.
Franzoni said the deal was designed to combine complementary technologies, strengthen vertical integration and broaden the group’s offering.
“I see now an opportunity, mostly in Italy, for further aggregation. We are looking for synergies for technologies and for production synergies,” he said.
Officina Stellare reinforced that strategy last month through the acquisition of electric motor specialist Mavel.
D-Orbit has also expanded through acquisitions, buying Earth observation specialist Planetek before raising fresh capital to fund further deals.
“The driver of our M&A [mergers and acquisitions] strategy is the acquisition of additional capabilities and services to offer to government, defense and commercial satellite operators,” Panesi said.
Recent contracts appear to reflect the shift. Officina Stellare this month secured a 6.5 million euro contract from Leonardo for optical communications terminals and another worth more than 7 million euros from the Italian Space Agency for an Earth observation program.
The company said the awards showed its ability to move beyond technology development and deliver integrated systems at industrial scale.
For industry executives, the question is no longer whether Italy’s space companies need to grow.
It is whether a sector built on specialized SMEs can secure the capital and scale needed to compete in a changing European market before competitors, or foreign acquirers, do it for them.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:55 UTC
01:45:55 KST

Continued from yesterday（延續自昨日）
https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/lang
While some healing economy trends focus on comforting products, others take the form of experiences. One recent example is puppy yoga, a class in which participants practice yoga as puppies wander freely around the room. The idea is simple: while people move through yoga poses, the presence of playful puppies is meant to create a joyful and relaxing atmosphere. Supporters claim the classes provide stress relief for humans. At the same time, they also help the dogs socialize with people.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片: AdobeStock
However, animal welfare experts have raised serious concerns about this trend. Some investigations have reported that puppies as young as six weeks old are used in these classes. Puppies should normally remain with their mothers for at least eight weeks to develop properly. Instead, they may spend hours in busy rooms filled with unfamiliar people.
Such environments can be overwhelming for young puppies. At this age, they need a sense of safety and the presence of a familiar caregiver when they are introduced to new experiences. Without this support, stressful situations may negatively affect their emotional and behavioral development.
For this reason, puppy yoga raises an important question about the healing economy. Although many wellness trends promise comfort and happiness for people, they may also create ethical concerns about how animals are treated.
有些療癒經濟趨勢著重在療癒人心的商品，其他則是體驗的形式。近期的一個例子是小狗瑜伽，在這樣的課程裡，參加者會在幼犬自由漫步於教室內的情況下練瑜伽。這個想法很簡單：當人們在做不同的瑜伽動作時，有愛玩的幼犬在場是為了打造歡樂又放鬆的氣氛。支持者宣稱這些課程能為人們提供壓力的紓解。同時，也有助於狗狗與人類互動。
然而，動物福利專家對這股趨勢提出高度疑慮。一些調查指出，這些課程中使用的幼犬年齡甚至只有六週大。幼犬通常應該與犬媽媽待到至少八週才能正常發育。牠們卻可能在充滿陌生人的忙碌教室裡待上好幾個小時。
這樣的環境對幼犬來說可能難以負荷。在這個年齡段，當牠們接觸新事物時，需要安全感以及熟悉照顧者的陪伴。若缺乏這樣的支持，充滿壓力的情況可能會對牠們的情緒與行為發展造成負面影響。
因此，狗狗瑜伽帶出了一個與療癒經濟相關的重要問題。儘管許多健康療癒的趨勢承諾能為人們帶來慰藉與快樂，但同時也可能引發如何對待動物的倫理疑慮。
What Did You Learn?
1-2. 請從第二天文章中找出最適當的單詞填入下列句子空格中，並視句型結構需要做適當的字形變化，使句子語意完整、語法正確，並符合全文文意。每格限填一個單詞（word）。（填充題）
Puppy yoga supposedly provides human relaxation and opportunities for dog __1__ with humans. However, experts warn that early introduction to busy environments without a safe caregiver hinders the puppies’ proper development and raises questions about the __2__ of using animals.
答案:1. socialization 2. ethics
3. From (A) to (F) below, choose the ONES that are true for both JellyCat and puppy yoga.（多選題）
(A) They both involve direct interactions with animals.
(B) They are promoted through videos on social media platforms.
(C) They show how businesses respond to people’s emotional needs.
(D) They both have sparked discussions about their possible negative effects.
(E) They are mainly intended to improve animals’ well-being and development.
(F) They reflect a growing interest in products or activities that support mental well-being.
答案:C、F
Words in Use
1. participant n. 參與者
Each participant in the marathon will receive a medal after they complete the race.
馬拉松賽事的每位參與者在完賽後都會收到一枚獎牌。
2. wander vi. 漫遊，閒晃
Holly wandered through the narrow streets of the old town.
荷莉在舊城區的狹窄街道上漫步。
3. presence n. 在場，存在
The judge requested the presence of a translator for the foreign witness.
法官要求為外籍證人安排一名翻譯員在場。
4. atmosphere n. 氣氛，氛圍
The live music added a festive atmosphere to the outdoor market.
現場音樂為戶外市集增添了節慶的氣氛。
5. socialize vi. 社交，交際
socialize with... 與……社交
Ken is socializing with the other hikers while they rest by the lake.
在湖邊休息時，阿肯與其他登山客交流互動。
Practical Phrases
1. be meant to V 意在（做）……
These exercises are meant to strengthen the lower back muscles.
這些運動意在強化下背肌肉。
2. be introduced to. . . 初次接觸……
Those students were introduced to basic chemistry during the summer camp.
那些學生在夏令營期間初次接觸了基礎化學。
3. for this reason 因此

Taiwanese badminton veteran Chou Tien-chen on Friday advanced to the men’s singles semi-finals at the BWF World Championships in India, securing the second world championships medal of his career.
He was to play against Japan’s Kodai Naraoka after press time last night.
The 36-year-old world No. 6 defeated Indonesian rising star Alwi Farhan 21-15, 21-15 in 50 minutes to guarantee himself at least a bronze medal.
Photo: Reuters
Chou, who entered the match with a 2-1 career record against the world No. 12, used his defense and experience to neutralize Farhan’s attacks and claim his third win in their four meetings.
Chou after the match said that he took care of many of the details well during the match and was able to respond to many of the opponent’s tactics.
“His attacks were actually very sharp, but I went all out. I was able to defend successfully a lot of the time and maintained my advantage,” he said.
The opening game was closely contested from the start, with Chou winning a 60-shot rally to take his seventh point.
After Farhan scored three consecutive points, Chou capitalized on a series of unforced errors by the Indonesian to produce a 7-1 run and lead 14-11.
Leading 16-15, Chou was awarded a point when Farhan was called for serving above the permitted height. Farhan then lost four more points in a row as Chou closed out the game 21-15.
The second game remained tight until 11-11, when Chou began to take the upper hand as he switched up between the pace, drops and timely smashes.
Farhan was called for another service fault with Chou leading 14-12. The Taiwanese player later earned six match points with a body smash before securing victory when Farhan sent a net shot into the tape.
Chou said winning several long rallies shifted the momentum in his favor and boosted his confidence as the match progressed.
A regular BWF world championships quarter-finalist since making his tournament debut in 2013, Chou won his first medal at the event with a semifinal appearance in 2022.
“I won’t think about a particular goal,” Chou said. “I will just fight as hard as I can without any burden and leave everything to Jesus. I believe God will make the best arrangements.”
Meanwhile, Taiwan on Friday also secured a medal in men’s doubles as Lee Jhe-huei and Yang Po-hsuan upset world No. 2 Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri of Indonesia 21-19, 21-16.
The victory made Lee and Yang only the second Taiwanese pair to reach the men’s doubles semi-finals at the world championships, following Chen Hung-ling and Wang Chi-lin, who won bronze in 2018.
Lee and Yang were to face China’s Olympic silver medalists and world No. 3 pair Wang Chang and Liang Weikeng in the semi-finals last night after press time.

Vietnam’s rise could stumble on growth push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:49 UTC
01:45:49 KST

Vietnam’s economy is on a roll. Hanoi, basking in the kind of praise that Southeast Asian peers won prior to the region’s financial crisis in the 1990s, wants still more rapid growth. However, leaders should be careful — such enthusiasm might well hasten the boom’s undoing.
Recent advances recall the glory days. In the second quarter, GDP climbed by more than 8 percent, easily exceeding forecasts. The closest to that, Malaysia, managed 6 percent. China, which for decades appeared largely insulated from business cycles, slackened to 4.3 percent. Vietnam’s government has its sights on a pace of at least 10 percent for the year.
Like the former Tiger economies that inspired it, Vietnam’s progress has been driven by breakneck industrialization and securing a lucrative niche in supply chains. Factories have churned apparel, furniture and electronics bound for shelves in the West, racking up enormous trade surpluses in the process. Tariffs on imports to the US were widely expected to slow things down. That has not happened, yet.
The performance has translated into meaningful gains in living standards. In July, the World Bank promoted Vietnam to the ranks of upper-middle income economies, joining Malaysia and Thailand. The Philippines also scored an upgrade. However, the pace at which Vietnam scaled the ladder is revealing. The bank had only elevated it to a lower-middle income economy in 2009.
It is reasonable to question how long a performance like this can be sustained. The more prosperous a country becomes, the harder it is to keep clocking up torrid rates of expansion, while a notable overheating would jeopardize financial stability and prod authorities to take firm steps to rein in activity.
Policy is increasingly geared to meet Vietnamese President To Lam’s objective of achieving high-income status by 2045, a century after the country declared its independence in the aftermath of World War II. Credit growth is running high: The central bank has set a target of 15 percent and has signaled it could indulge a greater amount. State spending is also being harnessed, with the budget deficit projected to widen. Managing this will be tricky. Officials want muscular growth, but do not want inflation to accelerate much beyond their target of 4.5 percent. Consumer prices jumped 5.6 percent from a year earlier in May, but have since increased at a more moderate pace. And they need to limit swings in the currency, which is allowed to fluctuate in a narrow band against the US dollar.
In an echo of how its neighbors ran into trouble during the Asian financial crisis, Lam also has his eyes on mega projects, including a US$2.5 trillion “master plan” to reconfigure large swathes of Hanoi. Ho Chi Minh City launched its own blueprint for a makeover. The risk is that such grand initiatives become an end to themselves. Waste and over-development are seldom far behind. While the ventures seem doable when times are good, they can sour when the economic and financial cycle turns. Recall the Vision 2020 program of former Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, who in 1991 beseeched citizens to reach for a Swiss-style standard of living by the second decade of this century. Years of strong growth did follow, but so did ostentatious projects like the Petronas Towers and a cavernous airport that is too far from Kuala Lumpur and too thinly staffed. (Mahathir eventually acknowledged the 2020 goal would not be reached.)
Another danger lurks in the dependence of Vietnam’s export machine on the world’s biggest economy.
Last year, the trade surplus with the US ballooned to a record US$134 billion, an increase of more than one-fifth. the US’ shortfall with the country is the third largest after China and Mexico. The levies that US President Donald Trump announced in April last year were regarded as a steep challenge for Vietnam.
At that time, the White House also made clear it wanted to crack down on transshipments from China, a hard-to-pin-down practice where parts of a product are routed through Vietnam to the US with Vietnamese duties paid rather than the steeper charges applied to its northern neighbor. The Trump administration is now renewing its focus on constraining such traffic.
Hanoi cannot control Trump, but it can take care to avoid a hard landing. Relaxing credit guidelines would be risky, and the central bank should watch that activity does not become too hot. It is important policymakers realize that outperformance cannot last forever. Pushing growth above 8 percent for a considerable period might see the country gallop further up the development ladder, but it could also easily lead to an unacceptable build up of bad debts and an economy increasingly vulnerable to shocks. China offers a sobering lesson: After growth tore along in excess of 10 percent a year in the early 2000s, the nation’s model hit a wall.
“If Vietnam does achieve sustained 10 percent growth, it’s more likely to be a warning sign than a reason for celebration,” Capital Economics senior Asia economist Gareth Leather wrote last week.
Vietnam has done very well. It could do even better if it learns the lessons of its neighbors and shoots for something less than perfection.
Daniel Moss is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian economies. Previously, he was executive editor for economics at Bloomberg News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Thousands of doses of Ebola vaccine arrive in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:46 UTC
01:45:46 KST

More than 16,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine arrived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) late on Friday, as the country faces the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history.
The DR Congo’s 17th Ebola outbreak, which has killed thousands of people, was declared on May 15, but is thought to have been spreading for several weeks prior. It has hit regions in the north and east where the presence of the state is weak, health infrastructure is largely lacking and myriad armed groups have roamed for decades.
The WHO on Thursday announced that DR Congo would receive a total of 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, produced in Germany.
Photo: AFP
The vaccine, developed by the pharmaceutical company Merck, is approved against the Zaire strain of the virus, but not against the Bundibugyo strain circulating in the country.
WHO experts still do not know whether Ervebo protects humans against the Bundibugyo strain, but early data, notably from animal trials, suggest it could offer some protection.
The Ervebo vaccine “has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak,” Congolese Minister of Public Health Samuel Roger Kamba said.
He was speaking on the tarmac of Kinshasa airport, where a batch of 16,250 doses was delivered by plane.
Of the 70,000 doses made available to the DR Congo, 20,000 are intended for a clinical trial, and 50,000 for “frontline and health workers,” the WHO said.
The Ebola outbreak in the country has already caused 2,516 deaths among 5,290 confirmed cases, the latest data published by the Congolese authorities showed.
“[It] is growing exponentially,” UN Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis said.
This month, WHO vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of Ervebo, the only existing approved Ebola vaccine, to see if it offered cross-protection against the Bundibugyo strain.
Two vaccines specifically targeting the Bundibugyo strain are in clinical trial phases: one is being developed by the US-based group Moderna, which uses mRNA technology, and the other by the UK’s University of Oxford.
An “rVSV Bundibugyo” vaccine, described by the WHO as “the most promising,” is to be developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories.

Ex-Chinese priest gets naturalized after decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:46 UTC
01:45:46 KST

A Catholic priest who was born in China and is now a US citizen has become a Taiwanese citizen after overcoming bureaucratic hurdles tied to his birthplace.
Xu Jingshan (徐景山), 67, who has been preaching in Taiwan for the past 20 years, said on Thursday that he first went to the US from China 33 years ago and later obtained US citizenship. He wrote off his household registration in China at the time.
He was assigned by the Catholic Church to Taiwan about two decades ago.
Photo: Hung Jui-chin, Taipei Times
Xu said that living in Taiwan without a national ID card had long caused practical inconveniences, such as difficulties in applying for a cellphone and obtaining a senior citizen card.
Upon learning about the government’s “Mackay Project” last year, he applied to become a naturalized Republic of China citizen for “making special contributions.”
His application was eventually approved by the Ministry of the Interior.
Because he was born in China, the National Immigration Agency (NIA) required that he provide documentation proving the cancelation of his Chinese household registration.
Xu said he had his relatives in China obtain the required documents from the local police station in his birthplace, but the NIA required the paperwork to be authenticated by Taiwan’s Straits Exchange Foundation.
However, the foundation only accepts notarized expulsion documents authenticated by Chinese notary offices, not expulsion documents directly issued by local police stations, Xu added.
A suspension in a Chinese notary office’s authentication service caused his application to stall, Xu said. In July, the office resumed the service, and his Taiwan ID card was ultimately issued.
During the process, he sought assistance from Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Yunlin County Councilor Tsai Yueh-ju (蔡岳儒), who in turn enlisted the help of DPP Legislator Liu Chien-kuo (劉建國). His case was also submitted to the Executive Yuan and the Presidential Office.
Tsai said Xu had previously served in churches in Yunlin County, where he devoted himself to grassroots education and helped establish a day center for seniors at Lunbei Catholic Church.
Xu was transferred to the Church of the Good Shepherd six years ago and has made significant contributions to rural communities and disadvantaged residents, Tsai said.

TikTok to pay US$400m in privacy lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:45 UTC
01:45:45 KST

TikTok has agreed to pay US$400 million to settle a lawsuit with the US Department of Justice over claims that the video-sharing platform contravened federal children’s privacy laws, the department announced on Friday.
Regulators around the world have been ramping up enforcement against social media companies that contravene laws about protecting children’s data, privacy and safety. Chinese company ByteDance — which sold off a majority stake of its US entity earlier this year to avoid a ban by the administration of US President Donald Trump — is also named as part of the settlement.
It has a 19.9 percent ownership stake in TikTok US, US media reported.
Photo: AFP
“Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly,” the department said in a statement.
“[It is] one of the largest recoveries ever obtained” from a case involving the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), the statement said.
The act bars Web sites from gathering the personal information of children younger than 13 without parental permission.
The justice department and US Federal Trade Commission jointly sued TikTok in 2024, alleging that it had placed the safety of millions of children in jeopardy by collecting their personal data without parental permission.
TikTok allowed children to use the app in addition to collecting and using personal data from young users without letting their parents know, they said.
Even accounts created in a “Kids Mode” intended for users younger than 13 gathered e-mail addresses and other personal information, the suit said.
In 2019, the US filed a COPPA lawsuit against an app called Musical.ly, which ByteDance bought in 2017 and then merged into TikTok.
TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
An ABC News report in May said that the Trump administration was considering using the funds for ongoing “beautification” projects, which have included resurfacing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, renovating the White House ballroom and building an arch.
It was not immediately clear what the settlement funds would be used for.
The US settlement comes amid a growing global crackdown on the video app.
Brussels began a probe into TikTok in 2024 under the Digital Services Act (DSA) — a content law and major weapon in the EU’s boosted legal armory that it has deployed to rein in Big Tech over the past few years.
Last month, the EU accused TikTok of failing to protect children through account settings that could expose them to risks such as cyberbullying and predatory behavior, putting the company at risk of a large fine.
Minors’ accounts should only be visible to those they have given permission to, the EU said.
Children ages 13 and over can use TikTok.
“A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default,” European Commissioner for Digital and Frontier Technologies Henna Virkkunen said at the time.
Under the DSA, children’s account settings have, by default, the strongest safety and security protections.
“TikTok’s account settings fail to meet this standard, as they expose minors’ accounts and content too widely,” the EU said in its preliminary view.
