South Korea makes billions, but takes home little
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:42 UTC
01:45:42 KST

South Korea, home to the world’s two largest memorychip makers, is in the midst of an AI-fueled exports boom. Generating wealth and keeping it at home are not the same thing, however.
Korea Inc is making a staggering amount of money this year. Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc are among the world’s five most profitable companies, earning more than Alphabet Inc or Apple Inc. Thanks to soaring memorychip prices, gross domestic income, a measure of the nation’s purchasing power, increased by 15.6 percent in the second quarter, far outpacing the 3.7 percent gain in GDP.
However, chronic capital outflows, which have haunted successive governments, are not going away. A sizeable chunk of export revenue is kept offshore, according to consultancy Capital Economics, which looked at deposits data in South Korea’s financial account for clues (Offshore corporate deposits would show up under currency and deposits of other sectors — other than the central bank, financial institutions, or the general government — in the country’s financial account.). In June, the government asked major exporters to repatriate funds held overseas to stabilize the South Korean won.
The main factors that contributed to money leaving the country are still present. Retail investors have flocked to the NASDAQ, developing a taste that first took hold during the meme stock craze in late 2020. They briefly sold their overseas holdings earlier in the year, but re-entered the US market in June, piling into leveraged semiconductor exchange-traded funds.
While less risk-loving than mom-and-pop traders, South Korean companies continue to invest abroad. SK Group has promised to put in a “much, much bigger” amount than the US$35 billion it has committed to in the US, while Samsung Group is also expanding manufacturing capabilities there. Still, the White House is pushing for more.
At home, though, there are worries that retail traders will abandon the Kospi for good after last month’s rout, returning to a perception long-held before the AI fever hit that the South Korean market is a value trap. Meanwhile, business sentiment is fragile. Private-sector investments fell in 2024 and last year.
In other words, South Korea has the same kind of dilemma as its north Asian neighbors, Japan and China.
The vast wealth created from its industrial success is recycled overseas — through foreign direct or portfolio investments — and does not necessarily translate into deeper equity markets, higher asset valuations, or a broad-based economic boom at home.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s administration is certainly doing what it can to address structural problems. Vowing to make a “great leap forward,” the government has unveiled public-private partnership projects in the less-developed southwest region, with SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics each promising to deploy about 400 trillion won (US$288.22 billion) in new chipmaking factories. It is injecting fresh capital into sovereign wealth funds for strategic investments in AI infrastructure. Last month, Seoul introduced 24-hour trading of the South Korean won to facilitate transactions at a level comparable to G10 currencies. South Korea is one of the world’s largest exporters, but its currency accounts for only 1 percent of global foreign-exchange turnover, according to Deutsche Bank.
Big question marks remain, however. Economists worry about the day the AI boom runs out of steam. The strength of South Korea’s export revenue comes mostly from soaring prices rather than volumes, so what would happen if Chinese competitors flood the market and drag down the entire industry’s profitability? Will Korea Inc suffer from over-investment?
Nonetheless, the government is wise not to waste the big fiscal windfall on socialist wealth transfers, instead leveraging state money to tease out domestic investments. After all, South Korea is a functioning democracy and Seoul cannot take a page out of Beijing’s playbook, which simply cracks down on cross-border stock investments and traps its capital at home as a way to develop domestic equity markets. For South Korea, improving business sentiment is the only way.
Shuli Ren is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian markets. A former investment banker, she was a markets reporter for Barron’s. She is a CFA charterholder. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

China investigates comedian who altered song onstage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:39 UTC
01:45:39 KST

One of China’s best-known comedians is under investigation and several of his shows have been canceled after he changed the lyrics of a revolutionary song during a performance.
Guo Degang (郭德?), the country’s most prominent performer of traditional xiangsheng, a form of Chinese comedic dialogue, is under investigation by Wuhan authorities, local media reported.
Guo’s show on Friday in Xi’an was canceled due to “venue issues,” a statement on ticketing platform Damai released by his promotion company showed.
Photo: AP
The company offered refunds for tickets as well as travel and hotel expenses. The exhibition center hosting the performance, which also cited “venue issues” on Wednesday, said the show had been “postponed,” without giving a new date.
Local media reports said several of Guo’s shows scheduled this month across cities were canceled.
The investigation highlights China’s stricter controls and censorship of the entertainment and arts industries, where performers and artists have to navigate an environment where “red lines” are often unclear and shifting.
Guo was reported to Wuhan’s culture and tourism authorities after he changed a lyric from “it is quiet along Weishan Lake” to “it is quiet in the Forbidden City” while performing at a show in the city last month, according to local media reports and videos on social media platforms.
The Forbidden City, once home to China’s emperors for hundreds of years, is now a museum that attracts more than 10 million visitors each year.
Guo’s performance had been approved in advance by Wuhan authorities, but the lyric change had not, which might have contravened regulations governing commercial performances, The Paper said.
The lyrics are from Playing My Beloved Pipa, a song from Railway Guerrilla, a well-known 1950s film about communist-led guerrillas fighting Japanese forces during World War II.
The pipa is a traditional Chinese stringed instrument, similar to a lute.
It is a popular song among the public. It was once played at CCTV Spring Festival gala in 1998, and was also selected in 2019 by the Chinese Communist Party’s Publicity Department as one of 100 songs recommended to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.
Guo is widely considered as the one who brought xiangsheng closer to the younger generation in China. The traditional art form was more regional and more popular among the older audience.
This is not the first time that performers face consequences over their work on stage. In 2023, comedian Li Haoshi (李昊石), known by his stage name House, sparked controversy after describing dogs chasing squirrels with a military slogan.
Xiaoguo Culture Media, the company he worked for, was later fined 14.7 million yuan (US$2.19 million), and Li has not appeared in public performances in mainland China since.

Printers’ group looks to future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:39 UTC
01:45:39 KST

Once a major force for spreading knowledge, printing is now at a crossroads as digital reading reduces demand for traditional print. To adapt, one of Taiwan’s oldest printing associations is turning to artificial intelligence (AI), new markets and talent development.
Established 80 years ago, the Tainan City Printing Commercial Association is looking to the next 80 years with a focus on technology, talent and cultural preservation.
“AI adoption is only just beginning, and every industry is essentially starting from the same line,” the association’s honorary chairman Huang Chien-tung (黃建東) said on Sunday last week.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Church Press
The precision and commitment to quality developed by printing professionals provide a strong foundation for adopting AI, he said.
The association is promoting AI-powered design and intelligent production to address labor shortages, while developing AI training programs and seeking government support for digital transformation and talent development.
Pan Ching-chu (潘靜竹), head of the Fucheng Old Books Store, said Taiwan has about 10,000 publishers, but many new books have initial print runs of only 500 copies, compared with several thousand in the past. Rising production costs have pushed up book prices as demand falls, while large quantities of nearly new secondhand books are being sold for a fraction of their original prices.
Photo: Hung Jui-chin, Taipei Times
Still, Pan said printing remains essential for packaging, advertising and other commercial applications.
Huang Chin-yi (黃進益), a section chief at Academia Sinica’s Southern Branch Service Office, said books connect design, editing, paper, ink, machinery, binding, logistics and sales into a cultural and creative industry chain. Rather than mass production, print could increasingly focus on high-quality materials, sophisticated design and collectible value, he added.
The renewed popularity of independent publishing, zines, art books and photography books among younger creators also suggests that demand for print and its tangible qualities remains.
The association’s 80th-anniversary publication showcases that craftsmanship. Its cover combines Oxford paper, laser-foil stamping and die-cutting inspired by traditional Tainan window patterns, blending traditional motifs with modern printing techniques.
Printer Sun Wen-shan (孫文山) hopes Tainan can establish a printing-themed tourist factory combining cultural history, technology demonstrations and hands-on activities.
Companies are also demonstrating how the industry can adapt.
Chairman Lu Jung-ta (盧榮達) said that printing companies must understand how to adapt to markets and customer needs while maintaining expertise in design, production and service.
Chien Sheng Enterprise, the first printing company to establish a facility in the Tainan Technology Industrial Park, helped usher traditional printing into the technology sector through computerized equipment, digital typesetting and precision printing.
Manager Huang Chien-tung (黃建東) said that the global industry has moved beyond simple contract manufacturing toward digitalization and knowledge creation. With product life cycles shortening, companies must continually invest in research and development and incorporate new technologies to remain competitive, he added.
Chairman Cheng Chun-ming (鄭俊銘) said the company’s green transformation goes beyond upgrading equipment to incorporating sustainability into its products and operations.
Cheng also emphasized the importance of talent, saying that traditional industries face difficulties recruiting workers, and Taiwan has few printing-related programs. He said medium and senior-level professionals returning to the workforce, particularly those with management experience in the electronics industry, could become an important source of talent if given appropriate printing training.
From movable type to AI-powered manufacturing, Tainan’s printing industry is attempting to preserve its traditional expertise while adapting to a digital, increasingly automated and environmentally conscious economy.

Legislature loses ‘friendship’ travel funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:39 UTC
01:45:39 KST

The legislature has suspended funding for overseas visits by lawmakers’ friendship groups after travel budget cuts, prompting mixed responses from the three major parties.
The central government’s budget for this fiscal year was delayed for 351 days before the Legislative Yuan finally passed it on Friday last week.
As part of across-the-board cuts, the budgets for overseas travel and training at central government agencies and their affiliated bodies were cut by 30 percent, with exceptions for legally mandated spending, Academia Sinica and the National Audit Office. Some agencies were subject to cuts ranging from 10 percent to 70 percent.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
In a letter sent to lawmakers, Legislative Yuan Secretary-General Chou Wan-lai (周萬來) said that after the cuts, the legislature’s overseas travel budget was insufficient to subsidize lawmakers’ visits organized by foreign parliamentary friendship groups, once existing expenditures and earmarked funds were taken into account.
Under Article 15 of the regulations governing parliamentary friendship groups with foreign legislators and other organizations, subsidies must be covered by the legislature’s budget.
The Legislative Yuan has stopped accepting applications for funding for overseas visits by parliamentary friendship groups, effective immediately.
“I think the legislature has only itself to blame,” Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) caucus secretary-general Fan Yun (范雲) said yesterday, adding that the cuts ended up affecting the Legislative Yuan itself, leaving lawmakers without subsidies and forcing them to pay out of pocket for overseas parliamentary diplomacy.
DPP Legislator Michelle Lin (林楚茵), who also chairs the Taiwan-France Parliamentary Friendship Association and other friendship groups, said that there were 114 parliamentary friendship groups as of the end of June, 78 of which are cross-national groups focused on parliamentary diplomacy.
At a time when Taiwan is facing pressure from China, parliamentary exchanges with other democratic legislatures are an important way for the nation to engage internationally, she added.
The subsidy for overseas visits by parliamentary friendship groups is about NT$60,000 per person, Lin said.
While that amount may cover trips to some Asian countries, an economy-class ticket to Europe could cost more than NT$60,000, she said, adding that there are also accommodation expenses.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said the cuts apply to the Legislative Yuan, which shows that they were intended to rein in government spending, rather than targeting the Executive Yuan.
Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) caucus whip Jacky Chen (陳清龍) said cuts have been made at a certain rate in previous years, adding that the 30 percent cut to overseas travel expenses was the version the three parties agreed upon during negotiations.
As DPP caucus whip Tsai Chi-chang (蔡其昌) signed off on the agreement, all government agencies would be able to adjust accordingly, Chen said.
TPP Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said parliamentary diplomacy is necessary, and lawmakers should continue traveling overseas to seek international support and deepen ties with democratic partners.
However, the importance of parliamentary diplomacy does not mean every expense should be given unlimited leeway, he added.
Hung criticized some government officials for taking aimless overseas trips and submitting poorly written reports, only to invoke national security confidentiality as a cover when their conduct was exposed.
Such misuse of travel funds was the main reason for the cuts, he said, adding that the legislature’s parliamentary diplomacy budget was simply collateral damage.
Hung blamed ruling party officials for misusing public funds, saying that they dragged down the budgets of the legislature and government agencies.

EDITORIAL: The devil in the omissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:38 UTC
01:45:38 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) failure to win the previous three presidential elections has been tied to its tenacious approach to cross-strait relations, with polls showing that the electorate remain profoundly suspicious of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
At first glance, it might be confusing as to why a political party aspiring to return to power would continue to flog the pro-China horse. The answer is that continued engagement with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) makes sense, as long as one is willing to ignore some glaring omissions.
An editorial in a pro-China newspaper said that few could deny that China is overtaking other countries, including the US, in multiple metrics.
Many countries are engaging with China, while Taiwan continues to cling to the concept of “resisting China to protect Taiwan,” and the nation would lose by refusing to engage with the world’s second-largest economy in tourism, education, industry and technology, it said. It also warned against the assumption that the US military would handily defeat the Chinese People’s Liberation Army in the Western Pacific.
These are all fair points, which the article suggests are largely omitted from the pro-Taiwanese independence side. At the same time, it neglects to point out that, in Taiwan’s case, there is no possibility of a mutually beneficial economic exchange with China, nor does it concede that siding with Washington over the CCP is far more than an ideological preference. The devil is not only in the details: It is also in the omissions.
During an online interview on Friday last week, KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) told host Dennis Peng (彭文正) that “Taiwan has never been independent, nor has it ever been a country.”
Cheng is incorrect in that assertion, although it is perfectly consistent with the KMT’s stance. The omissions in her statement are highly complex.
Cheng’s expression of the KMT position in this case is that the name of the country is not Taiwan, it is the Republic of China (ROC), bound to the ROC Constitution. This is not controversial from the KMT perspective, although pro-Taiwanese critics would certainly take issue with it. To Cheng, Taiwan only exists because of the ROC Constitution, which she called a “one China” constitution, omitting the logical conclusion that must be drawn: From the CCP’s perspective, the ROC no longer exists, and its constitution is little more than a historical document, albeit linked to the PRC’s own.
On how this inconvenient contradiction is to be cleared up, and how the KMT envisages “peaceful unification” with China, Cheng said her ideas would “be truly introduced and implemented as policy once the KMT retakes power.” She wants Taiwanese to hand her the presidency first before they find out what she has in store for them.
Cheng mocked the Democratic Progressive Party for “not daring to hold a referendum on Taiwanese independence.” Yet she knows what the political jeopardy to the CCP and the KMT, and the risk of war, would be if such a referendum were ever held. The list of omissions goes on.
After her meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) in Beijing in April, questions about whether Cheng would stand as the KMT’s presidential candidate in the 2028 election started to surface. Despite being the party chair, it is not necessarily the case that she would be the first option. A week, let alone two years, is a long time in politics, and if she ran, she would potentially be vying for the candidacy with three other strong candidates: Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) — currently the party’s highest-ranked elected figure — and Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕).
According to an opinion poll released on Wednesday by the online media outlet Z.Media (震傳媒), when asked about who they thought would be the preferred KMT candidate for the 2028 presidential race, 20.4 percent of respondents said that they supported Chiang, 18.9 percent Han and 16 percent Lu. The differences are hardly insurmountable. Cheng only received 3 percent of the support.
In politics, omissions are to be expected, but the times also call for clarity and honesty.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Chiang Kung missile specifications released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:38 UTC
01:45:38 KST

The National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) yesterday disclosed technical specifications of the Chiang Kung missile, amid a legislative deadlock that cast doubt over the program’s future.
The Chiang Kung missile, also known as Tien Chien IV, is intended to serve as the principal high-altitude interceptor of the proposed “T-Dome,” an integrated air defense matrix for Taiwan proper.
The Ministry of National Defense has confirmed that it would seek to fund Chiang Kung missile production via a supplementary budget, since the program was not included in the special defense budget passed by the Legislative Yuan.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
According to the NCSIST, the state-run defense research and development group, the Chiang Kung air defense system uses a land-based vertical launch system to fire hypersonic weapons capable of intercepting ballistic missiles at mesospheric altitudes.
The interceptor missile uses vectored thrust to ensure speed and maneuverability in the low-air-density conditions of high altitudes, the institute said.
The warhead of the Chiang Kung missile is mounted atop a two-stage solid-propellant rocket housed in molded composite materials to enable large-scale production at a low cost, it said.
The Chiang Kung’s radar can identify different types of targets, engage multiple tactical ballistic missiles, and is hardened against electronic warfare countermeasures, the NCSIST said.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, a defense official said that the Chiang Kung system’s ability to intercept ballistic missiles at altitudes up to 70km is a significant improvement over the Tien Kung III.
The Chiang Kung features a mobile active electronically scanned array radar vehicle developed jointly by Taiwan and the US, which possesses formidable detection and is designed to operate under heavy electromagnetic interference and GPS jamming, they said.
The Chiang Kung missile is a crucial part of the planned “T-Dome” air defense network, which incorporates multiple types of interceptors under the control of the US-made Integrated Air and Missile Defense Battle Command System, they said.
This system’s importance stems from its high-altitude capability, which is absent in Taiwan’s arsenal and cannot be otherwise obtained through foreign procurement, the official said.
The ministry’s budget woes have impacted the Chiang Kung system acquisition timetable, which has negative ramifications for the entire “T-Dome” project, they said.
The military cannot integrate its patchwork of air defense missiles when key pieces are missing, the official said, adding that Taiwan can ill afford this problem as Chinese capabilities grow by leaps and bounds.
The uncertainty surrounding the funding of key weapon systems, including Chiang Kung, is highly worrisome to the military’s leadership, they said.

YouTube paying to keep creators amid Netflix push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:37 UTC
01:45:37 KST

YouTube is offering millions of dollars to popular channels if they upload their videos to the site exclusively for a certain period of time, in an effort to halt Netflix Inc’s pursuit of its biggest stars, people familiar with the conversations said.
The payment would come in a couple of different forms. YouTube has discussed directly financing some programs, and it has also offered to allot a portion of major brand deals to creators. Although YouTube has not finalized deals with any creators, it is close an agreement with several partners, said the people, who declined to be identified because the negotiations are sensitive and ongoing.
Creators who do sign deals with Netflix face consequences, YouTube has said, according to the people. YouTube would be less likely to feature them in marketing campaigns or at events if they release videos on Netflix at the same time. YouTube would also exclude those creators from collecting a share of proceeds from some major brand campaigns.
Photo: AP
Netflix has been pursuing agreements with dozens of prominent YouTubers, paying creators such as Alan Chikin Chow and Nick DiGiovanni to post their videos on YouTube and Netflix concurrently. The company remains in active conversations with dozens of other creators, channels and programs, such as Hot Ones, a celebrity talk show.
The Netflix deals appeal to creators, because they are a way to get paid millions of additional dollars for videos they are already making and expose their programming to new viewers. Netflix has more than 325 million subscribers.
Yet YouTube has told creators cross-posting on its platform and Netflix hurts viewership on YouTube and conveys the idea that channels are deprioritizing the streaming platform as their primary distribution outlet.
Photo: Reuters
Some creators have already decided not to work with Netflix. The service requires them to deliver videos days in advance, which is not how many creators operate. It has also asked creators to remove certain brand sponsorships from their videos.
YouTube and Netflix have been the leaders in streaming video for the past 20 years. For most of that time, they have been friendly competitors largely operating in separate universes.
Netflix was the king of subscription streaming, focused on more expensive, Hollywood-style films and TV shows. YouTube was the undisputed leader in user-generated content, birthing a new generation of stars that people primarily watched on mobile devices. Its past efforts to fund original programming failed to produce many hit programs. One of those shows, Cobra Kai, went on to be a big hit for Netflix.
Yet the line between the two sites has blurred in the past few years. YouTube prioritized getting people to watch on TV and now accounts for more viewership on those devices than any other service. It has chased TV advertising dollars and taken the rights to major live events such as the Academy Awards and the NFL.
Netflix, which has long promoted its titles on YouTube, licensed the rights to popular shows such as CoComelon and Ms. Rachel. It sees YouTube stars as a way to draw in younger viewers and boost the amount of time its users spend on Netflix.
The competition has intensified over the past year as Netflix has stepped up its pursuit of YouTube’s most popular channels.
YouTube has weighed whether to respond. Chief executive officer Neal Mohan has long said that creators who do deals with competitors, be they Instagram or Amazon Prime Video, tend to drive viewers back to YouTube. Few of these creators are leaving YouTube, which is still their primary distribution outlet. Funding any individual channel also risks aggravating the thousands of channels that do not get any cash.
YouTube still does not want to serve as a studio for creators, which would involve funding and providing creative direction. However, over the past few weeks, Mohan and his team have decided that the steady stream of creators now posting on YouTube and Netflix at the same time was a problem that needed to be addressed. It is harder to sell advertisers on the appeal and value of a video on YouTube if it is also available on Netflix.
This is not the first time YouTube has responded to competitors in this manner. It offered money to creators who did not do deals with Vessel, a start-up cofounded and formerly led by Jason Kilar that was trying to get social media creators to post on its app before YouTube. YouTube also created a product for short-form video to compete with TikTok.

Wildfires expose, detonate old explosives in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:35 UTC
01:45:35 KST

The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames.
Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg Province in 1944.
Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict academic at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies.
Photo: AP
Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant.
“Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said.
Fires can ignite old munitions, and burn away the scrub and brush that hides them.
This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived.
Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, a World Weather Attribution study said last month.
As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent.
In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be WWII-era ammunition.
In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Governor Herve Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area.
No fire crews were in danger, he said, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.
During WWII, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province’s dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens.
In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said historian Bernard Collard, who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium’s border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war.
“When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said.
He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry.
The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens.
The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 US and 28,000 German troops.
Collard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases and a human skeleton.
“You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site.
Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.
Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires, because heat can trigger the explosives, North Rhine-Westphalia spokesperson Jonas Tepe said.
The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared with elsewhere in Belgium.
Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in WWI — call the annual tilling of the soil “ the iron harvest,” because it turns up so many war remnants.
Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tonnes of munitions left over from the world wars.
Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons.
In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition.
Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from WWII emerged at its base in receding water.

Thousands of invasive fish taken from Sun Moon Lake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:35 UTC
01:45:35 KST

More than 25,000 giant snakehead fry have been removed from Sun Moon Lake (日月潭) this year, marking a more than 30-fold annual increase from last year, the Nantou County Government said on Friday.
The county government has stepped up its effort to capture the invasive carnivorous fish species as its peak breeding season begins from this month.
The catch per unit effort ranged from 3,000 to more than 5,000 fry, it said, adding that a total of 4,808 giant snakehead fry were removed from the lake this week.
Photo courtesy of the Nantou County Government
While only slightly more than 800 fry were captured last year, this year’s catch via electrofishing has rapidly climbed to a cumulative total of 25,717 fry as of Friday, the county government said.
That is an annual increase of more than 30-fold from last year, it said, adding the annual total catch is projected to surpass 30,000 fry this year.
The giant snakehead, also locally known as “the bully of the lake,” came into the public eye in Taiwan about 20 years ago.
The fish species began to proliferate in Sun Moon Lake around 2020, requiring the county to conduct electrofishing removal in the summer of every year.
It is a carnivorous freshwater fish that hunts almost all kinds of aquatic life, including frogs, snakes, turtles and waterbirds.
A red devil cichlid — an invasive fish species commonly known as “the king of demons” in Taiwan for its aggressiveness — was found bitten when it was caught by a local angler at the lake on Thursday.
The angler, who has a Facebook page called “Sun Moon Lake No. 1” (日月潭一等高), posted a photo of the red devil cichlid showing that the bite left on its upper body was shaped like the mouth of a giant snakehead.
“Look who is the real underwater big boss of Sun Moon Lake,” he said.
“The bully of the lake can be so ferocious that it bit the king of demons even during Ghost Month,” the angler said, referring to this month of the lunar calendar.
Giant snakeheads can turn cannibal when their population grows too big in a single habitat.
While the giant snakehead’s breeding season could run through October, the county government said its removal effort might be coming to an end this year due to limited budgets.
The county government would provide guidance for local fishermen on how to capture giant snakehead fry balls, it said.
Fry balls are giant snakehead fry and juvenile fish merging into red-orange “balls” as they rise to the water surface to breathe or hunt small fry or shrimp.
Such fry balls have been nicknamed “death bubbles” by locals and have become a local specialty dish at restaurants around the lake, adding to local fishermen’s income.

China mulls bid to host 2028 UN climate talks: sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:32 UTC
01:45:32 KST

China is mulling a bid to host UN climate talks in 2028, two sources familiar with the matter said on Friday, as it seeks to burnish its reputation as a leader in the fight against global warming.
Beijing has not yet made a final decision regarding the proposal for the COP33 summit, the sources said, nor is there a clear timeline for doing so.
The host does not have to be decided this year.
Photo: Reuters
The UN’s annual climate gatherings rotate among regional blocs. This year’s COP31 is scheduled to take place in Turkey, followed by COP32 in Ethiopia next year.
The 2028 summit falls to the Asia-Pacific region.
In April, India withdrew its offer to host COP33 without specifying a reason. South Korea has previously expressed interest.
The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change secretariat said: “We have not been informed by the Asia-Pacific Regional Group on the nomination of the host country for COP33.”
“Regional groups hold consultations first to determine which country from their respective regions would offer to host on behalf of the group. Once agreed, the chair of that regional group formally sends an official nomination to the secretariat,” it added.
China has over the past few years positioned itself as a counterweight to the US.
Under US President Donald Trump, Washington left the Paris climate agreement twice while the administration seeks to boost fossil fuels.
Hosting UN climate talks could thus be an opportunity for China to boost its credentials as a climate leader.
The world’s second-largest economy also has an economic interest as the leading exporter of green technologies, including solar panels, electric vehicles, wind turbines and batteries.
However, hosting the gathering could also cast an unwelcome spotlight on China, which, with its population of 1.4 billion and massive manufacturing industry, is the world’s biggest greenhouse emitter, followed by the US, India and the EU.
Although it has pledged to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060, it is targeting only a modest 7 to 10 percent reduction in economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, compared with peak levels.
Another factor that China is considering is the US-China dynamic, one source said.
Climate cooperation had been a key feature of the bilateral relationship under former US presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, and COP33 could spur renewed collaboration if a Democrat is elected in 2028.

TASA launches new sounding rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:32 UTC
01:45:32 KST

The Taiwan Space Agency (TASA) yesterday in Pingtung County launched the nation’s first independently developed sounding rocket under its orbital launch vehicle program, completing its end-to-end communication verification with a maximum speed of Mach 1.2.
The rocket, named Maraho (島脈), blasted off at the county’s Syuhai rocket launch site in its first test flight at 7:10am yesterday.
The launch operations, including rocket ignition, flight and parachute deployment, were successfully completed, the agency said yesterday.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Space Agency
The agency in 2023 initiated the orbital launch vehicle program with the goal of establishing indigenous satellite launch capabilities by 2034, it said.
The program involves the target of delivering a 200kg payload to low Earth orbit, the agency said, adding that the test flight of Maraho was part of the effort.
Maraho propulsed for 18 seconds and generated 1,500kgf of takeoff thrust in this test flight, reaching a maximum supersonic speed of about Mach 1.2, it said.
It peaked at an altitude of 8.1km with a total flight time of 432 seconds, the agency said.
The whole flight process was completed in accordance with the plan and the desired verification data were successfully obtained, it said.
However, the rocket body could not be recovered due to unfavorable sea conditions, the agency said.
The test flight was aimed to verify the operation of the overall Maraho rocket system in a real-world flight environment, it said.
One of the key targets was to build an end-to-end communication mechanism between the ground and rockets to receive data in real time, the agency said.
Flight verification was conducted on independently developed subsystems: propulsion, structure, avionics, communication, tracking, ground support and recovery, it said.
The acquired actual flight data would next serve as a basis for rocket design improvements and the following test flights, the agency said.
TASA Director Wu Jong-shinn (吳宗信) said that Maraho’s rocket design, manufacturing, assembly, integration testing and the test flight were carried out fully by the agency’s research team.
Multiple test flights would be conducted to repeatedly verify critical technologies, rehearse the mission procedures and accumulate team experience, he said.
That would help reduce the development risks for large rocket research and gradually improve Taiwan’s capabilities of developing indigenous orbital launch vehicles, Wu said.
National Cheng Kung University astronautics professor Wu Chih-yung (吳志勇) said that Maraho maintained stable communications with the ground during the whole test flight process and sent back effective flight data.
It has become a successful example of orbital launch vehicle verification, he said.
Feng Chia University aerospace engineering professor Yeh Chun-liang (葉俊良) said the filling process of 90 percent hydrogen peroxide for the hybrid propulsion system is highly complex.
The completion of Maraho’s test flight can be recognized as a successful launch, he said.
The agency said that Maraho was named after Taiwan’s endemic butterfly species, Papilio maraho, or the broad-tailed swallowtail butterfly.
The broad-tailed swallowtail butterfly is known as Taiwan’s national butterfly, featuring broad red tails that resemble the flames trailing behind a rocket during liftoff, it said.
The butterfly species’ specific epithet originated from mrhuw in the Atayal language, meaning “a respectable wise person,” the agency said.
The rocket is expected to help upgrade Taiwan’s independently developed launch vehicle technology, it said.

Interpretive autonomy required
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:31 UTC
01:45:31 KST

Over the past few weeks, domestic and international headlines have been dominated by reports of what was described as a “joint naval drill” between China and Indonesia in the waters east of Taiwan, following an announcement by the Chinese Ministry of National Defense on Tuesday last week.
The two countries conducted the activity the following day, involving the Chinese naval vessel Honghe and the Indonesian Navy frigate KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai (332).
Beijing said that the exercise was intended to enhance the two navies’ operational capabilities, deepen practical cooperation and contribute to regional peace and stability.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council and Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the exercise, saying that China’s “reckless and irresponsible behavior” in repeatedly disregarding international norms and responsibilities continues to escalate regional tensions. The nation also sought clarification from the Indonesian government.
Indonesian officials — including the Indonesian Navy Information Service head and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ spokesperson — said that the activity was not a combat-oriented joint exercise, but rather a passing exercise. Such exercises are routine naval practices conducted when warships traverse a region, serving as a naval diplomacy, rather than a war-fighting drill.
The a passing exercise with China took place while KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai was returning home after participating in the joint exercise Orel-Garuda with Russia.
Technically, a passing exercise is a limited, short-duration exercise with a focus on non-warfighting exercises — in this case including communications drills and maritime replenishment — designed to build communication, trust, good relations and naval brotherhood.
A joint military exercise is normally more structured and deliberately planned, involving multiple phases and more complex scenarios such as simulated combat, amphibious operations or live-fire drills. Indonesia has also conducted similar a passing exercise activities with Japan and the US 7th Fleet, underscoring the routine, non-exclusive nature of these engagements.
Such naval interactions are consistent with Jakarta’s long-standing “free and active” foreign policy and its broader maritime diplomacy, which seeks to open cooperative avenues with a wide range of partners.
However, the concern here is not the technical content of the exercise, but its location. The waters east of Taiwan are geopolitically sensitive, sitting at the heart of cross-strait tensions.
Given this complexity, the combination of foreign participation and a flashpoint location inevitably carries geopolitical and strategic weight, even if it has no direct military impact on Taiwan. Indonesia’s naval presence in these waters, however routine, invites interpretations that transcend its operational intent.
What is particularly revealing is how the narrative around this a passing exercise has evolved, generating divergent readings across the international community. China described the activity as a naval navigation exercise; Taiwan characterized it an attempt to normalize Beijing’s presence in the waters to create a false international impression that China holds jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan; and Indonesia perceived it as a routine passing exercise in service of naval diplomacy.
Modern naval diplomacy is no longer simply about what naval forces physically do at sea. It is also about how those activities are framed, communicated and interpreted. Although Indonesia did not specifically intend to conduct an exercise only with China, the narrative that emerged around the low-intensity naval exercise could carry diplomatic risks and potentially affect Indonesia’s reputation.
This episode highlights a critical lesson: Indonesia must prioritize strategic communication before others define its actions and shape narratives that could misrepresent Indonesia’s intentions. Sensitivity to the operational details and the symbolic geography of any engagement should be carefully considered in foreign policy and defense decisionmaking.
At this level, strategic autonomy alone is insufficient. Indonesia must also cultivate what might be called interpretive autonomy — the capacity to proactively shape the narrative surrounding its actions to reduce misperceptions and maintain constructive relationships with various partners — without being boxed into narratives defined by others.
This is especially pertinent given the upward trajectory of Indonesia-China defense ties. Last year, the two countries held their inaugural 2+2 foreign and defense ministerial meeting, a clear sign of deepening strategic engagement.
Indonesia is also reportedly exploring defense industrial cooperation with China, including the potential procurement of 42 Chengdu J-10C fighter jets.
Under Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s administration, Jakarta has visibly expanded its defense cooperation beyond the traditional partner such as the US, reaching out to Beijing and Moscow.
The overarching message is clear: Even routine, low-level naval cooperation carries diplomatic weight when situated in contested waters.
Indonesia must ensure that its actions are clearly communicated — so that a standard naval interaction does not inadvertently entangle it in a diplomatic framing that distorts its true intentions.
Marina Ika Sari is this year’s Japan Foundation Southeast Asia Partnership visiting fellow and a researcher at The Habibie Center.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.
EDITORIAL CARTOON
Grab Holdings Ltd plans to acquire Taiwan’s No. 1 food delivery business, Foodpanda, for US$600 million. The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) is reviewing the proposal. Grab offers ride-hailing, dining, fresh food and grocery delivery, parcel delivery, payments, loans, insurance and digital banking services in 900 cities across eight Southeast Asian countries. Leveraging mapping data and artificial intelligence (AI) models developed in cooperation with China, it has built a comprehensive retail and consumer ecosystem. If Grab were to enter the Taiwanese market, it would have a major impact on the food service industry, convenience stores, supermarkets and e-commerce services. The ecosystem
On Wednesday last week an Indonesian frigate conducted exercises with the Chinese navy east of Taiwan, in waters Beijing has repeatedly used to demonstrate its capacity to encircle and blockade the nation. What was Indonesia doing there? The answer comes readily from Jakarta. Indonesia was practising bebas aktif, or “free and active” foreign policy, working with competing powers while reserving the right to belong to none of them. Indonesian personnel joined the US-led RIMPAC exercises in Hawaii this year, military contacts with Russia have continued, and the KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai met the Chinese frigate Honghe while sailing home from

Taiwan in Time: Vanished on Qilai Mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:30 UTC
01:45:30 KST

Aug. 24 to Aug. 30
Three pairs of chopsticks, stuck upright in the ground like incense, have become one of the most curious details in the story of three university graduates who disappeared on Qilai Mountain (奇萊) in 1972.
The case remains unsolved today. Despite an extensive two-month search, the three men’s bodies were never found. The incident came just a year after five National Tsing Hua University students died on the mountain on July 25, 1971, after being unexpectedly caught in a typhoon, prompting serious concerns about hiking safety.
Photo courtesy of National Taitung Living Art Center
Tunghai University graduate Chiu Kao (邱高) and Fu Jen Catholic University students Lee Fu-ming (李福明) and Hu Te-ning (胡德寧) were reportedly experienced hikers with sufficient wilderness survival skills, and had with them a transistor radio. Chiu wanted to summit Qilai Main Peak, part of the notorious “Black Qilai” range, known for its treacherous terrain, mercurial weather, thick fog and frequent accidents.
Reports in Wilderness Magazine (野外) say that Chiu’s original application was for the Nengao Traversing Trail (能高越嶺步道), but the three men changed their route on their own and headed for Qilai Main Peak, which was not advisable without a guide.
This case gave rise to supernatural legends and rumors that the mountain was haunted, while a mysterious “ghost photo” taken in 1996 prompted another month-long search for the hikers’ remains.
Photo courtesy of Wilderness Magazine
While their fate remains unknown, reports show that the Chiu Kao Incident helped spur the development of mountain search and rescue in Taiwan. Permanent civilian rescue groups sprang up afterward, building their skills through training and operations.
MASSIVE SEARCH
The hikers began their ascent from the Lushan Checkpoint (廬山) on Aug. 23, reaching Taipower’s Tianchi Wiring Maintenance Station (天池保線所), where they spent the night in the lodge. They left the following morning. It was the last confirmed sighting of the trio.
Photo courtesy of National Central Library
Chiu’s father reported the three men missing to police on Sept. 4. However, another three young men had stayed at the Dayuling Lodge (大禹嶺) the previous night and descended the mountain the following day, leading authorities to believe they were Chiu and his companions. This mistake delayed the rescue operations until Chiu’s father, still waiting for his son to return, called the authorities again on Sept. 9.
On Sept. 11, police from Nantou and Hualien counties finally began searching for the three men, assisted by Indigenous guides. The Air Force also dispatched a plane from Hsinchu Air Base, but found nothing.
The search soon intensified. The Air Force sent two helicopters and four planes, while ground teams found two white undershirts. On Sept. 14, searchers discovered writing scratched into the ground with a rock past Kalulou Peak. Most of it was illegible, but it appeared to indicate that the hikers had passed the most dangerous section of the route.
Still, there was no sign of the men. The Army also joined the search, while civic mountaineering associations began sending teams led by veteran climbers. More than 300 people had taken part by then.
On Sept. 19, the Chinese Alpine Association (中華民國山岳協會) dispatched a team of 15 experienced mountaineers and 25 Indigenous guides, led by Tsai Ching-chang (蔡景璋), one of Taiwan’s famed “Four Heavenly Kings of Mountaineering” (see “Taiwan in Time: The making of Taiwan’s ‘100 Peaks Club,’” May 17, 2026). Fellow “Heavenly King” Lin Wen-an (林文安) was also on the roster. With seven teams of 75 people searching in the rain, they still came back empty handed.
UPRIGHT CHOPSTICKS?
Photo courtesy of the Taichung National Park Administration
Nearly two weeks into the search, there was finally a breakthrough on Sept. 24. The United Daily News reported that Tseng Lung-hua’s (曾龍華) volunteer search team first found half a piece of bread on the ground west of Qilai Main Peak. Upon closer inspection, they found four mountaineering-association membership cards, two spoons, a ticket to the Provincial Museum and three pairs of chopsticks stuck in the ground pointing toward the sky. The China Times reported the same.
However, the Central Daily News reported finding two pairs of chopsticks and did not specify how they were placed. Searchers also detected a suspicious odor in the area, but a few days later discovered that it came from a decomposing mountain goat. And the 2005 book, History of Taiwan Mountaineering (台灣登山史) by Lee Hsi-sheng (李希聖) makes no mention of the chopsticks. However, the detail appears in most modern articles discussing the incident.
The search continued to expand, drawing in more people. On Nov. 7, the United Daily News reported that Chiu’s father, who had spent the previous 60 days in Hualien and Nantou, was returning briefly to Taipei. Tseng reportedly told him, “As long as Mr. Chiu doesn’t give up, I’ll keep helping until we get some answers.”
However, winter soon arrived. The snow made the mountains inaccessible, bringing the search to an end.
THE AFTERMATH
In September 1995, the United Daily News ran an article about the impact of the Chiu Kao Incident. It noted that the search and rescue efforts were of an unprecedented scale, mobilizing thousands of people.
Jen Tie-gang (任鐵鋼), then-head of the Taiwan Mountain Rescue Association, said that prior to this, operations were focused on “rescue,” as in most cases they knew where the hikers were.
Tsai told the paper that it was extremely bizarre that such an extensive search had uncovered so few clues about what happened to Chiu and his companions. He suggested that the three chopsticks stuck in the ground were meant to signal, “Come save us!” Yet aside from that, he said, there was little trace of them anywhere else in the mountains.
Rumors circulated that the three men had been attacked by wild animals, killed by robbers or even faked their deaths and secretly left the country.
“The concept of mountain search and rescue took root from this incident,” the article stated. “Permanent civilian rescue organizations were subsequently established, while repeated experience and training gradually refined search-and-rescue methods.”
“All of this can be said to trace back to the Chiu Kao Incident.”
A final chapter in the saga came about 10 years later. A hiker took a photo on the grassy plain between Nanhua Mountain and Qilai South Peak that showed a mysterious human figure in the distance, standing at an improbable spot high on the mountain. Hu Te-ning’s mother reportedly recognized the jacket the figure was wearing as one she had bought for her son, prompting one final search mission — that still yielded no results.

Even if Taiwan and the United States take steps to better prepare for a Chinese blockade, they face a greater threat from China than analysts previously believed.” The authors

Mentally ill prisoners need better options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:29 UTC
01:45:29 KST

There is a prisoner with a severe psychiatric disorder, exhibiting detachment from reality to the extent that they are unable to manage their own affairs, refusing treatment for nearly two years. Although this person continues to talk to themselves and experiences auditory hallucinations, paranoia and agitation, prison authorities can only place them in solitary confinement to prevent them from harming others.
This person with schizophrenia was sentenced to five years in prison for aggravated assault and other offenses, and is due to be released in a few months. From a psychiatrist’s perspective, it is simply absurd that a severely mentally ill person who has a history of aggravated assault cannot receive treatment in prison, leaving authorities to watch helplessly as they are released while still symptomatic.
This is not only a gap in the social safety net, but is unfair to people with psychiatric illnesses.
Correctional facilities are required to act in accordance with the law. Article 46 of the Mental Health Act (精神衛生法) states that “if correctional authorities, rehabilitation disposition facilities, and other institutions or facilities intended for detention and reformation have a patient or a person suspected of having the condition specified in Subparagraph 1 of Paragraph 1 of Article 3, they shall provide medical care or escort and assist such people in seeking medical care, and carry out the measures in a compulsory manner if necessary.” In this case, the correctional facility has provided psychiatric care, but the person has refused treatment. As they pose no risk of harming themselves or others, the facility has no legal basis to escort them to a hospital or apply for involuntary hospitalization.
However, the act actually provides a solution.
Article 54 of the act provides for compulsory “community treatment.” It states that if a severe patient “is not following medical advice, which is causing an unstable health condition or a risk of declining function, and the specialist doctor deems it necessary for the patient to receive community treatment, the local competent authority of the patient’s domicile or residence and the community mental health center must work together with the protector to help the patient access community treatment.”
The person in this case appears to meet the criteria for compulsory community treatment, and conducting that treatment while they are still in prison would be the most practical option. Medical personnel could make regular visits to administer medications, providing the most effective way to ensure continued care.
However, the authorities reportedly believe that a correctional facility is not a community, and therefore, compulsory community treatment cannot be applied for or carried out there. In my view, this is an unnecessarily restrictive interpretation of the law. In practice, compulsory community treatment is generally provided in people’s homes.
Article 5 of the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s guidelines for the home-based treatment of people with mental disorders (精神疾病病人居家治療標準) states that home-based treatment involves personnel providing professional services at a person’s residence or place of living. It does not restrict such treatment to a person’s own home.
In practice, people with mental disorders residing in nursing or residential care facilities also commonly receive home-based treatment.
I hope that the Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Health and Welfare and other government agencies would recognize the importance of treating incarcerated people with psychiatric illnesses and take steps to prevent these gaps in the social safety net.
Lin Jin-jia is a psychiatrist.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Lawmakers pass motion condemning the premier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:28 UTC
01:45:28 KST

Opposition lawmakers voted on Friday to fast-track a motion condemning Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) following his refusal to countersign legislation on creating savings accounts for youth passed by the legislature, alongside other bills.
The motion, proposed by the Taiwan People’s Party, accused the Democratic Progressive Party administration of “repeatedly abusing authority under the Constitution” to invalidate legislation passed by the legislature.
“Not only does this exceed official authority and disrupt the separation of powers, but it also treats the legislature with complete disregard,” the proposal read.
Photo: CNA
With the support from the main opposition Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), the proposal skipped committee review and moved directly to a second reading, setting up a potential vote in as soon as a month.
Under the legal system, a legislative motion to censure the premier is symbolic only, with no binding force or statutory authority.
Cho announced on Monday last week he would not countersign the Youth Development and Future Account Act (台灣兒少成長及未來帳戶條例), a bill creating government-funded accounts for Taiwanese under the age of 18, and an amendment to the Cable Radio and Television Act, passed by the opposition-controlled legislation.
Article 37 of the Constitution of the Republic of China stipulates that laws passed by the Legislature must be countersigned by the premier before the president can formally enact them.
The opposition argues that this authority serves as a check on presidential power, not on the Legislature, and that the premier should request a re-vote if the government does not support a law.
No premier had ever taken such action to block a law passed by the Legislature before December last year when Cho first declined to countersign the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法).
Since then, Cho has refused to sign legislation seven times, including amendments to legislative governance rules.
Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) slammed Cho on Thursday for “weaponizing” his countersign authority, calling the move a mistake.
Responding to Han, Executive Yuan Secretary-General Xavier Chang (張惇涵) said on Friday that Article 37 of the Constitution requires Cho to take action to “uphold the constitutional order.”
The Executive Yuan refused to countersign the bill on constitutional and equity grounds, contending that the measure encroaches on its constitutional authority to manage policies and the national budget, that allowing corporate sponsorship of the accounts could widen the wealth gap, and that vague tax exemptions violate the principle of taxation by law, its statement said.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:23 UTC
01:45:23 KST

A fire and subsequent explosion in a residential area in Tainan early yesterday injured 15 people and damaged 68 homes, the Tainan City Fire Bureau said.
The bureau said it received a report at 1:12am yesterday that a pile of waste in a vacant lot in Annan District’s (安南) Haidian Road had caught fire and exploded, adding that it dispatched 144 firefighters and 53 firetrucks to battle the blaze and evacuate nearby residents.
It took more than four hours to extinguish the fire, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Tainan City Government’s Environmental Protection Bureau
The incident damaged 11 privately owned vehicles, as well as eight fire engines, one ambulance and two disaster assessment vehicles, the bureau said.
The three homes closest to the blast site sustained the most severe damage, it added.
Twelve people and three firefighters were injured, sustaining cuts to the head or other minor injuries, the bureau said, adding that no one was seriously hurt.
The Tainan City Government’s air quality and pollutant sampling data showed no abnormalities after the incident.
A man surnamed Yang (楊) allegedly managed the land, allowing a Kaohsiung waste operator to illegally dump trash outside its jurisdiction in contravention of the Waste Disposal Act (廢棄物清理法), the bureau said, citing a police investigation.
The case has been referred to prosecutors, while the Kaohsiung Environmental Protection Bureau has been notified about conducting a joint investigation, it said.
Tainan Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲), who had been visiting Singapore, flew home after learning of the incident and arrived at the scene last night to assess the damage.
The city government would prioritize helping affected residents find temporary accommodation and restore their homes, he said, adding that lawyers would be hired to help them seek compensation and hold those responsible accountable.
The city government has activated emergency housing and relief measures for the 11 households that were most severely affected, Huang said.
Each household would receive NT$20,000 in emergency assistance, and civil engineers would be brought in to assess the structural safety of the homes to provide a basis for subsequent repairs and compensation claims, he added.

The Ciaotou District Court on Friday ruled that Chinese immigrant Zhou Manzhi (周滿芝) must serve an additional 18 months in prison for contravening the Anti-infiltration Act (反滲透法) after intervening in Taiwanese elections under orders from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
Zhou had once been a member of the Shanxi Province Patriotic Volunteer Association and the China Patriotism Volunteer Association, groups whose core missions are to promote Beijing’s “united front” rhetoric, the ruling said.
The court accepted the argument that the associations were controlled by the CCP’s United Front Work Department, a ministerial-level agency reporting directly to the party’s Central Committee.
Photo: Taipei Times
The associations are legally defined as sources of infiltration, and Zhou followed the instructions of such organizations in founding the Kaohsiung New Immigrants Care Association and the Taiwan New Immigrants Care Foundation to promote the “united front” rhetoric, the ruling said.
During the 2024 elections, Zhou used her influence with new immigrants to garner votes for Labor Party legislator candidate Zhan Xiuying (湛秀英) at in-person rallies and online, the ruling said.
The collegiate bench presiding over the case found that Zhou intended to increase the number of Chinese spouses in legislative seats to raise the number of pro-China voices within the government.
Zhou obeyed orders from a foreign force despite knowing the CCP’s intentions to infiltrate Taiwan militarily, culturally and through diplomatic actions, the ruling said.
Separate charges against Zhou of accepting Chinese hospitality, spreading falsified polls and garnering votes for then-independent presidential candidate Terry Gou (郭台銘) were dropped, the ruling said.
Co-defendant in the case Hsu Wei-fu (徐維甫) was handed one year and 10 months in prison, while Wang Min (王敏), Hsu’s girlfriend, was given a sentence of one year of prison with a four-year deferral.
Taiwan New Immigrants Care Foundation secretary-general Kuo Yung-tsung (郭永聰) was found not guilty of related charges.
The ruling can still be appealed.

Stars selling Greece to a new wave of US tourists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:45:13 UTC
01:45:13 KST

The idyllic beaches of the Greek islands have long been a draw for European holidaymakers, but now a new wave of US tourists is waking up to their charms, driven by stars such as Madonna, Katy Perry and Justin Bieber.
Madonna celebrated her 68th birthday on Corfu, sharing a whirl of parties and boat trips against the backdrop of the island’s landscape with her 20 million Instagram followers — earning her rapturous thanks from Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
Experts say the huge popularity of Christopher Nolan blockbuster The Odyssey would only fuel the trend — although holidaymakers would be hoping for an easier trip home than the one endured by Matt Damon’s eponymous hero.
Photo: Reuters
While Madonna partied in Corfu, singer Bieber took his family to the Peloponnese. Perry and her partner, former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, sampled the delights of Mykonos.
All of them chronicled their holidays on social media, giving the Greek tourism industry a massive hit of free advertising.
“Celebrities are voting for the Greek summer,” public broadcaster ERT said on Friday, devoting a report to these stars from across the Atlantic.
The newspaper To Vima hailed this “new wave” which “helps raise the country’s international profile.” It cited British singer and actress Rita Ora, who shared her holidays with “her millions of followers” on social media.
Paris Tsartas, professor of tourism development at Harokopio University in Athens, said the deluge of celebrity endorsements gave Greece a powerful boost as a summer destination — particularly with the lucrative US market.
After a decade of financial woes following the debt crisis of 2009, and the devastation of the COVID-19 pandemic, Greece has pumped money into the sector, which accounts for about 30 percent of GDP, according to the Association of Greek Tourism Enterprises (SETE).
About 1.55 million Americans visited Greece last year. They represent the third-largest source of tourism income, behind Germans and Britons, with an average spend per tourist of 1,120 euros (US$1,308), the SETE said.
To answer growing demand, the main US airlines have significantly stepped up services, American Airlines increasing its total available seat capacity by 30 percent compared with summer last year. This year Greece has had its highest-ever number of direct flights, with 103 connections a week between Athens and the US.
Some of the new enthusiasm is driven by the phenomenon of “set-jetting” — people traveling to a destination after seeing it in a movie or TV series.
In a study for online travel giant Expedia, 13 percent of American travelers said they had booked a trip after seeing a destination on screen. Greece is well acquainted with the trend, after hit musical Mamma Mia, filmed on the island of Skopelos, triggered a jump in US visitors.
Tsartas predicted The Odyssey would have a similar impact. Key parts of Nolan’s film, recounting the travails of Damon’s Odysseus as he seeks to return home from the Trojan war to his wife Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, were shot in the Peloponnese region of Greece. According to EasyJet Holidays, cited by ,
Bookings to Greece increased by 18 percent in the weeks following the film’s international release in last month, the Greek newspaper Kathimerini cited EasyJet Holidays as saying.
There is more small-screen exposure for Greece’s charms to come: Netflix had chosen the country for the sixth season of hit series Emily in Paris.
Lead actress Lily Collins and the rest of the production team were spotted this spring in Mykonos, Paros and Santorini.

Takaichi confronts her mentor’s mixed foreign policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:11 UTC
01:45:11 KST

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has inherited a lot of things from her mentor, the late prime minister Shinzo Abe: Her support base, conservative credentials, and even her favored slogan of “Japan is back.”
This is true of foreign policy, too. The sight of US President Donald Trump pulling the rug from under one of the US’ closest allies by ordering joint military drills with South Korea to be scaled back is but one reminder of the risks and rewards of Abe’s playbook in dealing with Washington. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to islands controlled by Russia but claimed by Japan drags up the late premier’s biggest international failure. And talk of summits with North Korea recalls an event that made Abe’s early career, before turning to bitter regret.
Takaichi should put a little distance between herself and her mentor, and work through a new foreign policy to decide what should stay and what should go.
Illustration: Tania Chou
Start with Trump. Japan’s leader can learn many of the right lessons from his relationship with Abe. Whatever Trump’s true reason for abruptly hamstringing the South Korea drills — his affinity for North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, Seoul’s supposed failure to help with Iran or, as reports suggest, the slow pace of investment in the US — the move has startled Tokyo. Officials are no doubt concerned that as in 2018, Trump will increase demands on Japan ahead of the midterm elections.
One of Abe’s greatest diplomatic achievements was showing the world how to engage with the capricious president. He understood earlier than most that dealing with Trump meant flattery, copious reciprocity, big promises of spending, and a willingness to hold one’s nose. Despite periodic calls for higher spending on US troops and increased imports of US cars, Japan remains one of the few traditional allies that has largely dodged his opprobrium.
Takaichi has mostly followed that model, and for now Tokyo looks better placed than Seoul. She has turned US demands for investment into an opportunity to secure rare-earth and energy projects that will boost economic security. And she understands that Trump does not care if these do not add up to US$550 billion — the official amount Japan agreed to invest during last year’s tariff war — so long as he gets a good headline.
There are lessons to take away from Abe’s dealings with North Korea, too, amid reports that the US president is looking for another summit with Kim. As a young politician, Abe made his career with his hardline stance during then-Japanese prime minister Junichiro Koizumi’s historic summit with Kim’s father, Kim Jong-il, in 2002, which paved the way for the return of some of the Japanese citizens that North Korea had kidnapped.
Abe also sensibly avoided being used as a tool by Pyongyang, a concern that does not seem to bother Trump. Japanese media reported following his assassination four years ago that Abe had rejected a 2014 proposal to repatriate just two of the abductees, something he deemed a bad deal. Yet he was never able to secure his own visit to Pyongyang as leader, and was sidelined by Trump’s overtures to Kim.
Takaichi must similarly balance the risks of being bypassed against those of being used as a political pawn. Having taken up the abductee issue herself, a summit with North Korea would be a potential political win.
The question is leverage: This is a very different state from the impoverished one in 2002. Arms sales to Russia and crypto thefts leave Pyongyang with a diminished need for assistance. Without tangible results, Takaichi should not lend legitimacy to the Kim regime in return for a mere photo op.
For all his clear-eyed vision on China, Abe had a terminal blind spot for Putin. He burned years of political capital seeking a deal to reclaim the territory Moscow calls the southern Kurils and Japan dubs the Northern Territories, seized by the Soviet Union in the dying days of World War II. It was the unfinished legacy of his own father, Shintaro, who as foreign minister believed he could break the impasse.
Shinzo Abe held summits with Putin, seeking “hot-tub diplomacy” at an onsen resort, while officials from a northern prefecture gifted the Russian president an adorable dog. All to no avail, with Putin stringing Japan on so long that the dog died of old age last year.
Any attempt to restart such talks should stay dead, too, but there are concerning signs that some around the prime minister want to return to this failed strategy, and re-engage with Moscow. Takaichi is notably the only G7 leader yet to hold a bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. She must not make the same mistake Shinzo Abe did: allowing the ghosts of the past to dictate the present.
Shinzo Abe’s skill was in understanding that personal relations could create room for Japan where it might be militarily outmatched, but his mistake was sometimes to confuse relationships with actual results. Takaichi needs to know the difference.
Indeed, it is important to know when to change tactics when needed. That is what Shinzo Abe, at his best, would have done.
Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan and the Koreas. He previously led the breaking news team in North Asia, and was the Tokyo deputy bureau chief. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.
