====================================================================================================

Huckabee attends screening of ‘The Bridge,’ about Israelis finding joy through music after Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:14 UTC
17:00:14 KST

The Bridge, a documentary about 10 Israelis whose lives were shattered by the October 7 attacks and who traveled to Los Angeles to rediscover the joy of making music at the legendary Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp, was shown at an emotional screening at the Menachem Begin Heritage Center in Jerusalem this week. The audience included US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and several of the Israelis featured in the film.
Huckabee, an enthusiastic musician who has played bass guitar for decades, said the film moved him deeply. “Music has the power to take our worst moments and help us to put them behind us,” Huckabee said. Songs, he said, express “our struggles, our trials, our tears, and our joys. That is why music is so powerful.”
He thanked the Israelis who took part in the film, as well as David Fishof, Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp’s founder and director, who also attended the screening, for allowing the audience “to see the power and the healing that music brings.”
That idea that music can provide a way back into life after devastating trauma is at the center of The Bridge.
The tagline for the movie is, “Ten survivors. One way to rock,” and that captures the essence of the film.
The Bridge, which was produced by Kevin S. Bright (who addressed the audience via video) and directed by Brad Allgood, follows a group of young Israelis affected directly by October 7 as they travel to Los Angeles for the Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp, where participants rehearse, form bands, take master classes, and perform with veteran rock musicians. Musicians who performed with bands such as Guns N’ Roses, Van Halen, and Black Sabbath mentored the Israelis.
The movie opens with clips of the October 7 attacks and features interviews with the 10 camp participants about how they survived that day. Among them was Tuval Haim, whose brother, Yotam, also a musician, was kidnapped by Hamas. Yotam managed to escape but was killed in a tragic instance of friendly fire. Another participant, Bar Rudaeff, had to cope with the kidnapping of his father, Lior, on October 7. After the conclusion of the rock camp, Rudaeff learned that his father had been murdered.
Nova survivor describes her emotions after October 7
Raz Shifer, a Nova survivor, spoke in the film about feeling tormented about why she survived when so many around her were killed. Throughout The Bridge, she takes every opportunity to speak out for the release of the hostages, including Romi Gonen, her friend’s sister. Ben King of Kibbutz Be’eri tells about how he survived with his wife in their safe room after terrorists entered their home and set it on fire.
Valeria Dvorkin sat alone in the safe room of her house in Kibbutz Nir Am with her dog for over 24 hours, hearing fighting outside. Many of her friends were killed and kidnapped, including Emily Damari, who was released in early 2025, as well as twins Gali and Ziv Berman, who were ultimately brought home in October 2025. Dov Engel, a reservist, was wounded while fighting in the South on October 8.
All 10 suffered devastating losses, and all had a passion for music prior to the attack, but most said they stopped playing music in the aftermath. Watching them gradually open up to each other and to the musicians and rock-camp participants, and begin to find joy through music again, however haltingly, is incredibly moving.
At the discussion following the screening, Fishof said that one of the most important parts of the experience was not only giving the Israelis a chance to play alongside famous musicians, but putting them in a room with Americans who, in many cases, had never met an Israeli. The camp itself became a kind of bridge in precisely the way the documentary’s title suggests.
“It was just so amazing to see how we changed all these people’s visions about Israel,” Fishof said. “And that these guys could rock out too.”
The trip took place in March 2024, when anti-Israel demonstrations were intensifying in the United States. Fishof and some of the other organizers said they had been genuinely nervous about how the Israeli delegation would be received. But when the group was introduced to the other rock-camp participants, and they told their stories, the response was overwhelmingly warm.
Sam Grundwerg, world chairman of Keren Hayesod–UIA (United Israel Appeal), who helped organize the project and who attended the screening, recalled how the Israelis were embraced by the other campers and by the musicians.
“What we’re hoping that it will do is for people that love music, that genre or any genre, people who are brought in by this human story,” Grundwerg said. “They’re also hearing these stories about real people and about real horrific things that they went through on October 7.”
Fishof said former Skid Row singer Sebastian Bach, who knew little about Israel or October 7 before he met the Israeli delegation, came to love them. Bach subsequently posted publicly in support of Israel, including posting the phrase, “Am Yisrael Chai.”
Israeli film participants discuss the meaning behind the trip
For the Israeli participants, the trip was about reclaiming parts of their lives that had become inaccessible after October 7.
Valeria Dvorkin, one of the participants in the Jerusalem screening, said that after October 7, she found herself unable even to listen to music.
“It was very difficult to hear music after October 7. Even in my car, in my room,” she said.
But the Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp experience changed that. “After this experience, I am running on it, full power,” she said. “I’m doing music. It fills me. It makes me happy. So, I think it helps me all the time.”
She has continued making music with Rudaeff, who also attended the screening.
“You appreciate, first, that you live to enjoy this experience, and then, again, that people are fighting for the freedom that we have,” Rudaeff said at the screening. “So even though you experience fighting, you also feel grateful.”
He described how his family discussed what song should accompany his father’s burial, after Lior’s remains were returned to Israel in 2025, since music had always been such an important part of Lior’s life. The family chose Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven.” As the last bits of earth were placed on the grave, he said, the final notes of the song were playing.
“It was the way to be buried for him,” he said.
Only after the burial, Rudaeff said, did he feel that he could begin focusing more fully on his own life again. He has since built a music studio in Tel Aviv and returned to creating music.
Fishof said the experience convinced him that it was time to bring Rock Camp to Israel.
“Sam and I, I think our goal is to bring Rock Camp here, and to really have these rock stars come and share their music.”
He said he also hopes to give Israelis affected by the war opportunities to write songs and work directly with professional musicians.
“We want to give this opportunity to people to get into writing songs and meeting these celebrities and change people’s lives through music.”
Fishof spoke about how the recent wave of antisemitism following October 7 had affected him.
“All my life… I never had any problems, I worked with rock stars, never had problems,” he said. “But when I made this film... for the first time in my entire career, I really felt it,” said Fishof, a former sports and music agent who produced many revival tours.
He said he had difficulty obtaining the rights to one song the participants played and hoped to use in The Bridge, adding that the Tribeca Festival rejected The Bridge because its selection committee feared it would be considered too pro-Israel.
But while he has recently encountered some anti-Israel sentiment, he emphasized that others were happy to help with the Rock Camp journey. He recalled that songwriter Linda Perry heard Dvorkin perform one of her songs and allowed the production to use it without charge. Award-winning songwriter Diane Warren contributed a peace song for the Israeli participants to perform, and he said that gestures like these encouraged him.
It all went back to Huckabee’s heartfelt words immediately following the screening: “Music is able to touch us where we are,” he said, “and take us where we need to be.”

Layers of history: Egypt unearths 6,000-year cemetery spanning Predynastic to Ptolemaic eras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:08 UTC
17:00:08 KST

Egyptian archaeologists unearthed an ancient cemetery whose roots stretch back through the Greco-Roman era to the Predynastic period, the Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced earlier this month.
Discovered at the Kom El-Khalgan archaeological site in Dakahlia Governorate, the oldest finds at the site date back to the Lower Egyptian prehistoric cultures, Buto I and Buto II, in the first half of the fourth millennium BCE.
In the cemetery, archaeologists found a group of tombs with simple oval pits carved into the sandy layer, containing remains buried in various funerary positions, indicating the different burial rites of the time.
The tombs were also characterized by the simplicity of their funerary furnishings, such as small handmade pottery vessels and some seashells, even though the density of burials point to the area being heavily populated at the time.
A second group of tombs dating to Egypt’s Second Intermediate Period (circa 1782 to 1550 BCE) to the New Kingdom era, were also found at the site.
Confirms settlement in region during Hyksos’ reign
The finds confirm that the area had been settled during the Hyksos’ reign during the 15th Dynasty given its proximity to Avaris, which had served as the capital city at the time.
Among this group, the there are two styles of tombs: mastabas, which are flat-roofed, rectangular structures with inward sloping sides, and tombs with cornices.
Similar to the earlier group of burials, preliminary research here points to a diverse set of burial positions, varied age groups, and funerary customs.
Funerary furnishings found within these tombs include jewelry, amulets, scarabs, bronze tools and weapons, pottery vessels and Tell el-Yahudiyeh (TEY) style juglets.
A mudbrick tomb containing a collection of pottery vessels and bronze tools and dating back to the early Eighteenth Dynasty was also found.
From the Ptolemaic period, excavations revealed a number of simple burial pits, including the burial of a child inside two amphorae that had been reused as a burial vessel.
Remains of ancient residential buildings also found
Alongside the cemetery, archaeologists also uncovered the remains of residential area dating to the Second Intermediate Period, including mudbrick buildings, grain storage silos, ovens, and hearths.
Surrounding the residential and funerary infastructure, researchers at the dig found a group of sinusoidal (wavy) walls, commonly seen in Egyptian architecture between the Middle and New kingdoms.
As well, the excavations yielded a collection of other artifacts, including pottery vessels, stone tools, and large quantities of fish, bird, and animal bones.
The foundations of a building with thick mudbrick walls, pottery shards, and stone tools dating to the beginning of the New Kingdom were also found.
Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy praised the archaeologists efforts and affirmed the importance of the find.
Dr. Hisham El-Leithy. Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities secretary-general, noted that the discoveries offers insight into ancient settlement patterns, funerary practices, and the way people interacted with nature in antiquity.
He added that excavations at the site are still ongoing.

Ferguson job losses were entirely avoidable warns Sweeney
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:55:30 BST
16:55:30 KST

The decision to place the first phase of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme with a Polish yard rather than Ferguson Marine directly caused the job losses now being announced at Port Glasgow, Paul Sweeney MSP has told the UK Defence Journal.
Ferguson Marine confirmed on Tuesday that it had opened a voluntary redundancy programme expected to see up to 70 employees leave, around a quarter of the workforce, as work on the ferry Glen Rosa winds down.
Mr Sweeney, a former shipyard worker and Labour MSP for Glasgow, said: “This is yet another example of the completely incoherent industrial policy of the Scottish Government over many years. We’ve had over half a billion pounds worth of shipbuilding contracts awarded to overseas shipyards in the last four years, and not a single contract awarded to Ferguson Marine, despite the shipyard being under the ownership of the Scottish Government.”
He said one government agency had excluded another government-owned asset from bidding for work. “Caledonian Maritime Assets Ltd froze out another government-owned asset, Ferguson Marine, from even tendering for the Lord of the Isles ferry replacement recently, and instead shortlisted only overseas shipyards and essentially drafted the tendering qualification requirements to exclude any British shipyard.
“This is completely perverse, and it shows that we are seeing a government risk averse and run by essentially lawyers rather than by people with an understanding of industrial and engineering policy and what will produce good economic outcomes, prosperous jobs, and a thriving competitive industrial base in our shipbuilding sector.”
‘A criminally negligent opportunity missed’
Mr Sweeney was most critical of the phase one award, which went to Remontowa in Gdansk.
He said: “They could have awarded directly to Ferguson Marine the phase one of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme. Instead, they gave it to Remontowa in Gdansk in Poland. That decision alone has directly caused these job losses at Ferguson Marine.
“They could have, and as has been demonstrated by their subsequent stated intention to directly award phase two of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme to Ferguson Marine, shown that all along they could have directly awarded that phase one contract for those relatively straightforward, repeatable series build ferries to Ferguson Marine.
“That would have given them a robust drumbeat of orders and a stable production cycle through the whole shipyard, going right through from steel production and fabrication to outfitting trades, and then the sea trials and so on. So you have every part of the shipyard flowing well, and you’ve got that flowline production model going.”
He said the opportunity to put the yard into what he called ferry factory mode had been squandered. “It’s astonishing, the incompetence around not doing that and not using that opportunity with the Small Vessel Replacement Programme to get Ferguson Marine into basically a ferry factory mode. That could have been the game changer there. And it’s a criminally negligent opportunity missed.”
Why the work has run out
Sweeney set out the immediate cause of the crunch at the yard, pointing to the end of subcontract work alongside the completion of the ferry. He said: “The Scottish Government have been in no rush to verify their ability to award that second phase contract to Ferguson Marine. They’ve been dragging their heels on that now for months, and we’ve now seen the consequences of that. The lack of mobilisation at the yard as Glen Rosa leaves, there’s simply no work coming through. The BAE Systems subcontract for Type 26 has come to a conclusion, so that is why we’re seeing this crunch for the shipyard, and it’s completely avoidable.”
On the loss of skills, he said: “It’s devastating to see that institutional memory being eroded, that critical mass of skills being undermined, because they’re very hard to re-establish once you lose them. It is simply going to make it more expensive, more difficult for that shipyard to be competitive in the medium to long term if you lose that capacity. You can’t just flick it on and off like a light switch.”
The subsidy control argument
Sweeney also said he had put forward a legal route for direct awards and been rebuffed.
He said: “I have repeatedly tried to offer constructive suggestions to the Scottish Government over several years now about how they can get this to work properly. Most recently, I spelled out quite clearly the opportunities in the Subsidy Control Act to directly award using national security provisions, and they simply responded with a load of legalistic guff.
“It has subsequently been made clear by the Treasury and by the Cabinet Office that national security powers can be used to directly award contracts in the shipbuilding sector, and are actively encouraging government agencies to do this. So why the Scottish Government isn’t using this massive opportunity with the verification provided by the UK Government to directly award is beyond me.
They need to get a grip and get a grip quickly, because lives, livelihoods, and people’s wellbeing are at stake here, as well as the future existence of a shipbuilding industry in Scotland. It’s not unexpected news, but it’s certainly something I thought we could have avoided. And the government ministers seem to be completely asleep at the wheel, as this thing unravels on their watch.”
He also pointed to the wider pipeline, noting that the National Shipbuilding Strategy identified a cross-government pipeline of orders over the next 30 years, and that Scotland is seeing what he described as massive leakage of that pipeline overseas.
Defending the yard’s record
Sweeney has also pushed back on the suggestion that Ferguson Marine’s own track record has made it an unattractive prospect for commercial customers, “It successfully completed a major frigate fabrication contract for BAE Systems recently. Many shipyards have had bad contracts in the past and successfully rebounded, but you need some fundamentals to sustain a commercial shipbuilding industry, and state financing is one of them.”
He argued that heavy industry of this kind cannot operate without state involvement anywhere. “Shipbuilding is similar to aerospace, in that the barriers to entry are so high that the state inevitably becomes involved in some way. Even Europe’s most successful shipbuilding firm, Meyer Werft in Lower Saxony, was jointly nationalised by the state and federal governments in 2024, but it then secured a 10 billion Euro contract with MSC Cruises last year. The problem is that the Scottish Government just tinkered with state intervention rather than taking the comprehensive measures necessary to be effective and competitive internationally.”
‘The yard has a record’
Asked publicly on social media whether the yard’s record would deter commercial customers, Mr Sweeney rejected the idea that its history rules it out of future work.
He said: “It successfully completed a major frigate fabrication contract for BAE Systems recently. Many shipyards have had bad contracts in the past and successfully rebounded, but you need some fundamentals to sustain a commercial shipbuilding industry, and state financing is one of them.”
On why the state has a role at all, he said: “Shipbuilding is similar to aerospace, in that the barriers to entry are so high that the state inevitably becomes involved in some way. Even Europe’s most successful shipbuilding firm, Meyer Werft in Lower Saxony, was jointly nationalised by the state and federal governments in 2024, but it then secured a 10 billion euro contract with MSC Cruises last year.”
He said the failure was not intervention as such but the extent of it. “The problem is that the Scottish Government just tinkered with state intervention rather than taking the comprehensive measures necessary to be effective and competitive internationally.”
He has also said the yard cannot win commercial work because Scotland does not provide shipbuilding project finance through its state investment bank, something he says every other shipbuilding nation does, leaving Ferguson Marine dependent on government contracts that have gone abroad.
The government and the yard respond
Stephen Flynn, the Economy Secretary, said the redundancies would put the yard on a more competitive footing and were necessary to help secure a viable future, adding that he was assured they would not affect Glen Rosa and that the intention to directly award four vessels is going through due diligence.
Graeme Thomson, chief executive of Ferguson Marine, said: “Shipbuilding capability relies on continuity and while changes of this nature are difficult, taking proactive action now ensures we protect the long-term viability of the yard and remain lean, modern, and ready to cut steel on the new fleet as quickly as possible.”
The Scottish Government said in March 2026 that it intended to make a strategic direct award to Ferguson Marine covering two ferries for Caledonian Maritime Assets under the Small Vessel Replacement Programme, along with a marine protection vessel and a marine research vessel.

Russian and Ukrainian attacks kill 10 people, a day after deadly shopping mall drone strike
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian drone and missile strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine, officials said Saturday, while a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Krasnodar region killed three people there.
The attacks came a day after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian shopping center killed at least 16 people and wounded some 130.
Moscow’s forces have recently intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine’s chronic shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down the missiles.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that one person was killed and another wounded in the latest attacks when ballistic missiles hit railway infrastructure in the capital, Kyiv, overnight.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces had hit a locomotive depot.
In a separate attack, local authorities said two people were killed Saturday afternoon in a Russian ballistic missile strike on the Kyiv region, which surrounds the capital.
Russian drone strikes also killed one person overnight in the Zaporizhzhia region, local officials said Saturday, and a daytime attack killed three others and wounded 15. Zelenskyy said that three people were also wounded in an attack on a minibus in the regional capital, also called Zaporizhzhia.
In Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, authorities said that three people, including two children, were killed and two adults were wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike.
A day on from a deadly attack on a shopping center
The latest attacks came a day after Russian drones struck a shopping center in the city of Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said in the early hours of Saturday that the death toll had risen to 16. Later on Saturday he said four people remain missing after the attack, which wounded a further 130.
Kryvyi Rih is the hometown of Zelenskyy, who described the attack as a double-tap strike, in which an initial wave of drones hit the area followed by a second wave as rescue workers responded. The Ukrainian leader said the fire, which spread across 9,000 square meters (around 97,000 square feet), had been extinguished and rescue efforts were underway.
Kryvyi Rih has been hit multiple times during the 4½-year all-out war between Russia and Ukraine, with one of the deadliest occurring in April 2025, when 20 people were killed, including nine children.
Large-scale Russian strikes have become a regular occurrence this summer, with Friday’s attacks landing just 24 hours after Russia pounded Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime assault that killed 16 people. The United Nations said last week that Kyiv was one of the hardest-hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 wounded.
Ukraine pounds Russia with long-range strikes
At the same time, Ukraine has shifted the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities that have caused fuel shortages across Russia. It also has unsettled the Russian public by striking warehouses of Wildberries, the country’s biggest online retailer.
The Russian online news outlet Astra reported Saturday that a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil refinery in the Samara region. Local officials said that damage was recorded at an unidentified “industrial facility” and a logistics center for Ozon, a competitor to Wildberries.
Zelenskyy said Saturday Ukrainian forces struck the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Samara, noting it is some 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) from the front line.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said in remarks to state TV reporter Pavel Zarubin, who posted them Saturday on his Telegram channel, that strikes on civilian targets “cause economic damage to our country” and “lead to losses,” but that “no turning point” in the conflict had been reached and that Kyiv “will never gain any advantage.”

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto meets with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, and Defense Minister Dong Jun at his official residence in Jakarta, Indonesia, Aug. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng)
JAKARTA, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Indonesia welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest and do business in the country, will continue to provide a sound business environment for Chinese companies, and opposes any ill-intentioned instigation and hype, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has said here.
Prabowo made the remarks on Friday while meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, and Defense Minister Dong Jun at his official residence.
Prabowo positively evaluated the role and achievements of the Indonesia-China Comprehensive Strategic Dialogue Mechanism and the 2+2 dialogue mechanism.
He said that China has successfully lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty and achieved great accomplishments in the economic, scientific and technological, and military fields, setting a good example for Global South countries to learn from.
Prabowo said China treats Indonesia as an equal with mutual respect, and provides Indonesia with valuable confidence and support.
Indonesia looks forward to deepening all-round strategic cooperation with China in such areas as politics, economy, science and technology, the Indonesian president said, noting that he expects to attend the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in November this year to further enhance strategic communication and collaboration with the Chinese side.
For his part, Wang said that under the president's leadership, Indonesia has overcome various difficulties in recent years and its national construction has entered into a stage of rapid development.
Both the Chinese and Indonesian governments are committed to developing the economy and delivering benefits to their people. No force can stop the continuous rise of developing countries such as China and Indonesia, Wang said.
Noting that China and Indonesia have obvious complementary advantages, Wang said China is a reliable, long-term and stable partner in Indonesia's national development process.
Wang said China has the ability and willingness to deepen cooperation with Indonesia to help Indonesia turn its resources into development momentum, accelerate the pace of industrialization and modernization, and bring more tangible benefits to its people.
The development of human society has proved that openness leads to continuous progress, while isolation only results in backwardness, Wang said.
The more turbulent the world becomes and the more complex and severe external challenges grow, the more China and Indonesia should strengthen solidarity, deepen mutual trust and support, uphold openness and cooperation, safeguard common interests, achieve their respective national development, and set a model of cooperation for Global South countries, Wang noted.
China stands ready to work with Indonesia to earnestly implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, as well as the outcomes of the first Conference of China-Indonesia Comprehensive Strategic Dialogue Mechanism and the second ministerial meeting of the 2+2 dialogue mechanism, Wang said.
The two sides will comprehensively advance cooperation in areas including politics, economy, energy and mineral resources, military and security, so as to continuously inject fresh impetus into their respective national development and rejuvenation, as well as make positive contributions to regional peace and stability, Wang said. ■

Ukrainian drones kill at least 10, hit warehouse of Russian online retailer Ozon

Ukrainian drones kill at least 10, hit warehouse of Russian online retailer Ozon
Aug 22 - Ukrainian drones killed at least 10 people in attacks against targets across Russia and Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine, including a warehouse owned by online retailer Ozon and an industrial facility, Russian officials said on Saturday.
Russia and Ukraine are both ramping up drone campaigns aiming to cripple each other's economic infrastructure, often striking targets far beyond the war's front lines, as fighting on the battlefield grinds toward the 4-1/2-year mark.
On Friday, at least 16 people were killed and more than 130 wounded when several Russian drones struck a shopping centre in central Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine's strikes, which Kyiv says seek to choke off financing for Moscow's war effort, had opened a "Pandora's box" of Russian retaliation.
French President Emmanuel Macron, meanwhile, promised to accelerate the delivery of new French equipment to Ukraine, after discussing Kyiv's shortage of air defences in a call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
DRONE STRIKES ACROSS RUSSIA AND RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE
In a post on Telegram on Saturday, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, governor of Russia's Samara region, said that an elderly woman had been killed in a strike on the city of Novokuibyshevsk, which he said caused damage to industrial facilities. Ukraine's military said it had struck the city's oil refinery, causing a fire.
Ozon, Russia's second-largest online retailer, said in a statement on Telegram that work at its Samara region logistics centre in the town of Chapayevsk had been halted after the strike, which it said caused injuries.
The attack is the first on Ozon following weeks of drone strikes on its larger rival Wildberries, which Ukraine has cast as part of a wider campaign against economic infrastructure underpinning the Russian war in Ukraine.
Elsewhere, in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said that three people, two of them children, had been killed and another adult was wounded in a strike on the Sea of Azov port town of Yeysk. He said a fire had broken out at an unnamed facility at the town's port.
The governor of Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, said two people had been killed and 13 wounded in Ukrainian attacks. In Bryansk, another frontier region, four people were wounded, the local governor said.
On the Crimean peninsula, seized from Ukraine by Russia in 2014, the Moscow-backed governor of Sevastopol, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said that at least two people had been killed and 10 injured when a Ukrainian drone struck a city bus.
In Luhansk region, an eastern Ukrainian province almost all of which is controlled by Russia, Moscow-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said that two civilians, including a 16-year-old boy, had been killed and nine more were wounded.
Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed a total of 457 Ukrainian drones overnight. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

‘Young want to leave’: Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:41:10 UTC
16:41:10 KST

Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
Professionals who left a country in turmoil say they are unlikely to return soon as more in Libya could be planning to leave.
London, United Kingdom – Sarah Mizran, a 32-year-old architect, was a teenager when Tripoli fell in August 2011, as opposition fighters swept into the capital.
It was the beginning of the end for Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. Having ruled for 42 years, he was soon captured and killed near Sirte.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Hundreds protest in Libya outside UN agency against undocumented migrants
- list 2 of 4Protests erupt in Libya’s Tripoli as anger grows over power cuts
- list 3 of 4Drone attacks on energy infrastructure deepen Libya’s energy crisis
- list 4 of 4Can diplomacy end the conflict in Libya?
Eight years ago, Mizran left the city for the United Kingdom.
“Libya loses more than just skills when young professionals leave,” she told Al Jazeera. “It loses a sense of possibility when an entire generation grows up feeling that they have to leave in order to build a future, and that leads to a loss of hope in the country itself.”
Already drawn to the concept of sustainable architecture and what it could mean for Libya, Mizran pursued a master’s degree in architecture in southern England. She has spent recent years studying sites in Tripoli, working out what rebuilding the city might mean beyond simply putting up new buildings.
“Ultimately, as an architect, I want to be part of rebuilding Libya’s architectural landscape,” she said. “I don’t know exactly what that return will look like yet, but I know that remains part of the future that I’m working towards.
“A sense of stability in the country will prompt a stronger wave of the diaspora wanting to return,” she said.
She was 24 when she arrived in the UK on a scholarship to study at the University of Kent.
“I had to learn a different professional culture, a different way of working, and in many ways just find my place again,” she said.
She is far from alone.
Nader Elgadi, 36, was running his own media company in Tripoli when, in late 2014, fighting broke out around the capital’s airport during Libya’s second civil war.
He also came to the UK for a master’s degree and had planned to go home, but as threats to activists mounted, he stayed instead.
“I went from running my own business and living comfortably in Libya to starting my life from scratch in the UK,” he said. “The first two years were really hard.”
Elgadi founded Libya in the UK in 2018, a cultural charity “to create the Libya that we wanted to have after we managed to end the dictatorship”.
The group hosts events for the diaspora community trying to build “a sense of that country we always wished for”.
Home, ‘something we create again and again’
Fifteen years on, both describe the UK as home, even as Libya pulls at them.
“Home is not something we find once and keep forever,” Mizran said. “It’s something we create again and again.”
Elgadi calls himself “a nomad” who has stopped expecting to return for good, even as his consultancy still works with Libyan clients.
Whether that dispersal of talent has held Libya back is up for debate.
Tarek Megerisi, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said “tens of thousands of very good, technically proficient people” are still working in Libya’s ministries, but claimed they are blocked from doing their jobs by more senior officials with little interest in governing.
Much of that took root soon after the revolution, he believes.
“After the revolution there was a mass return of Libyans from all across the world. Many skilled young professionals, but also older Libyans, whose qualifications and whose experience were often vastly overstated, used their standing to secure political positions and promised to lead the country to democracy. Instead, they basically just acted like Gaddafi’s government did,” Megerisi said.
He said corruption plagues some ministries in an environment that has driven away the generation that came of age after 2011.
“Young professionals who gained qualifications and had early experience working in the late stage of Gaddafi’s Libya, which was a bit more open,” were genuinely excited the revolution might catalyse their careers, he said. “All of that kind of just got run into a quagmire.
“It’s very sad to see … now all the young generations who have any ambition for their life, they just want to leave the country.”
He summed up Libya’s governance by paraphrasing Kahlil Gibran’s poem, Pity the Nation, “Pity the country that has two governments and nobody interested in governing.”
Megerisi said the talent pool “would come back in a heartbeat should there be a real, valid, credible opportunity”.
Toby Chitayat, an associate at CRI Menas, a UK risk consultancy, is more sceptical that the brain drain is doing much damage.
Set against Libya’s east-west split, its volatile oil revenue and endemic corruption, he argued its effect on governance or investor confidence “is comparatively minimal” but acknowledged that it remains “far too early to say anything definitive about the prospect of serious re-engagement with the country.”

World Bank projects war-hit Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:35:08 UTC
16:35:08 KST

World Bank projects war-hit Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent
Conflict with Israel derails Lebanon’s economic recovery as inflation and consumer prices rise, the global lender says.
Lebanon’s economy is projected to shrink by 6.4 percent this year as conflict turns a brief post-crisis recovery into a sharp downturn, says the World Bank.
The global lender’s Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor, titled A Conflict-Torn Economy, noted that the country entered the year on stronger footing after expanding by 4.2 percent in 2025, its highest real gross domestic product (GDP) growth since the 2019 financial collapse.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Canada boosts Lebanon aid to $50m and condemns Israeli ‘unlawful invasion’
- list 2 of 3What’s happening in Lebanon’s ‘pilot zones’?
- list 3 of 3Displaced Lebanese watch southern Lebanon’s ‘pilot zones’ from afar
“The rebound was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the report said on Friday.
“Real GDP is projected to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026, reflecting the collapse in tourism, weaker consumption, disrupted supply chains, heightened insecurity, and prolonged displacement,” it added.
Consumer prices are also under renewed pressure, with inflation expected to accelerate to 17.5 percent. The World Bank attributed the rise to supply disruptions, elevated shipping costs, and volatile fuel prices.
“Advancing reforms, particularly on banking sector restructuring and fiscal management, will be critical to restoring confidence, protecting stability, and mobilising the financing needed for reconstruction and recovery,” said Dahlia Khalifa, World Bank division director for the Middle East department at the launch of the report.
Parliament recently passed key amendments to the bank resolution law, designed to restructure failing financial institutions and map out a framework for the broader financial sector crisis.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) endorsed the legislative progress, calling the measure “a very good step that reflects Lebanon’s commitment to aligning its legislation with the best international practices”.
The IMF, which has maintained ongoing discussions with Lebanese officials to secure a formal bailout program, confirmed it plans to resume technical meetings in Beirut next month to evaluate further structural policy measures.
“Economic stability in Lebanon is possible amid the current regional chaos, but the likelihood of achieving it in the short term is also conditioned by politics and security, not by economic affairs alone,” said former Economy and Trade Minister Alain Hakim in an interview with Lebanese news outlet Akhbar Al Yawm.
“There is no reason for extreme pessimism because we have the elements available in the country on all fronts, including the existence of constitutional institutions, in addition to indicators of economic activity improvement in the pre-war period,” Hakim said.
“Therefore, when this war ends, this activity will return, especially from the private sector and individual initiatives.”

Russia and Ukraine trade attacks that kill at least 10 after deadly mall drone strike
Russian drone and missile strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine, officials said Saturday, while a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Krasnodar region killed three others.
The attacks came a day after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian shopping mall that killed 16 people and wounded more than 130 others.
Moscow's forces have recently intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine's shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one person was killed and another wounded in the latest attacks when ballistic missiles hit railway infrastructure in the capital, Kyiv, overnight.
Russia's Defense Ministry said that its forces had hit a locomotive depot.
In a separate attack, local authorities said two people were killed Saturday afternoon in a Russian ballistic missile strike on the Kyiv region, which surrounds the capital.
Moscow's forces have recently intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine's chronic shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down the missiles.
Russian drone strikes also killed one person overnight in the Zaporizhzhia region, local officials said Saturday, with a daytime attack killing three others and wounding 15. Zelenskyy said that three people were also wounded in an attack on a minibus in the regional capital, also called Zaporizhzhia.
In Russia's southern Krasnodar region, authorities said that two children were killed and two adults were wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike.
The latest attacks came a day after Russian drones struck a shopping center in the city of Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine on Friday.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said in the early hours of Saturday that the death toll had risen to 16 and nine people remain missing after the attack, which wounded another 130.
Large-scale Russian strikes have become a regular occurrence this summer, with Friday's attacks landing just 24 hours after Russia pounded Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime assault that killed 16 people.
Germany's foreign minister, who is visiting Kyiv on Saturday, sharply criticized Russian President Vladimir Putin for stepping up his "brutal war of aggression." The minister, Johann Wadephul, pledged more aid for Ukraine.
"Russia's brutal war of aggression ... has in no way abated," Wadephul told a press conference, AFP reported. "On the contrary, Putin has even increased the intensity of his war. He is deliberately terrorizing civilians, attacking civilian infrastructure with rockets and swarms of drones."
Wadephul, who announced an additional $58 million in humanitarian aid for Ukraine, said: "I want to emphasize once again here: the people of Ukraine have our full support. Germany stands behind Ukraine."

Former world champion boxer Zolani Tete killed in South Africa
JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (AP) — Former world champion boxer Zolani Tete has been shot and killed at his home in South Africa, government officials said Friday.
Gayton McKenzie, South Africa’s sports, arts and culture minister, said the 38-year-old Tete was killed in his car and that a 27-year-old woman who was in the vehicle with him was shot multiple times and is in hospital.

Taiwan to give repeat foreign visitors NT$5,000 credit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:22:52 UTC
16:22:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will launch a NT$33.3 billion (US$1.05 billion) tourism program in September that includes a new NT$5,000 spending-credit incentive for qualifying repeat international visitors.
Under the program’s international-tourism component, eligible foreign independent travelers who have previously visited Taiwan may be selected to receive NT$5,000 (US$157) in stored-value spending credit. CNA reported that a companion traveling with a selected repeat visitor may receive an additional NT$3,000, bringing the potential combined benefit to NT$8,000.
The repeat-visitor initiative will run from Oct. 10 through March 31, 2027. Online registration will open at 10 a.m. on Oct. 1, according to the Taiwan Tourism Administration. The program will apply to qualifying international visitors entering the country from Oct. 10 onward.
To qualify, a traveler must have entered Taiwan at least once after Jan. 1, 2023. The initiative targets independent travelers and excludes some organized group-tour arrangements.
The administration said separate incentives will be available for groups of at least four people if repeat visitors account for at least 10% of the group. Eligible groups may receive between NT$10,000 and NT$30,000, depending on the program’s conditions.
Domestic travelers are also set to benefit from an accommodation bonus of NT$800 per person per night and an additional NT$400 for the second consecutive night. A birthday accommodation fee of NT$1,200 is also available, the administration said.
The new international-tourism measures are part of the broader “Tourism Dual-Engine Drive Program,” which will begin rolling out Sept. 1. The package also includes weekday lodging subsidies, birthday accommodation vouchers, incentives for international conventions and support for overseas companies organizing incentive trips in Taiwan.
Taiwan is seeking to encourage longer and repeat visits as international tourism recovers. Japanese arrivals reached 1.48 million last year, up more than 12% from the previous year and nearly 70% of the 2019 level, the administration said in June, as reported by CNA.

Taiwan High Speed Rail recruits 45 drivers and 80 maintenance staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:22:27 UTC
16:22:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A week after the arrival of the first new N700ST high-speed train from Japan, Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation is recruiting 45 drivers and 80 maintenance staff, reports said Saturday.
The new train has been moved to Kaohsiung’s Yanchao District depot for tests and will start service on July 1, 2027. An additional 11 train sets built by Hitachi Toshiba Supreme Consortium are scheduled to arrive by the end of Sept. 2028.
The need for new staff is also the result of the company having to operate the original 700T and the new trains simultaneously, per Liberty Times. Once the number of services increases, the company will also consider recruiting more frontline service personnel.
Once train drivers have completed their training and obtained their license, they can expect a starting salary of between NT$60,000 (US$1,880) and NT$70,000 per month, the report said. For maintenance staff, the wage structure is more complicated, as it also includes overtime and nighttime bonuses, but newcomers can expect close to NT$50,000 per month. Over the past five years, the company has implemented five wage rises.
Taiwan High Speed Rail is also planning to spend NT$30 billion on a wide range of upgrades. The changes included safety fences on train platforms, new service desks at stations, new interiors for trains, and adjustments to the online ticket purchasing system, Liberty Times reported. 
The company also plans a second repair facility near Zuoying Station in Kaohsiung and changes to the Yanchao depot.

Bangladesh’s new President Mirza Fakhrul assumes office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:21:04 UTC
16:21:04 KST

SM Najmus Sakib
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
Bangladesh’s newly elected President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was sworn in Friday as the 23rd president of the South Asian nation.
Acting Parliament Speaker Kaiser Kamal administered the oath of office to Fakhrul at Bangabhaban, the presidential residence, in the presence of state guests, including the prime minister, Cabinet members and opposition lawmakers.
After taking office, the new president administered the oath of office to six new members of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Cabinet, including four full ministers and two state ministers.
The Cabinet has now total number of ministers to 51 after reshuffling, change and withdrawal, according to a government gazette notification early Saturday.
Fakhrul, a leader of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), was elected president Thursday for a five-year term, comfortably defeating retired Col. Oli Ahmed, the nominee of the opposition alliance led by Jamaat-e-Islami.
Fakhrul received 255 votes, while the opposition candidate secured 88. Six lawmakers were absent from the vote, while one parliamentary seat remains vacant.
Bangladesh’s parliament has 300 elected seats, in addition to 50 reserved seats for women.
The presidential election was held after a 35-year gap, as no opposition candidate had contested the largely ceremonial post during that period.
Fakhrul, 78, emerged as the de facto leader of the BNP while its late chairperson, Khaleda Zia, was imprisoned and then-acting Chairman Tarique Rahman was in exile in the UK for 17 years, mainly during ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s 15-year rule.
Mohammed Shahabuddin, who served as president under Hasina’s Awami League government, resigned on July 24, citing health reasons, two years before completing his five-year term.
Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed subsequently assumed duties as interim president.

pyramids and maya forms shape coco brun and sten studio’s stone vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:13:11 UTC
16:13:11 KST

French artist and designer Coco Brun joins forces with Mexico City-based Sten Studio for Echoes of Mexico, a collection of sculptural vessels rooted in the country’s lapidary traditions. Hand-carved from red travertine, veined marble and multicolored onyx, the pieces translate references to ancient Mesoamerican architecture and ornament into a contemporary design language. Developed with support from the Institut Français d’Amérique Latine (IFAL), Mobilier National and Galerie Territorio, the project was recently recognized in the fourth edition of Le French Design 100 at Art Paris.
The collaboration unfolds through two capsule collections, each limited to a maximum of 10 pieces. Rather than sourcing new blocks, Brun and Sten Studio work with remnants from the workshop’s existing production, including red travertine, white Venetian marble, black Orizaba marble, and pink and green onyx. Variations in veining, translucency and color are therefore not treated as imperfections to be corrected, but as part of the final composition — which is fortunate, considering stone rarely agrees to repeat itself.
marble and onyx define the sculptural vessel series | all images courtesy of Sten Studio and Coco Brun
PYRAMIDS, MASKS AND POLISHED MASS
The Místicos series takes its geometry from the structural logic of Mexican pyramids. Faceted silhouettes, sloped surfaces and flattened summits abstract architectural forms into compact vessels, balancing the visual weight of polished marble against the translucent depth of onyx. Rather than reproducing specific monuments, the pieces distill their proportions and mass into a smaller, more domestic scale.
A different set of references informs Abstracted Ancestry, which looks to the layered geometry of Maya ceremonial masks and, in particular, the oversized ear ornaments worn by dignitaries. The resulting vessels feature oval bodies, sweeping curves and two straight perforated fins that extend from either side. These openings reference the form of historical ear ornaments while also introducing voids into otherwise dense stone objects, shifting the pieces somewhere between vessel, sculpture and architectural fragment.
each piece is shaped from reclaimed stone fragments
LEFTOVER STONE GOES ON TOUR
Material reuse runs through both collections. By working with offcuts from Sten Studio’s primary production, Echoes of Mexico gives fragments that might otherwise remain unused a new formal role. The project therefore connects a highly traditional craft process with a contemporary concern for material efficiency, while preserving the irregularities that make each vessel distinct. The result is not so much recycling disguised as luxury as a demonstration that the leftover piece can occasionally be the most interesting one.
The collection is also conceived as a traveling dialogue between France and Mexico. Following its presentation in Europe, the works are set to appear at the Lake Como Design Festival, before continuing to Mexico City Design Week as part of Inmersiones Creativas at Casa Ortega, an exhibition marking 200 years of diplomatic relations between France and Mexico. The journey concludes in Paris at 1000 Vases, staged at Espace Commines during Art Basel week, extending the project’s conversation between craft, geography and cultural memory across several very different contexts.

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says
The drought-stricken country has recorded a 32 percent jump in the number of children treated for severe malnutrition.
Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
Life-threatening malnutrition among children is spiking in Somalia as more than 200 health and nutrition facilities were forced to shutter following cuts to international aid, the United Nations has warned.
The East African country has seen a 32 percent jump in the number of children admitted to facilities with severe acute malnutrition and complications in the first six months of 2026, UNICEF said on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
- list 2 of 3Suspected Somali pirates seize tanker near Yemen amid wave of hijackings
- list 3 of 3Somali army clashes with rebel forces for control of key city Baidoa
Nearly 1.9 million children are projected to be malnourished this year.
“In Somalia today, aid cuts are closing doors to healthcare, shutting down nutrition services, and pushing water, education and protection further out of reach,” UNICEF spokesman James Elder told reporters in Geneva, speaking via video from Nairobi.
As many as 618 health facilities could close nationwide under “severe funding scenarios”, Elder said. “This is the wrong moment to retreat.”
Somalia faces a severe drought that has killed livestock, ruined harvests and destroyed livelihoods. Aid groups estimate that drought displaced about 500,000 people between January and April, adding to roughly 3.3 million Somalis already uprooted.
One-third of Somalia’s population of 19 million people is facing severe food shortages.
Yet funding for addressing acute malnutrition in parts of Somalia has dropped by more than 80 percent this year, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said earlier this month, with the United States and several other Western countries slashing aid.
Somalia was also excluded from the $2bn global humanitarian aid pledge announced by the US for this year due to allegations of aid diversion and corruption.
The cuts have compounded the effects of the current drought, curtailing access to water even as prices in rural and pastoral areas have quadrupled, according to UNICEF.
At the same time, fuel and fertiliser costs have risen because of the US-Israel war on Iran, while a record-strength El Nino climate pattern is forecast to worsen the humanitarian crisis with severe flooding, Elder said.
Nearly a million children below five, adolescent girls and women risk losing access to nutrition services.

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says
Health chief defends higher charges for less urgent services in Hong Kong as full fee waivers increase from 14,000 since new regime began on January 1
About 280,000 patients have secured full fee waivers since Hong Kong’s public healthcare charges were overhauled at the start of the year, a 20-fold increase from the previous figure of 14,000, the health minister has said.
Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau revealed the figures on Saturday as he defended the reform, which raised user fees for non-urgent and less serious services to reduce the government subsidy rate. He said the changes were intended to optimise the use of existing resources and strengthen protection for vulnerable groups.
“Since its implementation, just in eight months the number of people benefiting from full medical fee waivers has increased from 14,000 to 280,000 – a growth of over 20-fold,” Lo said.
The new public healthcare fee regime was introduced on January 1 to ensure the sustainable development of the healthcare system amid challenges posed by an ageing population.
Under the new structure, a visit to an accident and emergency department at a public hospital costs HK$400 (US$51) for less urgent cases, up from between HK$50 and HK$150 per visit.
The number of people eligible for subsidised or free healthcare will also expand significantly, from 300,000 to 1.4 million, following the relaxation of income and asset limits.

Ukraine says death toll from Russian drone strike in Kryvyi Rih rises to 16

- Russian authorities say Ukrainian drones strike industrial facility, logistics complex in Samara region
The death toll from a Russian drone strike on a shopping complex in the city of Kryvyi Rih in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region rose to 16, local authorities said Saturday.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, said on Telegram that search and rescue operations were still ongoing at the site, stating that nine people, including two children, remained missing.
“16 civilians from Kryvyi Rih died in the Russian strike. 130 people were injured, including 25 children,” Vilkul said, noting that, as of 7.30 am local time (0430GMT), 61 injured people were currently being treated in hospitals, while 23 of them were in serious condition.
He added that a day of mourning would be observed in the city on Sunday for the victims of the attack.
On Friday, Vilkul stated that the largest shopping complex in the city was attacked by Russian drones, sparking a fire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack an "act of terrorism,” saying: “The attack drones struck in two waves – half an hour after the first hit and the fire, there was a second strike targeting the emergency responders.”
Russian authorities have not yet commented on the strike.
Ukrainian authorities further reported overnight strikes in the country on Saturday morning, with the Kyiv City Military Administration saying a fire broke out in an unspecified warehouse in the capital’s Darnytskyi district after reporting a ballistic missile threat over the city about an hour earlier.
“According to preliminary information, unfortunately, there is one dead and (one) injured. The relevant services are working. The information is being clarified,” the statement said, without providing further details.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, CEO of Ukraine’s national railway company Ukrzaliznytsia, said in a statement on US social media company Facebook that one of the company’s enterprises was hit with ballistic missiles.
He also said that the Rozdilna railway station in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region has been damaged, adding that the consequences of the attack are being eliminated and that it has not affected railway traffic.
Ukraine's Air Force claimed that it downed 182 out of 217 drones, as well as destroyed nine missiles, launched by Russia overnight.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a morning statement that it launched a massive strike against transportation infrastructure facilities and a logistics center in Kyiv and the surrounding Kyiv region.
It said that the strike hit the “Darnytsia” locomotive depot, where “technical maintenance and repair of the locomotive fleet was carried out, ensuring the transportation of weapons and military equipment for the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”
It also claimed strikes on a logistics center in the city of Brovary in the Kyiv region, as well as on “warehouses with military equipment and fuel tanks intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” in the Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi ports in the Odesa region.
Strikes in Russia
A later Defense Ministry statement said Russian air defenses shot down 457 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, governor of Russia’s Samara region, said that his region was targeted in a “massive” Ukrainian drone strike, claiming several dozen drones were shot down during the attack.
“Damage was sustained at one industrial facility. Additionally, a hit was recorded at the Ozon logistics complex,” Fedorishchev said, noting that several casualties are known, all of whom are receiving medical assistance.
Ozon, a Russian e-commerce company, confirmed the strike on its logistics complex in the Samara region, saying a fire broke out in its warehouse and that over 500 employees were evacuated from the site.
"Unfortunately, there were casualties. We will certainly provide them with all the necessary support," the statement said, adding that the warehouse has been closed indefinitely.
Separately, Krasnodar Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said civilian infrastructure and residential buildings in the southern region's Yeysky district came under attack, noting two children were killed and two others injured as a result.
Kondratyev said drone debris also fell on an enterprise located on the territory of the district's administrative center, and that firefighters are currently extinguishing a fire that consequently broke out.
Ukraine's General Staff claimed it struck and caused a fire at the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region during an overnight attack, alleging that the facility's products are “used to supply the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.”
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Belarus to present project in St. Petersburg ahead of 85th anniversary of Siege of Leningrad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

An archive photo
                    MOSCOW, 22 August (BelTA) – A unique Belarusian project – the requiem concert Every Third – will be presented in the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall in St. Petersburg on September 8 and 9, BelTA learned from the Standing Committee of the Union State of Belarus and Russia.
 
8 September 2026 marks the 85th anniversary of the start of the Siege of Leningrad – one of the most tragic pages of the Great Patriotic War of 1941-1945. On the Day of Remembrance for the Victims of the Siege of Leningrad, more than 100 Belarusian artists will take the stage at the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall to honor the memory of the victims and heroes of the Great Patriotic War and to speak out against the resurgence of Nazism.
 
The project Every Third presents an unusual fusion of concert, theatrical performance, and documentary narrative based on photographic and video documents related to various periods of the Great Patriotic War and the postwar era as well as figures and information refined by modern research. For a long time it was believed that one in four residents of Belarus perished during the war. However, data refined in recent years indicates that Belarus lost one in three of its population during the war.
 
The requiem concert will feature both well-known musical works from the Soviet era and new compositions by contemporary Belarusian composers: Valery Shmat, Anna Seluk, Yevgeny Oleinik, Anna Blagova, and others. The poetic foundation of the concert is Anatoly Vertinsky’s Requiem for Every Fourth. The requiem concert was created on the initiative of OOO Musical Media Company with the support of Belarus’ Defense Ministry and Culture Ministry. The project’s director is Vladislava Artyukovskaya, artistic director of the Youth Variety Theater. The script was written by Vladislava Artyukovskaya and Anna Seluk.
 
Between 2024 and 2026, the requiem concert Every Third was seen by thousands of viewers in Belarus and was performed twice each in Moscow and Kazan. In 2025, the project was awarded the Belarus president’s prize For Spiritual Revival for preserving historical memory and strengthening spiritual values.
 
During the days of the requiem concert the foyer of the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall will host thematic exhibitions that have become iconic for Belarus. The photo exhibition Fates Folded into a Triangle is based on the joint online project of the same name by BelTA and the Belarusian State Museum of History of the Great Patriotic War. The exhibition tells the stories of those who perished and those who survived the entire war through authentic personal letters, postcards, and greeting cards sent from the front lines to loved ones as well as archive photographs. Visitors will have a rare opportunity to write and fold a triangular letter themselves, following the front-line model.
 
The exhibition Partisans of Belarus – a joint project of the publishing house Belarus Today and the National Archive of Belarus – consists of an archival database of award sheets, personal files, and combat records of partisans. Using the interactive display of the Partisans of Belarus project, every visitor will be able to find a relative among the partisans and underground resistance fighters of Belarus and learn new facts about the partisan movement during the Great Patriotic War.
 
Performances of the requiem concert at the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall are organized as part of the Year of St. Petersburg Culture with the support of the St. Petersburg government.

Economic Watch: Chinese robotics fair draws crowds as industry brews innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
14:55:17 CST
15:55:17 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Unitree Robotics' blockbuster IPO, the bustling World Robot Conference (WRC), and the upcoming World Humanoid Robot Games, amount to a string of high-profile events which have combined to make this week a "super week" for Chinese robotics.
Underpinning these events is a clear trend: China is swiftly becoming a global epicenter of robotics innovation, which is poised to reshape the way products are manufactured and the way people live.
The numbers confirm China's significant rise in robotics. Data from the country's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology show that revenue of industrial enterprises above designated size in China's robotics sector had exceeded 300 billion yuan (about 44.24 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with an average annual growth rate of more than 20 percent over the past five years.
Also, a report by California-based research firm Smart Analytics Global indicates that global humanoid robot shipments totaled approximately 19,100 units in the first half of 2026, with Chinese-made units accounting for over 97 percent of the total.
More broadly, exports of industrial robots increased 13.2 percent in the January-July period, while shipments of surgical robots surged 3.3-fold year on year in the first half of 2026.
Robots, AI products and innovative drugs are three new drivers of China's export growth, according to Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun.
This momentum has played out at this year's WRC, which is being held in a southeastern technology hub in Beijing.
On weekday mornings, traffic ground to a halt for kilometers around the WRC exhibition hall, forcing the organizers to issue daily "travel advisories," a task that speaks volumes about the sector's red-hot vitality in China. Inside the venue, crowds are so dense they rival the throngs at CES in Las Vegas.
WRC exhibitors this year have topped 300, up 69 percent from 2025, with the event featuring over 3,000 products, and roughly 300 making their debuts. Additionally, many are powered by large AI models, cloud computing and big data.
China's vast and sophisticated manufacturing sector is providing a massive testing ground for embodied AI technologies, which are now being deployed on a large scale in factories and training facilities.
According to an industry research report, by June this year, China had launched over 70 training grounds for robots, with another 46 either under construction or in the planning pipeline.
"This week's IPO is just the start of the journey," said Aron Kisdi, managing director of Autodiscovery and Unitree Robotics' U.K. distributor, at the company's WRC booth. Unitree Robotics, based in Hangzhou in east China, went public on China's A-share market on Wednesday, the same day the WRC opened, and its shares skyrocketed 629.44 percent to open at 1,100 yuan.
"It signals that the time in the lab is nearing an end, and we're pushing robots into the real world," Kisdi explained.
On the exhibition floor at the WRC, many booths are displaying robots operating in real-world work scenarios. A logistics robot sorts parcels at a rate of more than 1,000 items per hour, while nearby, a pair of dexterous robotic hands smoothly folds a cardboard sheet into a packaging box.
At UBTECH's display zone, robots perform automated loading and unloading of automotive sheet metal parts with zero human oversight, building on earlier trials at several car plants. Chinese robotics firms have, notably, already put robots into factories to test their capability of doing more sophisticated jobs beyond just basic handling.
Elsewhere at the show, automakers like Xiaomi feature their own humanoid robots, underscoring how industry demand is fueling robotics innovation.
The bustling expo floor in Beijing also features robots designed for emotional companionship, housework, convenience-store retail and coffee brewing, which can tap into China's massive consumer market, the world's second-largest in terms of commodity consumption for more than 10 consecutive years.
"Robots are no longer only about flashy concepts and specs. They're increasingly focused on tackling real-life challenges," said Ren Jingwei, a manager at Zhiyuan Research Institute in Hangzhou.
Also, this year's WRC fair is no longer just for curious onlookers. Industry players up and down the supply chain are busy exchanging business cards and phone numbers there in bids to forge new partnerships.
One noteworthy shift this year is the considerable presence of dexterous-hand sensor makers, joint module suppliers and chip manufacturers at the WRC. These component suppliers, once supporters behind finished robots, have now also taken center stage in their own niche sectors -- a sign that China's robotics industry is maturing into a more sophisticated ecosystem.
Humanoid robots could spur investment across precision transmission, smart sensors, AI chips and intelligent software, generating a huge market from R&D to after-sales service, said Xu Xiaolan from the Chinese Institute of Electronics.
To many attendees, Beijing's robot show points to an upcoming transformative change in the industry. The "ChatGPT moment" for embodied AI will come in two to three years under an optimistic outlook, or within five to ten years at the latest, said Wang Xingxing, Unitree Robotics founder and CEO, when speaking at a WRC forum. ■

TOKYO, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- The torch relay for next month's Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games began Saturday at Nagoya Castle, with three-time Olympic wrestling champion Saori Yoshida carrying the flame on its opening leg.
The official Games flame was formed shortly before the relay by combining three fires collected in Tokyo, Hiroshima and Nagoya. Former Japan football star Homare Sawa and retired tennis player Kimiko Date brought the fires kindled at Tokyo's National Stadium on August 18 and in Hiroshima two days later.
Takeru Goto, a member of Japanese boy band INI and an official ambassador for the Games, kindled the Nagoya fire with a concave mirror before the three fires were merged.
Yoshida, who competed at four Asian Games and won gold, said the continental event holds special memories for her.
"I hope the feelings of every torchbearer will give strength to the athletes competing at the Games," she said before setting off from the castle.
The flame was then handed to local torchbearers and carried through central Nagoya. Saturday's route included Meijo Park, Hisaya-odori Park, the Oasis 21 complex and the Nakagawa Canal. The flame will be divided after the opening-day relay and carried along two routes across Aichi Prefecture.
Around 1,000 torchbearers, including members of the public and prominent figures, will carry the flame through 40 local government areas and a number of schools before it arrives at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on September 19 for the Games' opening ceremony.
Japan will host the Asian Games for the third time, following Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994.
The 20th Asian Games will be held from September 19 to October 4, featuring 43 sports and athletes from 45 countries and regions across Asia. ■

Japan's FY 2027 budget requests may exceed 130 trln yen, hitting new record high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
14:54:51 CST
15:54:51 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Budget requests from Japanese government ministries and agencies for fiscal 2027 are expected to exceed 130 trillion yen (around 818 billion U.S. dollars), a significant increase from the current fiscal year's initial budget of 122.31 trillion yen, Kyodo News reported on Friday.
The report said that the actual budget could rise further when finalized at the end of this year, as spending for many items is yet to be determined.
Among the requests, the Ministry of Defense plans to seek a record of about 8.9 trillion yen. Previous media reports said key spending areas will include procuring large numbers of interceptor drones, introducing artificial intelligence into command-and-control systems, and further deploying long-range missiles with what Japan calls "counterstrike capabilities."
Expenditures on social security, such as pensions and medical costs, are expected to rise by around 390 billion yen due to the country's continued aging of the population.
Ministries and agencies are required to submit their budget requests for fiscal 2027, which runs from April 2027 to March 2028, by the end of this month, after which the Ministry of Finance will compile the budget by the end of the year.
It is worth noting that the Japanese government has previously imposed caps on budget requests to control the scale of spending. This time, however, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government launched a major budget drafting reform by not setting limits on some of the investment projects it is promoting. This is seen as a major factor behind the unusually large increase in overall budget requests.
The report said that with the Japanese government forecasting tax revenue of about 83 trillion yen for fiscal 2026, budget requests topping 130 trillion yen will likely lead to new debt issuance, further straining the debt-ridden country's fiscal health.
Amid growing concerns over the country's deteriorating fiscal situation, Japanese government bond yields have continued to rise recently, increasing the government's debt-servicing burden and putting further pressure on public finances. (1 yen equals 0.0063 U.S. dollars) ■

MANNHEIM, Germany (AP) — A German Cup match between Waldhof Mannheim and Kaiserslautern was halted for about half an hour on Friday as fans threw fireworks and other objects and invaded the pitch.
The match was tied at 0-0 and heading into extra time when fans at both ends of the ground threw flares and objects, narrowly missing some of the players as they ran from the field.
Some Mannheim supporters made it on to the pitch before officers in riot gear and mounted police fanned out to push them back.
German news agency dpa says the match resumed after a delay of just under 30 minutes. Ibrahim Kanate scored in the last minute of extra time, giving second-division Kaiserslautern a 1-0 win to advance to the second round of the German Cup.

Beyblade battles drive up sales at Hong Kong malls, but how long will the trend last?
Struggling to attract patrons, shopping centres are embracing resurgent popularity of Japanese toy, drawing fans who stay and spend – at least for now
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.
In shops across Tuen Mun Town Plaza, children, teens and young adults hunch over small plastic battle arenas, unleashing their tops into the “Beystadiums” in head-to-head competitions where the top that remains spinning the longest wins.
The toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Asia early this year, and gatherings are attracting crowds of local players eager to put their models to the test.
Spotting the economic potential behind the hobby, shopping centre operators across Hong Kong are converting open spaces into free battle zones to drive up foot traffic and sales.
Tuen Mun Town Plaza went a step further by scaling up the concept into a mall-wide strategy ahead of a major Beyblade tournament in August, encouraging shop operators to take part in the game and offer discounts to shoppers who present their tops.
“The strategy is about how a tenant can engage with customers through a shared interest, instead of directly selling to them,” said Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer of Sino Group, which owns the plaza.
“It’s a soft-selling approach that allows staff and shoppers to start a conversation, drawing people into the store before making a sales pitch.”

A video released by Trabzonspor to announce the signing of Egyptian football star Mohamed Salah has given a boost to the international visibility of Trabzon’s cuisine, drawing attention to traditional dishes among visitors to the Black Sea city.
