The spread includes kuymak, a hearty dish made with cornmeal, cheese and butter; stuffed collard green; cornbread; locally produced butter; and kaygana, a traditional egg-based specialty.
Emre Murat, head of the Trabzon Gastronomy Association, said the video had generated significant interest in the dishes featured, particularly among international visitors.
“People began coming to Trabzon to see the products featured in the commercial. There were many inquiries about what Salah had eaten and, particularly from foreign tourists, where they could find those dishes,” Murat said.
Salah’s arrival in Trabzon, he noted, offered an opportunity to showcase not only the football club but also the city’s culinary traditions and way of life to a global audience.
Murat said food suppliers in contact with the association reported unusually strong demand during the week of Salah’s arrival, with some working late into the night to meet interest in local products.
The renewed attention comes as Trabzon’s cuisine has gained wider exposure through television productions filmed in the region and international events. Murat also cited the inclusion of Trabzon butter in the menu of an official gala dinner held for leaders during a NATO summit as another example of the city’s culinary heritage reaching international audiences.
Mamal Jeri, a tourist from Kuwait, said kuymak was among his favorite dishes in Trabzon. After seeing the transfer video on social media, he said he was inspired to try it himself.
“Salah is known by everyone. His arrival here was a big surprise, but it was very good,” Jeri said.

Excavations to resume at Antalya’s ancient city of Rhodiapolis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:47:51 UTC
15:47:51 KST

Excavation work at the ancient city of Rhodiapolis in Antalya’s Kumluca district is scheduled to resume next year, following a period of suspension, as efforts continue to uncover and preserve the site’s archaeological heritage.
Kumluca District Governor Bahadır Güneş recently visited the ancient city with a delegation, describing Rhodiapolis as “a window into Kumluca’s history.” Excavations at the site began in 2006 and have since brought much of the ancient settlement to light.
Beste Tomay, an archaeology faculty member at Adıyaman University who advises the excavation project, said Rhodiapolis holds an important place among the ancient cities of Lycia, both historically and culturally.
Tomay said preparations are being carried out this year, including field surveys, assessments of previous excavation work and an inventory of artifacts held in storage. Full excavation activities are expected to resume next year under the coordination of the excavation leadership.
The site contains remains spanning the Lycian and Byzantine periods, including a theater, bathhouse, agora, temples, a church, cisterns and monumental tombs. Archaeologists believe further excavation could reveal additional elements of the ancient settlement and deepen understanding of the region’s cultural history.
Tomay said bringing the entire city to light would make a significant contribution to Kumluca’s historical and cultural profile, while strengthening the connection between the district and its ancient past.

Nemrut’s ancient statues undergo nanolime treatment for preservation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:38:37 UTC
15:38:37 KST

Conservation work continues at Nemrut Mountain, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in southeastern Türkiye, where experts are using nanotechnology to protect its monumental ancient statues from further deterioration.
The restoration and conservation program, launched in 2022 to preserve the site’s colossal sculptures for future generations, focuses in part on sealing fine cracks in the stone with nanolime. The material is injected into cracks to prevent water from penetrating the sculptures and accelerating their deterioration.
Ayşe Ebru Çorbacı, director of the Gaziantep Regional Restoration and Conservation Laboratory, said teams are currently working on the head of Kommagene Tyche and the statue of Zeus Oromandes on the site’s western terrace.
The nanolime treatment is designed to fill microscopic cracks and strengthen vulnerable sections of the sculptures, she said, noting that earlier conservation work had produced positive results.
“2022 works produced results,” Çorbacı said, adding that the next phase began in 2025. During that campaign, conservation teams reinforced the head of King Antiochos and eagle heads on both the eastern and western terraces. This year, work has shifted to the heads of Kommagene Tyche and Zeus.
The monumental statues are part of the sanctuary built by the Kingdom of Commagene in the first century B.C. at the summit of Nemrut Mountain. The site, located at an altitude of about 2,150 meters, is known for its enormous stone figures representing deities and rulers, as well as its monumental eastern and western terraces.
Mehmet Alkan, director of the Adıyaman Museum, said the conservation project was essential to ensuring that the sculptures, which have survived for more than 2,000 years, remain intact for future generations.
“Restoration and conservation works at Nemrut Mountain resumed in 2026 with the support of the Culture and Tourism Ministry,” Alkan said, adding that the work is being carried out by specialists from the Gaziantep Regional Restoration and Conservation Laboratory.
The long-term effort reflects the challenges of preserving Nemrut’s sculptures in an exposed mountain environment, where water infiltration and weathering can gradually weaken the ancient stone. The conservation teams are therefore seeking to reinforce the statues while minimizing intervention and preserving their historic fabric.

In search of Longjing: The hands behind China’s most revered green tea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:38:22 UTC
15:38:22 KST

I feel as though I am in a dream. I am standing in the very place where my favourite green tea in the world is grown. Yet Longjing goes far beyond my own personal passion; it is one of China’s most revered teas and among the world’s most prized green teas. For three days, I stayed in an ancient village tucked among Hangzhou’s tea-covered hills, where Buddhist monasteries and tea gardens have existed side by side for centuries. Each morning, when I opened my door, there was no hotel corridor waiting for me, but a stone village path, bamboo groves, tea gardens and people making their way towards the temples.
This is Amanfayun. Set along a pilgrimage route formed by seven ancient Buddhist temples, it is an extraordinary place where 46 old village buildings, some more than a century old, have been transformed into places to stay. It is not easy to tell where the hotel begins and the village ends. Rather than constructing a new and ostentatious world, Amanfayun seems to have quietly settled into the one that was already here. Walking along stone paths, through bamboo groves and shaded courtyards, you feel less like a guest in a large hotel operation and more like a temporary resident of the village. Perhaps Amanfayun’s greatest achievement is that, rather than drawing attention to itself, it makes you notice the place around it.
In China, tea is not simply a leaf steeped in hot water; it belongs to a vast culture in which agriculture, craftsmanship, history, philosophy and everyday life intersect. During the Qing Dynasty, Emperor Qianlong visited the place we know today as Longjing Village and granted imperial status to 18 tea bushes in front of Hu Gong Temple. Those 18 bushes remain among Longjing’s most powerful symbols today. The prestige that once carried this tea all the way to the imperial table continues, centuries later, to shape its value.
One of the most striking things here is that tea does not exist as an agricultural product separate from village life. Families sell tea outside their homes, meticulously ordered rows of tea bushes cover almost every hillside, and people carry glass cups of Longjing with them throughout the day. Even the waffle served at breakfast comes flavoured with Longjing.
So what makes Longjing so precious? To begin with, its production area is extremely limited. The leaves are picked by hand while still very young in spring, and it is after this that the craftsmanship defining the tea’s character truly begins. In traditional, high-quality Longjing production, the leaves are hand-roasted in heated, wok-like pans. The master presses, lifts, shakes and turns the leaves with the palm of the hand. This is far more than a drying process; it is a craft that gives Longjing its flat, slender and almost flawless form.
The most prized teas are made from the youngest leaves harvested early in spring. The picking season is brief and quantities are extremely limited. This scarcity partly explains reports over the years of exceptional batches of Longjing commanding prices per kilogram higher than gold. The precise day of harvest is critical. Pick a leaf a day too early and it may not be fully developed; a day too late and it may already have lost some of its delicacy. With Longjing, a window of just a few days can determine both the character and the value of a tea.
And then there are the Longjing masters. These are the people who determine the fate of the tea with their hands in a matter of minutes. They read the heat not through a thermometer, but through the memory of their palms. Over years, they learn exactly when the leaf has lost enough moisture, when it needs to be pressed and when it must leave the pan. Give the same fresh leaves to two different masters and you will not end up with precisely the same tea. That is the essence of their craft.
Because my journey fell in August, I should not, in fact, have had any chance of seeing Longjing being produced. The harvest and production take place in spring. Amanfayun, however, arranged something I will not forget. They invited the local tea master who produces tea from their own gardens especially for me and sourced fresh tea leaves so that he could give a small production demonstration. Within minutes, the entire room was filled with the scent of warm leaves, toasted nuts and that unmistakable Longjing aroma. After eight years of reading about, tasting and talking about this tea, I was finally watching it take shape right in front of me. Aman’s own approach to experiencing this landscape includes walking through bamboo forests and tea fields to Longjing Village and, during spring, witnessing local people harvesting and pan-roasting the leaves as a way of understanding this region.
In fact, this was far more than a small gesture; it was a revealing example of where Aman looks for luxury. For me, luxury that day was not the size of my room, the marble used in it or the number of people attending to me. It was making something I could not possibly have witnessed in August possible for a few hours, simply because they had genuinely listened to why I was there. That, to me, is personalized service: Before anticipating what a guest might want, understanding why that guest has come in the first place. This is also where Aman’s particular skill becomes apparent: Rather than using the culture of a destination as decoration, it attempts to become part of it. Perhaps this is why Aman properties in different corners of the world do not feel like replicas of one another, but rather like different geographical expressions of the same idea. Among the core values the brand says it continues to protect are privacy, service, architecture sensitive to its surroundings and pioneering locations.
The same approach can be felt in the kitchen. The summer menu at Steam House foregrounds produce from the lakes and waterways of the Jiangnan region, including Taihu prawns marinated in Shaoxing yellow wine. The continuation of age-old cooking methods in the semi-open kitchen feels like an extension of the same philosophy. Aman itself speaks of architecture that remains true to its destination and of experiences shaped by culture, community and nature. At Amanfayun, there is little need to read the theory; you need only look around.
Perhaps what truly distinguishes Amanfayun is the sense that it positions itself not as the owner of this village, but as one of its temporary custodians. The character of the old village houses has been preserved; the stone paths continue along their old course; the surrounding temples, tea gardens and village life are not a stage constructed behind the hotel, but life itself. This idea of seasonality extends all the way to the spa. Traditional Chinese Medicine holds that the body should be supported in accordance with nature’s rhythms; summer is believed to place greater demands on the heart, and treatments therefore focus on supporting circulation and restoring balance. You encounter a similar philosophy in the kitchen, in the tea and in the gardens: rather than resisting the season, you move with it. In the morning, you might pass a Buddhist monk, step into a tea garden a few minutes later and then have breakfast inside a centuries-old building. And gradually, you understand more clearly that Longjing is not simply a tea. Perhaps luxury can be exactly this: not making a place resemble you when you arrive, but allowing it, for a while, to bring you closer to itself.

Fishermen expect abundant bonito as season opens in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:38:01 UTC
15:38:01 KST

Turkish fishermen anticipate the most abundant bonito catch in recent years as the new industrial fishing season opens across the country’s seas on Sept. 1, a fishery cooperative head said.
Central Union of Fishery Cooperatives (SÜRKOOP) Board Head Ramazan Özkaya said all signs point to a highly productive bonito season. He said an expected increase in bonito will likely reduce anchovy populations across Turkish waters since the larger fish naturally prey on them.
Fishermen completed their vessel maintenance and net repairs despite continuously rising input costs, particularly fuel. Noting aquatic resources belong equally to the country’s 86 million citizens, Özkaya urged consumers to reject illegally caught fish while calling on authorities to strictly enforce size and location bans.
Declining marine stocks drive younger generations away from the sector, resulting in aging crews, Özkaya said. “We want young people to stay in this profession,” he said, calling for sustainable fishing practices to pass the marine resources to future generations.
For the first time this year, the Agriculture and Forestry Ministry allowed small-scale fishermen using gillnets to begin catching bonito on Aug. 15. Özkaya said the 15-day head start protects traditional fishers from fierce industrial competition, allowing them to sell their two to three crates of catch profitably before large fleets arrive.
Türkiye imposes seasonal fishing bans annually from April 15 to Sept. 1 to preserve aquatic ecosystems and allow fish populations to spawn. The industrial fleet accounts for the vast majority of seafood production, while small fisheries remain crucial for coastal economies and traditional livelihoods.

Mediterranean talks shape Türkiye’s plastic strategy under Zero Waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:37:51 UTC
15:37:51 KST

Türkiye is stepping up efforts to curb plastic pollution in the Mediterranean under its Zero Waste initiative, with Adana and Mersin hosting the first two of four regional coordination meetings ahead of a national plastic waste workshop in Istanbul.
The consultations, also held in Muğla and Antalya, bring local experience into a common national approach to plastic waste management.
Adana represents a key upstream source of pollution. The agricultural and industrial province has about 5,000 kilometers of irrigation canals and more than 4,000 kilometers of drainage channels, through which plastic waste can contaminate water and agricultural land before reaching rivers and the Mediterranean.
Governor Mustafa Yavuz said authorities were considering more frequent canal cleaning, identifying pollution hotspots, installing waste-capture systems and using cameras to detect illegal dumping.
Adana has 186 licensed waste recovery facilities. Authorities conducted 1,785 environmental inspections through Aug. 15, including 487 focused on waste. Four facilities without the required permits were ordered to halt operations, while fines totaling 48.6 million Turkish Liras were imposed for violations. An Adana Provincial Action Plan covering waste, wastewater treatment and microplastic pollution is being prepared. Yavuz said it would include clearly assigned responsibilities, deadlines and a monitoring system to ensure measures continue.
In Mersin, where plastic waste reaches the Mediterranean directly, Governor Atilla Toros said 20 plastic recycling facilities had been inspected and two penalized. Samples from urban wastewater treatment plants were also being analyzed.
Toros noted that currents in the eastern Mediterranean can carry pollution from other countries toward Türkiye’s shores. Authorities are coordinating environmental safeguards at Mersin Port with public institutions and the port operator.
Samed Ağırbaş, chairman of the Zero Waste Foundation, said the priority was preventing plastic from reaching the sea rather than simply cleaning it up afterward. He said reducing unnecessary plastic use, preventing waste at source and strengthening reuse and recycling must be addressed together.
The process will culminate in an Aug. 31-Sept. 1 workshop in Istanbul bringing together 17 ministries, more than 40 general directorates, local authorities, universities, industry and civil society. Discussions will cover the plastics cycle from production and consumption to waste management and recycling, as well as microplastics, health, financing, governance and international cooperation.
The meetings are expected to contribute to a national roadmap aimed at reducing plastic leakage into waterways and the sea, strengthening the circular economy and protecting Türkiye’s coastal and marine ecosystems.

TCG Anadolu takes robotic surgery to sea in 5G trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:37:06 UTC
15:37:06 KST

Türkiye has tested a 5G-linked robotic surgery system aboard the TCG Anadolu, with doctors on land providing real-time guidance to a surgical team on the ship, as part of efforts to expand medical care during missions far from shore.
The demonstration, conducted by the Turkish Naval Forces and Kocaeli University during Teknofest Blue Homeland at Gölcük Shipyard Command, was performed on an organ model and did not involve a patient.
The trial used telementoring, allowing specialists at Kocaeli University to monitor the procedure and guide the team aboard the vessel.
Full telesurgery, in which a surgeon ashore directly controls a robot on the ship, remains a later phase of the project.
Officials involved in the initiative said the test was the first of its kind aboard a combat vessel and could pave the way for Türkiye to become the first country to conduct full robotic surgery on a military ship with Role 2 medical capabilities.
Kocaeli University Rector Nuh Zafer Cantürk said the systems at the university hospital and aboard the ship were synchronized through 5G.
The connection recorded latency of around 135 milliseconds, allowing movements to be transmitted with little delay, he said.
Cantürk said the project would progress through teleconsultation, telementoring, teleproctoring and experimental robotic surgery before moving to fully remote operations.
Procedures involving the gallbladder and appendix, as well as some gynecological operations, could eventually be performed using the system, he added.
Saadettin Hülagü, a Kocaeli lawmaker and former rector of Kocaeli University, said the project was launched after the team examined whether robotic surgery could be supported aboard a naval vessel operating far from Türkiye.
Tests indicated that vibration levels aboard the TCG Anadolu were sufficiently low for the initial work, while 5G provided the required connection, according to Hülagü.
TCG Anadolu commander Navy Col. Nadir Kılınç said the ship’s Role 2 medical facilities include a 32-bed patient unit, an eight-bed intensive care unit, a burn treatment unit, two operating rooms, dental facilities, advanced imaging equipment, a blood bank and a laboratory.
He said the technology could eventually enable surgical procedures to be conducted aboard the vessel while it is operating hundreds of miles from Türkiye.
Kocaeli University professor Önder Kara said the next phase would pair two control consoles and move the project from telementoring to full telesurgery.
Tests would initially be conducted on an animal model before progressing to procedures involving patients, he added.

Iran says new US sanctions violate sovereignty of other states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:35:06 UTC
15:35:06 KST

Sahin Demir
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
Iran on Saturday condemned new US economic sanctions against Tehran, arguing that Washington’s use of secondary sanctions violates the sovereignty of other countries and international law.
“The United States’ declaration of new economic sanctions on Iran is far more than continued unlawful ‘economic warfare’ against a single country,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on US social media company X.
“It is an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent Member State of the United Nations,” he added.
Baghaei argued that no country can lawfully force foreign banks, companies or airports under the jurisdiction of other sovereign states to stop lawful trade with a third country.
He said secondary sanctions have “no foundation in international law,” arguing that they violate the principle of sovereign equality under Article 2(1) of the UN Charter and the customary prohibition on intervention affirmed by the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case.
Baghaei also linked the sanctions to a US naval blockade, saying the combination reduces the sovereignty of other states to something “provisional, conditional, and revocable at the whim of another power.”
He warned that such measures could ultimately erode sovereignty as a foundation of the UN-based international system and lead to what he called a return to “full-scale classic colonialism.”
On Wednesday, US President Donald Trump announced his intention to launch “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country,” describing his maximum-pressure campaign against Iran as “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”
He vowed to cut financial channels supporting Tehran, warning that countries providing Iran with an economic “lifeline” through financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities would face severe economic consequences.
Calling the campaign an “Economic D-Day,” Trump urged US allies to join the effort to financially isolate Tehran.

The statement said Israeli settlements in the West Bank were illegal under international law, a position reaffirmed by the U.N. Security Council.
Resolution 2334 states that settlements established in Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, have no legal validity.
Israel opened bidding on Aug. 18 for the construction of 1,234 homes in E1, part of plans for a total of 3,401 units.
The E1 area lies east of East Jerusalem between the city and the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim.
Opponents say construction there would separate the northern and southern West Bank and further isolate East Jerusalem from surrounding Palestinian communities.
The residential plans received final approval in August 2025.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signed a development agreement covering Maale Adumim and E1 the following month.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas welcomed the joint statement and called for the project to be halted immediately.
Abbas said the plan threatened the establishment of an independent Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
He urged the signatories, the European Union and the U.N. Security Council to take concrete steps against E1 and further settlement activity.

AI-assisted vehicle inspections to begin in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:30:48 UTC
15:30:48 KST

Türkiye has presented the technologies planned for a new vehicle inspection system that will begin operating on Aug. 15, 2027, including artificial intelligence-assisted imaging, contactless tire checks, underbody scans and robotic headlight tests.
TURKA, which will operate the country’s vehicle inspection services for 20 years from that date, demonstrated the system on real vehicles at a pilot center in Istanbul’s Arnavutköy district on Aug. 21.
The facility will serve as a testing, training and research center until the system is introduced across all 81 provinces.
Türkiye had more than 34.7 million registered vehicles at the end of July, according to official data.
Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu said the new stations would use AI-assisted image processing, high-resolution cameras, laser measurement technologies, advanced sensors and robotic systems.
He likened the planned inspections to giving vehicles “an MRI and CT scan.”
TURKA Chairman Halis Ezer said the company had spent about 18 months examining vehicle inspection technologies and operating models around the world.
“Rather than transferring the model of a single country to Türkiye, we combined the strengths of different systems in line with Türkiye’s needs,” Ezer said.
The pilot center will be used to compare equipment, test software updates and assess operating procedures and the experience of vehicle owners.
Employees who will work at inspection centers around the country will also receive practical training there.
Among the systems being tested is technology that can read tire sidewall information while a vehicle is moving, check whether the tires are compatible with the vehicle and measure tread depth without contact.
AI-assisted imaging will also be used to detect cracks, cuts and bulges.
High-resolution cameras will scan vehicle underbodies and bodywork and measure vehicle dimensions, while robotic systems will carry out headlight measurements and other lighting checks.
The AI systems will flag possible defects and provide technicians with supporting data, with the aim of reducing differences between individual assessments.
Vehicle owners are expected to be able to follow each stage of the inspection and access the results digitally.
Plans also call for inspections to be viewed live from waiting areas, while new technology and operating procedures are intended to shorten waiting times.
TURKA plans to operate 249 fixed and 103 mobile inspection centers with about 900 inspection lanes.
The network will cover passenger and commercial vehicles, motorcycles and agricultural vehicles such as tractors.
The company said locally developed technologies would be used alongside expertise provided by its partners in the United States, Spain and Argentina.
TURKA is also working with public authorities on plans to equip its 249 fixed centers to support the initial response to forest fires.
The facilities could also be made available for use as field hospitals during disasters and emergencies.

Odyssey effect: Stars sell Greece to a new wave of US tourists
ATHENS – The idyllic beaches of the Greek islands have long been a draw for European holidaymakers, but now a new wave of US tourists is waking up to their charms, driven by stars like Madonna, Katy Perry and Justin Bieber.
Madonna celebrated her 68th birthday on Corfu, sharing a whirl of parties and boat trips against the backdrop of the island’s landscape with her 20 million Instagram followers – earning her rapturous thanks from Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
And experts say the huge popularity of Christopher Nolan blockbuster The Odyssey will only fuel the trend – though holidaymakers will be hoping for an easier trip home than the one endured by Matt Damon’s eponymous hero.
While Madonna partied in Corfu, singer Bieber took his family to the Peloponnese. Perry and her partner, Canada’s former prime minister Justin Trudeau, sampled the delights of Mykonos.
All of them chronicled their holidays on social media, giving the Greek tourism industry a massive hit of free advertising.
“Celebrities are voting for the Greek summer!” public broadcaster ERT said on Aug 21, devoting a report to these stars from across the Atlantic.
The newspaper To Vima hailed this “new wave” which “helps raise the country’s international profile”. It cited British singer and actress Rita Ora, who shared her holidays with “her millions of followers” on social media.
Paris Tsartas, professor of tourism development at Harokopio University in Athens, told AFP the deluge of celebrity endorsements gave Greece a powerful boost as a summer destination – particularly with the lucrative American market.
After a decade of financial woes following the debt crisis of 2009, and the devastation of the Covid-19 pandemic, Greece has pumped money into the sector, which accounts for nearly 30 per cent of gross domestic product, according to the Association of Greek Tourism Enterprises (SETE).
Around 1.55 million Americans visited Greece in 2025. They represent the third-largest source of tourism income, behind Germans and Britons, according to SETE, with an average spend per tourist of €1,120 (S$1,660).
To answer growing demand, the main US airlines have significantly stepped up services, American Airlines increasing its total available seat capacity by 30 per cent compared with summer 2025.
And in 2026, Greece has had its highest-ever number of direct flights, with 103 connections a week between Athens and the United States.
Set-jetting
Some of the new enthusiasm is driven by the phenomenon of “set-jetting” – people travelling to a destination after seeing it in a movie or TV series.
In a study for online travel giant Expedia, 13 per cent of American travellers said they had booked a trip after seeing a destination on screen.
Greece is well acquainted with the trend, after hit musical “Mamma Mia”, filmed on the island of Skopelos, triggered a jump in American visitors.
Professor Tsartas predicted The Odyssey would have a similar impact.
Key parts of Nolan’s film, recounting the travails of Damon’s Odysseus as he seeks to return home from the Trojan war to his wife Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, were shot in the Peloponnese region of Greece.
According to EasyJet Holidays, cited by the Greek newspaper Kathimerini, bookings to Greece increased by 18 per cent in the weeks following the film’s international release in mid-July.
And there is more small-screen exposure for Greece’s charms to come: Netflix had chosen the country for the sixth season of hit series Emily in Paris.
Lead actress Lily Collins and the rest of the production team were spotted in the spring of 2026 in Mykonos, Paros and Santorini. AFP

New licensing for game shoots could stop poisoning of birds of prey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

From the end of August, Land Rovers load up with tweed-clad shooters, who go off to large estates and compete to fill the biggest “bag” of game birds, often shooting dozens at a time – a practice which has long appalled bird conservationists.
Soon, the years-long campaign to stop the poisoning of birds of prey, as well as the release of tens of millions of pheasants into the countryside, could be victorious as a result of government plans for a new licensing scheme for shoots.
The scheme could end the centuries-long tradition, or at least severely curtail it. Currently, about 30 million pheasants are set loose each year by shooting estates for people to pay to shoot.
This number could be reduced if shoots are given licences to release only a certain number of birds. The introduction of licences would also mean estates that are linked to the poisoning or shooting of birds of prey could lose their ability to host shoots.
Beccy Speight, the chief executive of the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), has been campaigning on this issue for many years and is preparing documents to send in an “evidence sprint” to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which has committed to consider only allowing estates to shoot under licence.
“We think this is a totally reasonable step to take. It is not to ban shooting in any sense; it is about saying we need shooting to be in a sustainable form, and it needs to be licensed so this wildlife crime can’t continue,” Speight says.
There is currently a licensing scheme for grouse in Scotland. Estates are given five-year licences to host shoots as long as they follow a code of practice, including protecting habitat for other birds such as waders. Shoots that are linked to the poisoning of birds of prey can lose their licence. Speight thinks a similar scheme could work in England.
Deaths of raptors such as buzzards, eagles and hen harriers are often linked to shooting estates because of fears from gamekeepers that they will prey on birds including grouse, partridge and pheasant.
Magnificent white-tailed eagles can now be found swooping in the skies of south-west England thanks to a reintroduction programme. But raptors have faced persecution. Natural England recently found five white eagles in Dorset that had died from the same brand of rat poison. The Health and Safety Executive is investigating whether the poison was used in accordance with legal requirements designed to protect wildlife.
“It makes me feel sick,” Speight says. “All that work, these eagles are amazing birds. It is why we need licensing.”
Seven satellite-tagged hen harriers were found poisoned or shot on or near grouse moors last year. Speight adds: “We find the satellite-tagged bodies and that is probably just the tip of the iceberg- buzzards, for example, aren’t satellite tagged so we can never find or test their bodies. It’s a serious problem that is going on in our natural world.”
Many people shoot sustainably, killing what they can eat or give to friends and family, and keep estates in a wilder condition, promoting biodiversity beyond just the birds which are kept to shoot.
Under a licensing system, this would be preserved. Speight explains: “Shooting is a continuum, from small walk-up shoots up to very intensive bag-driven shoots, and it would probably result in more shooting at the start and middle rather than at that extreme end.”
The shooting industry has been furious at Speight’s campaigning. Roger Seddon, of the Countryside Alliance, recently described her as a “pied piper” and a “puppeteer controlling the environment secretary like a marionette”.
Asked about this, Speight was exasperated: “It’s absolutely not true. It’s the job of the RSPB to drive its cause, which is a world where people and nature thrive side by side.”
Speight is exhausted after dealing with the fallout from three devastating wildfires on RSPB reserves this summer. “They still have people putting hotspots of fire out,” she says.
This is relevant to the shooting debate, too. For example, large intensive grouse moors are made up of dry heather habitat, which involves draining wet peatland and creating a monoculture of one plant. “Heather is incredibly flammable. Dried out peat is releasing carbon into the atmosphere but also becomes very susceptible to fire,” Speight says.
Speight says recent claims that wildfires are caused by rewilding are “nonsense”. “There is no evidence to back that up,” she said. “With rewilding, you get these more broken, natural mosaics with water in the landscape, which creates breaks and holds water in the landscape more. That has to be good from a wildfire perspective.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “Sustainable shooting has an important place in our rural communities, and we want to make sure high environmental and animal welfare standards are in place so that the practice succeeds and we’re protecting our ecosystems.
“We will work with key groups to explore other moves, such as licensing or other conditions for recreational game bird shooting and release. This will begin with evidence gathering and any changes will be subject to public consultation.”

‘Friday afternoon fraud’: warning for UK homebuyers on bank scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

You are poised to move house and are awaiting the solicitor’s instructions that things are ready to go and it is time to hand over your deposit. When the email arrives giving you their bank details, you set up the transfer and move the cash. And then the solicitor calls to ask where the money is.
Conveyancing fraud involves criminals getting access to an email chain between homebuyers and their solicitors or estate agents and requesting payment to a bank account they control. Sometimes the solicitor has been hacked, but often the homebuyer has been the victim of a phishing exercise.
The scam is sometimes known as “Friday afternoon fraud” as it tends to take place at the end of a sale, which is often timed before a weekend.
The sums of money involved in a property sale mean the fraudster only have to land a few victims to make a lot of cash.
Report Fraud (formerly known as Action Fraud) says there were 3,657 scams involving persuading people to pay into the wrong bank account in the 2025-26 financial year, and these cost victims a total of £101m.
Conveyancing fraud is a subset of this. Between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025 Report Fraud recorded 140 property cases with an average loss of £78,393. In the worst case the Guardian has covered, a homebuyer transferred the entire £300,000 purchase price to the wrong account.
City of London police has warned that this type of fraud isn’t limited to purchases – it’s also been reported by renters who have lost money they thought they’d paid to their letting agent, and in probate transactions.
What it looks like
The message looks just like an email from your solicitor or estate agent. It asks for you to make a payment you are expecting to make but may come earlier than you were expecting.
It may say that the solicitors’ firm has new bank details and the payment needs to be made quickly.
If your solicitor’s email has been hacked the message could come from its genuine address, but usually the fraudsters will be using a spoofed email address so if you look carefully you may spot something slightly different from the genuine company’s one. There may be a missing letter or extra punctuation mark, for example.
What to do (and not do)
Don’t post about your impending move on social media as fraudsters could spot this and realise that you are a good person to target.
Make sure your side of the email chain is secure by setting a strong password for your account and using any extra protection that’s offered, such as two-factor authentication.
Avoid logging into public wifi and using it to check your emails as this gives fraudsters a potential access point.
If you are expecting to exchange on a property soon, make sure you have asked for the solicitor’s bank details either in person or over the phone in a call that you have made to it.
Any message suggesting your solicitor has changed its bank details should be checked out – again ask them in person or by phone.
Take heed of any warnings from your bank as you try to transfer the money. It should tell you if the name of the account does not match what you expect, and when this happens you should stop and check everything is as it should be.
Contact your bank straight away if you have made a transfer that was not legitimate.

Lovech’s rich history is attracting an increasing number of young visitors thanks to the new permanent exhibition at the city’s Regional History Museum. Opened at the beginning of July, it has already become the museum’s second most visited attraction, with particularly strong interest among students, families, and local residents, said Silvia Vuteva, curator and ethnographer at the Regional History Museum-Lovech, during a special press conference.
Silvia Vuteva
PHOTO BTA
Located along the Osam River in northern Bulgaria, the city holds an important place in Bulgarian history. During the 19th century, Lovech was a major center of trade and craftsmanship and was associated with the activities of Vasil Levski, who established one of the most important centers of the Internal Revolutionary Organization here in the period before Bulgaria’s Liberation in 1878.
PHOTO BTA
The Regional History Museum’s newest exhibition is spread across seven themed halls and traces the development of Lovech and the surrounding region from antiquity to the present day. Among the nearly 5,000 exhibits on display are archaeological finds, everyday objects, documents and materials related to the city’s cultural, spiritual and economic life.
PHOTO BTA
The history is presented through digital technologies, multimedia and educational materials. Some of the halls also feature reconstructions, including a Neolithic dwelling, a military trench, and the interior of a home from Bulgaria’s socialist period.
Visitors spend an average of between one and one and a half hours exploring the exhibition. Since the beginning of August, it has welcomed 17 groups, including 43 university students.
PHOTO BTA
One of the exhibition’s main objectives is to present local history in the context of the nation’s broader history and to show how the past has shaped the identity of Lovech and its residents.

Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia

Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia
The Level 2 storm which hit Estonia on Saturday has started to subside, though strong winds and rain are still forecast for Sunday.
Heavy rain — with some locations receiving the average monthly rainfall in the space of 24 hours — and strong winds swept across Estonia over the weekend, bringing down trees, causing power outages and disrupting ferry services.
The weather warning has been downgraded to Level 1 (yellow) in western and southern Estonia as of Sunday morning. Eastern Estonia – Ida-Viru, Lääne-Viru, Järva, Jõgeva and Tartu counties – are now not subject to the warning and the weather map is showing green as of the time of writing.
Heavy rain is to continue over Estonia on Sunday morning, with 24-hour totals of 50–70 millimeters and up to 90 millimeters in some areas. These higher figures are roughly the same as the overall average rainfall for August, usually the wettest month, in Estonia.
Wind gusts reached as high as 30 meters per second on Saturday and the Rescue Board (Päästeamet) has been notified of fallen trees on roads and power lines.
The storm also left households without power: On Saturday evening, 3,410 households were without power according to Elektrilevi. As of 9 a.m. Sunday, that figure had fallen to around 2,600, though around half the outages were in southeastern Estonia.
Heavy rainfall of 50–100 millimeters overnight threatened Tallinn's sewage and drainage system, and Tallinna Vesi issued flood prevention advice, including clearing gutters, avoiding parking in flood-prone areas, and reducing water use during the rain.
Urmas Kütt, head of pipeline operations at Tallinna Vesi, noted that during and immediately after heavy rain, the public should avoid using large amounts of water to avoid placing additional strain on the wastewater system. Stormwater should not be directed into the sewer network to avoid overloading the system, and Kütt stressed people should avoid flooded basements and manholes due to electrocution and other hazards.
Ferry services were subject to cancellation during the storm but are back online as of Sunday morning. The 8.30 a.m. sailing from Rohuküla to Heltermaa (Hiiumaa) went ahead, and the 10 a.m. service in the other direction is also on schedule. No changes to the Virtsu to Kuivastu (Muhu/Saaremaa) route timetable are currently expected.
The storm also hit Latvia and Lithuania. Latvia's weather service issued a storm warning, outdoor events were canceled and roads were flooded in several places. In Riga, water accumulated beneath viaducts, disrupting traffic. According to Lithuanian media, at least one person was killed after being struck by a falling tree and over 150,000 households were left without power.

Reports credit North Korea’s newest missile of terror with 2.5-ton warhead and 900-km range. Expert explains why those numbers can’t both be true
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:17:12 UTC
15:17:12 KST

Russia may soon get 150 more missiles from North Korea, and their inaccuracy is precisely what makes them dangerous to civilians. This characteristic makes them above all weapons of terror, military expert and Defense Express director Serhii Zghurets said on Espreso.
The particular danger may carry the KN-30, credited with a range of up to 900 kilometers and a 2.5-ton warhead. For comparison, the warhead in Russia's Kalibr cruise missile is 450 kilograms, as in the Iskander ballistic missile, and even those destroy large objects. A missile carrying anything near five times that payload would hit far harder than any weapon already devastating Ukrainian cities.
The claimed specs don't add up
Zghurets urged skepticism toward the most hyped missile. The KN-30's credited figures can hardly be combined in one missile, he said. Physics forces a trade-off.
"If we are talking about a missile that can fly 900 km, then it has a significantly smaller warhead weight. If we are talking about 2.5 tons, then the range will be much shorter," Zghurets explained.
Either version remains dangerous, but the claims as advertised describe a missile that likely does not exist.
A 150-missile delivery is under discussion
North Korea keeps feeding Russia's arsenal. Pyongyang continues to strengthen Russia's military potential with missiles of several types, including the KN-23, KN-24, and KN-30, and a possible supply of about 150 North Korean missiles to Russia is now actively discussed, Zghurets said.
Even if the missiles' real characteristics differ from the claims, such a number would be a substantial addition to the Russian arsenal, he noted, more missiles for the campaign Russia fires at Ukrainian cities regardless of how well each one performs.
Inaccuracy makes them terror weapons
The missiles' precision is their defining flaw. By one estimate, Zghurets cited, missiles flying about 800 kilometers can deviate from their target by 18 kilometers, an error radius wider than most cities.
That rules out military precision but not harm.
"There is definitely no talking about any accuracy with these missiles. But as a weapon of terror that supplements the Russian arsenal, the Russians will of course need it now," Zghurets said.
A missile that can land anywhere within 18 kilometers of its aim point cannot reliably hit a military target, but if fired at a city, it will hit something, which is how Russia has used North Korean missiles against Ukrainian civilians.
Both sides get what they want from the axis
Moscow's interest goes beyond missiles. Russia is also interested in bringing in North Korean troops, which would free part of its own forces for combat against Ukraine, Zghurets said.
Pyongyang is paid in money and technology. North Korea seeks military-technological advantages from the cooperation, including improving its submarine-launched ballistic missile technology, and over the years of the war, may have received about $20 billion from Russia, Zghurets estimated.
The Moscow-Pyongyang military alliance is a serious challenge for the West, he said, though it is hard to predict how actively the US will try to limit the two countries' cooperation.
